items.title: Westchester Knicks 2026-27 Season Primer
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
New York’s G League affiliate opens its 2026-27 season tonight against the Maine Celtics in the Tip-Off Tournament. The roster features three players on two-way contracts, a returning fan favorite (hint: he’s great on toast), and a collection of prospects hoping to dribble their way up to an NBA court.

With the Knicks operating near the second apron, Westchester provides a way to develop young players without committing additional standard roster spots. Two-way players can spend most of the season in White Plains while remaining available for NBA duty, subject to a limit of up to 50 games on the active roster. The G League has also given players like Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek opportunities to get more work. Here’s a peek at the players worth watching.

Dalton Knecht: A second chance in New York

Of everyone on Westchester’s roster, Dalton Knecht has the clearest path to helping the big club this season. The 2024 first-round pick (17th overall) arrived after the Lakers waived him, with New York releasing Kevin McCullar Jr. to make room for Knecht on a two-way contract. This low-risk move could pay off if the former Tennessee star rediscovers his shooting touch and improves his court awareness, which was a criticism raised in the comments section at Silver Screen and Roll.

The 25-year-old made a promising debut for the New York Knicks this week, scoring 10 points on efficient 4-of-6 shooting (including two threes) with seven boards, a dime, and a block in 16 minutes off the bench in a rout of the Bulls. Finding consistent playing time will be difficult, however. With Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, Pacôme Dadiet, and Mohamed Diawara competing for minutes on the wings, Knecht will probably need an injury or another opening to receive an extended look. (TBH, he already looks ahead of Dadiet.)

Coach Mike Brown has said he’d rather see Knecht playing meaningful minutes in the G League than sitting on the NBA bench. Makes sense. Knecht needs opportunities to shoot, make decisions, and work through mistakes. He has shown he can score, but questions remain about his defense, shot selection, and ability to contribute consistently as a role player.

If Knecht performs well enough, the organization could eventually consider converting him to a standard NBA contract, which would require sufficient roster and financial room. For now, he should get plenty of opportunities to let it fly against G League competition.

Speaking of flamethrowers . . . Tyler “Silent K” Nickel might be the most straightforward fit for what the Knicks need. New York selected the Vanderbilt sharpshooter with the 47th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft after an impressive senior season. He followed that with a promising Summer League showing and signed a two-way contract.

From what we’ve seen, Nickel moves well without the ball, finds open space, and punishes defenses for leaving him unattended. The big league Knicks have several players capable of creating offense, and a dependable perimeter shooter who doesn’t require many touches could fit nicely alongside them (see: Landry Shamet).

His defense will help determine how quickly the 23-year-old advances. He needs to prove he can handle quicker, stronger NBA bodies while maintaining his shooting efficiency against more aggressive closeouts. Westchester should give him plenty of reps to work on both.

Nickel doesn’t seem to have Knecht’s offensive versatility, but his shooting gives him a clearly defined role. If he can hold his own defensively, he could become a useful option for additional spacing. For the time being, Westchester might have its very own set of Splash Brothers to keep you entertained (at a reasonable price).

Jaden Akins: Defense and versatility

Jaden Akins took a less direct route to New York. Undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025, he spent last season with the Motor City Cruise after earning All-Big Ten third-team and All-Defensive recognition as a senior. His combination of scoring, secondary playmaking, and defense caught the Knicks’ attention. Westchester acquired his returning player rights in September, and he secured a two-way contract before the season.

Akins faces considerable competition at the one- and two-guard spots. His best chance of separating himself is to use his time at Westchester to polish his defense and his work off the ball. Can he defend multiple positions, run an offense for stretches, and make open shots? Can he contribute consistently without committing unnecessary fouls or turnovers? Those qualities will probably matter more to New York than his individual scoring averages.

Dink Pate: Back for another season

The fan favorite returns! Dink Pate returns to Westchester after a confusing offseason. The 6’8” wing, still only 20 years old, averaged approximately 16 points, seven rebounds, and four assists across 50 games with the club last season. He subsequently attempted to play college basketball at Providence, but that plan fell through amid questions about his NCAA eligibility. The Knicks signed and waived him on an Exhibit 10 contract, and he returned to Westchester, which already held his G League rights.

Pate has length, can create his own offense, and contributes as a rebounder and passer. His combination of physical tools and professional experience makes him one of Westchester’s more interesting developmental players. Decision-making and efficiency are where he needs improvement.

Unlike Knecht, Nickel, and Akins, Pate doesn’t have a two-way contract. He would need an available two-way or standard roster spot and a new NBA contract to join the big club. Westchester’s rights also don’t prevent another NBA team from signing him. Thus, his time in White Plains is a prove-it run for a broader audience—so we expect to see some inspired hooping from him this season.

Frontcourt depth: Robbins, Dante, and Miličić

Westchester’s frontcourt includes several players who could provide useful depth. , a seven-footer who went undrafted out of Vanderbilt in 2023, is probably the most recognizable. He showed some encouraging work around the iron during Summer League with the Knicks, and Westchester subsequently acquired his G League rights.

Robbins brings size, rebounding, and shot-blocking ability. The big league club could use more reliable center depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond, with James Wiseman slow to make an impression. Robbins could use his time in White Plains to convince the team he deserves a look—perhaps before the front office starts eyeing its surplus of guards as trade bait.

, the 6-foot-11 former Oregon center, is working his way back from an ACL injury. His size and athleticism lift our eyebrows, but getting healthy and regaining his previous form will be the immediate priorities.

, a 6-foot-10 forward out of Tennessee, brings international experience and positional versatility after spending time with the Delaware Blue Coats last season. Improving his outside shooting and defensive consistency would help him take the next step.

The wings: Jourdain, Okani, and company

Westchester also has several forwards competing for rotation minutes. returns after averaging roughly eight points and more than five rebounds last season. The former Memphis forward provides rebounding, energy, and defensive effort. His journey from local tryout to returning player is a nice story, even if an NBA opportunity remains a longer shot.

, the former West Virginia wing, brings length and athleticism after spending time with multiple G League organizations. , an undrafted forward out of Duquesne, and are also trying to establish roles after joining the training camp group.

The guards: Shooting potential

Westchester’s backcourt includes several capable players. is worth watching after arriving from the Stockton Kings. The 6’5” guard shot approximately 42% from downtown last season, giving Westchester another option to stretch the floor.

returns as a scoring option at guard and on the wing, while joins the club after being selected 25th in the 2026 G League Draft. Spears brings extensive college experience, including a productive stint at UTSA, and spent last season playing professionally in Mexico.

The three two-way players will receive the most attention this season, although we’ll also keep an eye on Pate (‘cuz he’s kinda electric). The rest of the roster will compete for minutes and try to establish themselves as dependable professional players. Westchester opens its Tip-Off Tournament schedule tonight at 7 p.m. against the Maine Celtics at the Portland Expo, then faces the same opponent at the same venue Sunday at 12:30 p.m. Both games will air on MSG Network.

items.title: World Champion Brandon McNulty to debut rainbow jersey on home soil at El Tour de Tucson - North American Roundup
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
World champion Brandon McNulty debuts his rainbow jersey on home soil on November 21 at El Tour de Tucson. A native of Phoenix, Arizona, McNulty will make his first appearance at the Tucson event, now in a 43rd edition that has grown in size to 12,000 participants across three routes, the longest 103 miles.

A number of former pro athletes are also part of the front corral of starters including four-time triathlete world champion Leanda Cave and former Grand Tour riders George Hincapie, Bob Roll, Bobby Julich, and Frankie Andreu.

All riders compete for prestige and bragging rights in a choice of three distances, as there is no prize money.

El Tour de Tucson is the flagship event for El Tour America, a non-profit that produces cycling events and helps raise funds for more than 120 other non-profits. Many of the current and retired pros participating in the ride will also participate in The Prologue, an exclusive camp for limited attendees to raise additional funds.

RNRNYC Racing p/b R1 will support former WorldTour rider Ide Schelling for a second season, this time with a focus on gravel racing, and will be the the new home for New Zealander Ethan Craine as the team grows their roster for 2027.

RNRNYC, which takes their name from cycling apparel brand Rubber N' Road that has a design studio and manufacturing in New York City, launched last season as an elite club team. They promote inclusivity and give riders opportunities to develop and race at a high level alongside experienced pros.

Schelling had a limited role with RNRNYC Racing last year, participating in a limited calendar of road and gravel, taking 10th place in The Gralloch. The Dutch rider retired from an 11-year pro road career in 2025, which included six years at the WorldTour level with Bora-Hansgrohe and XDS Astana. He will continue as a brand ambassador for RNRNYC and be supported as a privateer in gravel.

"Ide will be racing a lot more by himself, but remains part of the bigger ecosystem, the RNR and L1 racing family. Maybe he'll do a couple of races with the team, but really he will focus on doing gravel events, which are mostly in Europe. Maybe doing Big Sugar and a couple more in the US," Gil Lavi, co-founder of Rubber N' Road and RNRNYC Racing, told.

Lavi said the cycling apparel brand benefits greatly from an international roster of riders, since the company has production facilities in three countries and customers around the globe.

"Having Ethan [Craine] is huge. César Marte and Wiley Close are very talented racers, super young, super talented," Lavi said about some of the new riders that have been announced so far.

Craine, 25, joins from five years with Project Echelon Racing, where he had stage wins in the Green Mountain Stage Race, Salt Lake Criterium and Chicago Grit. Close, 22, moves from ENVE MOG Squad's gravel team, where he finished eighth on the queen stage at Green Mountain Stage Race in his first road race in September.

Marte, a sprinter from the Dominican Republic, earned top results in the US across multiple teams at the Tour of Somerville, Gateway Cup, and Tour of America’s Dairyland since 2022 and als has multiple stage wins at the Vuelta Independencia.

The full roster will be disclosed in the coming weeks, with 12-15 riders expected to compete on a heavy road racing calendar, with a few gravel races mixed in.

Retirement news is typically reserved for riders, but this time organisers for Crusher in the Tushar confirmed Thursday that the Utah gravel race would permanently close after 14 years.

Taking its name from the Tushar mountains of central Utah, the highest range in the state, the Crusher was cancelled twice in the last three years due to impact from active wildfires in the area.

Life Time purchased the event from founder and former road pro Burke Swindlehurst in 2019, and included the race as part of the Life Time Grand Prix series from 2022 to 2024, though the third instalment was not held due to the fires. Keegan Swenson won the two Grand Prix editions while Haley Smith and Sofia Gomez Villafañe split the wins for elite women.

"We made the decision to retire Crusher in the Tushar," Life Time posted Thursday on social channels and the web site for the event.

"Since its founding, Crusher in the Tushar has played a pivotal role in shaping gravel cycling, challenging athletes on one of the sport's most demanding and memorable courses.

"We are deeply grateful to founder Burke Swindlehurst for his vision, the greater Beaver community for its incredible hospitality and partnership, and the athletes, volunteers and partners who have made Crusher such a special event over the years.

"Our thoughts remain with the Beaver and Piute County communities as they continue to recover and rebuild following this year's devastating wildfires and flooding."

A total of 12 US teenagers will be part of EuroCrossAcademy's November block of training and racing, with the first competitions set for the Netherlands November 14-15 including Vam-Berg Cross in Wijster.

The squad will have multiple skills training sessions in Alphen, Netherlands and Lichtaart, Belgium, with a focus on forest trails and sand, then complete the two-week trip with racing in Hilversum, Netherlands and Maldegem, Belgium.

This is 24th year EuroCrossAcademy, led by Geoff Proctor, and a third consecutive year for a unique block for 15-16 year olds. The programme began in 2003 as EuroCross Camp to help athletes prepare for the Cyclo-cross World Championships. It has grown into a non-profit, EuroCrossAcademy (ECA), which now provides summer camps in Montana and Vermont as well as blocks of European racing experience in the development process for young US riders.

The group of 15-16 year olds are the focus for November, with the 17-18 year old riders taking part in a separate experience in December.

"The emphasis at the ECA November block is specifically on development, not results or outcomes. Are are they becoming better people by improving their character/continuing to find purpose?" Proctor told about what measuring success.

He said ECA coaches measure success based on the level of "finding joy in a safe, kind, supportive environment" as well as learning life skills, not just riding skills, from their teammates, mechanics, support staff, and themselves.

For both blocks of training and race, will provide coverage with rider dairies, the athletes providing first-person accounts of the 'character development' and competition.

A Literal Love Letter to Steel: The Custom Cicli Barco Road Bike
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: This is how you solve modern bike problems in steel when you consider aesthetics as an equal partner with usability.
items.lbText:
When it comes to steel frames, there’s always a story about a legendary frame that was built by someone with no credit. One name on the down tube, but different hands building it. It’s often talked about in hushed whispers—“did you know?” But for the people actually building those frames, it’s an opportunity.

Cicli Barco is a custom steel frame builder in Italy, but it’s also a contract build shop, and the story we heard from Gianluca Barco at Bespoked Osaka was one of pride in that history. The company website tells of “Granda Mario,” who built “handcrafted frames used by legends like Freddy Maertens and Eddy Merckx” without real recognition. Barco spoke with pride, though, saying that the family’s reputation for high-quality fabrication has shifted that dynamic. Today, while Cicli Barco still splits production evenly between a company label and contract work, the Barco name carries such prestige that other brands now proudly advertise when their frames are “made by Barco.”

Under the Cicli Barco label, the brand produces around 100 frames a year, blending traditional craftsmanship with modern design concepts. For Barco, this contract work isn’t just about paying the bills; it provides a valuable avenue to experiment with new techniques and view frame building from different perspectives.

At Bespoked Osaka, Cicli Barco brought a literal “love letter” to this craft. To be clear, that’s literal as in half of the frame is covered with a handwritten “love letter,” creating a stop-in-your-tracks aesthetic. As Barco explained, while anyone can source tubes and parts, developing a unique signature that makes a bike undeniably a “Barco” is one of the hardest achievements for a frame builder.

The true engineering standout on the bike, however, is a zero-stack head tube designed to integrate seamlessly with modern cockpits without resorting to oversized tubing. Instead of a standard straight head tube, Barco uses a modular central section that can be adapted to specific sizes and geometries. The main tubes are spot-welded to this central part, and a special tool is used to shape the tube to fit the headset cup. Once the cup is inserted, the weld is finished and then reinforced with silver brazing, resulting in an incredibly narrow and clean aesthetic.

It’s an elegant solution to a problem that modern metal bikes are plagued with, but the execution is mirrored throughout the rest of the bike. Look at the seatpost clamp, and you’ll see TIG welding and silver brazing used once again to solve a modern bike problem that, once you see it, you can’t unsee. On this bike, there is no collar. Instead, the seat stays have a bolt through them that, when tightened, closes the cut in the seatpost and acts as a clamp without the visual bulk of one. Like the head tube, it’s so genius it has to be highlighted, but it’s not simple. Using both welding techniques together allows the builders to tightly control material deformation, giving them the freedom to explore complex designs without compromising the structural integrity of the steel.

To finish off the build, the parts have to match. Just like the metalwork, there’s a beautiful balance of clean lines, high technology, and functionality. The drivetrain is SRAM RED XPLR AXS with a CeramicSpeed OSPW and an INGRD crank. The handlebars—featuring an integrated stem—and the wheels come from Polymer Workshop, a brand that has also staked its reputation on solving modern integration problems and fitting into as many contemporary frames as possible. In this case, the definition of modern is slightly turned on its head, but aesthetically, everything is a perfect match. The deep wheels bring a contrast of black that matches the handwritten text, the fork, and the INGRD chainring. There are pops of chrome in the RED drivetrain, and there are even easter eggs of red in the script that match the Italian flag at the back of the bike.

items.title: Surprise Ducati pacesetter on Qatar MotoGP Friday
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
VR46 Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio set the pace to end Friday practice at the Qatar Grand Prix, delivering a new record lap in the process.

Di Giannantonio led points leader Marc Marquez by 0.142s in a Ducati 1-2. The Italian is a known Lusail specialist, having taken the first of his two MotoGP wins at the track back in 2023. 

Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) and a resurgent Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati) completed the top four. Bezzecchi's three Aprilia peers - Raul Fernandez, Jorge Martin and Ai Ogura - all secured automatic Q2 spots within the top 10, too, though it was a close call for Ogura.

Other direct spots in Q2 were picked up by Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM), Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) and Brad Binder (KTM).

For once, Pedro Acosta had no answer to his fellow KTMs and was only 14th. He now faces the possibility of being outqualified by a team-mate for the first time ever in MotoGP, should he fail to advance from Q1 on Saturday.

It was a notably credible first day as a Honda MotoGP rider for Jake Dixon, standing in for Joan Mir.

Dixon lapped 1.987s off the pace in the end, just two tenths back from out-of-sorts LCR Honda regular Diogo Moreira.

items.title: The Knicks have a bench guard conundrum
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
When you’re the defending champions, there are not many holistic things to complain about.

Sure, the Knicks started 0-3 with a very unsettling offense, but all they needed was their medicine (the Nets and Bulls) to get back to .500?

Worried about losing to Philadelphia twice in October? Joel Embiid’s plantar fasciitis has already acted up; calm down.

Any “problems” this early in the season are either short-term, regarding the looming extension talks, or good problems, which are more conundrums than actual problems.

The biggest of those conundrums has to do with the Knicks’ rotation, specifically with their copious amounts of guard depth.

Jalen Brunson is the head of the snake, but after him? There are a lot of players with minutes who could fluctuate on any given night.

Tyler Kolek and Jose Alvarado duel over backup ball-handler minutes. Jordan Clarkson and Deuce McBride grapple over bench two-guard minutes. Landry Shamet’s strong play is actively pushing starters Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart over their minutes with the three entrenched parts of the team’s nucleus.

It does qualify as a good problem to have, as injuries will undoubtedly give each of these guys ample opportunity over the course of 82 games, but when they’re all healthy, like they are right now? It probably gives Mike Brown a bigger headache than watching Andre Drummond attempt layups.

All of these guys provide something that the Knicks could use more of, but have warts that can limit their playing time.

Kolek is the best true playmaker, but he’s a poor defender, and his jump shot has been consistent throughout his young NBA career. This basically also describes Alvarado, but the defense is better from the New York native.

McBride has stretches where he’s the team’s best rate shooter and is a tremendously pesky point-of-attack defender… but is that not what the team is getting out of a taller two-guard in Shamet?

Clarkson has been a sparkplug every game he’s played this year, but the 35-year-old showed his maddening inconsistency in his first year in New York.

It’s created an extremely volatile rotation, which isn’t surprising when you have a coach who opened the year saying only five players on this team have minutes that are secured.

Despite zero Knicks players averaging more than 33 minutes a game except Brunson (who’s at 34.1), only Shamet is averaging more than 18 minutes a game off the bench.

McBride is at 17.5, Kolek is at 12.2, Alvarado is at 11.3, and Clarkson is at 9.9, but even these are deceiving.

Kolek has played steady rotation minutes, but didn’t play at all in the first two games before Alvarado’s ankle injury. Alvarado played 16 and 11 minutes, got hurt, got benched after nine minutes on Monday, and was on track to be a DNP-CD against the Bulls on Wednesday.

Clarkson’s gone from playing three, five, or eight minutes to his spurts of 15 and 17 in the two games against the Bulls and his 11 to spark the incredible fourth quarter against Brooklyn.

McBride, who’s served as the Knicks’ sixth man for over two years now, has topped 17 minutes just twice. He played a season-low 11 minutes on Wednesday and hasn’t had a clear role.

To get these guys more minutes, it would mean cutting minutes from Hart or Bridges. While both have their warts, and the latter continues to look somehow less involved than he was during his lowest moments last season, some of the Knicks’ best lineups are coming with them on the court… just separated.

We’ve seen Brown deploy line changes significantly more in the early going, opting to sub in three or four players at a time to deploy uniform units, but that’s not helping how erratic this all feels.

The depth is making players redundant on the court, especially with how unwise it is to run four-guard lineups in an NBA that’s prioritizing size and length more and more.

And with the Knicks’ extremely shallow forward and center depth? This glut might have to be sorted out at the trade deadline. As much as McBride has shown his tremendous value to the Knicks over the course of his contract, if he isn’t going to play more, is it even a net positive to keep him for the playoff run?

For now, it’s merely a conundrum that Coach Brown will be scratching his head over every game.

By the time we hit February? Things better be sorting themselves out.

items.title: What happened in first Brazil F1 practice
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Lando Norris edged the new Formula 1 world champion Kimi Antonelli to top the first practice session at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as Colton Herta completed his F1 superlicence mission.

Norris set the pace with a 1m11.717s, lapping just 0.082s quicker than Antonelli.

McLaren is the only team that has brought upgrades to Brazil with a new front and rear wing, modified floor furniture and a beam wing.

Max Verstappen (Red Bull), who complained of "unacceptable downshifts", and Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) made it four different teams in the top four, all within just over three tenths of a second.

George Russell was fifth fastest ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull.

Gabriele Mini was the fastest of the six FP1-only rookies in seventh place for Alpine in his second successive FP1 outing, 0.852s off the pace and just under a tenth ahead of regular driver Franco Colapinto, who was ninth.

On home soil, Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi was eighth between the two Alpine drivers while Liam Lawson rounded out the top 10 for Racing Bulls.

McLaren's reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli was 11th ahead of Haas's Ollie Bearman and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

Rafael Camara finished his first FP1 session in 18th place, eight and a half tenths behind Bearman, as he builds up slowly to his unexpected grand prix debut this weekend - replacing Esteban Ocon.

Herta picked up the final point he needs to qualify for his F1 superlicence, as he surpassed the 100 kilometres of running required to earn the 40th and final point, when combined with his four other qualifying FP1 runs and his IndyCar results.

Cadillac thought it was mission accomplished in Mexico until it emerged that its FIA-verified calculations included an error on IndyCar's website. That meant Herta needed another FP1 outing in Brazil to finally get him over the line, removing a key obstacle to him replacing Valtteri Bottas in 2027, should the team decide to do so.

Bottas was 15th, and nine tenths quicker than Herta in FP1.

Freddie Slater's second FP1 outing ended up being even shorter than his first, as he'd completed just seven laps before his Audi ground to a halt, bringing out an early red flag.

It means Slater has been able to complete just 21 laps between his back-to-back first F1 practice outings in Mexico and Brazil.

Ferrari's Dino Beganovic also had a disrupted FP1 session as he lost a lot of time to his team needing to change his floor mid-session. He ended up with just 11 laps, having been told to abort his soft tyre lap for a car problem.

items.title: TotalEnergies team survives as new three-year sponsor announcement imminent
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
After months of uncertainty and the loss of half of their riders, the TotalEnergies squad have found new life, according to Ouest France.

An official announcement from managers Jean-René Bernaudeau and Stéphane Heulot is expected on November 9, according to .

At the time, Bernaudeau said, "We need to have ten riders under contract and a sponsor providing a bank guarantee before being interviewed in December to finalise the budget. The end of the month is obviously the deadline; we promised ourselves we wouldn't go beyond October 31st."

Bernaudeau appears to have met that cutoff with the imminent announcement of a title sponsor for the next three years.

However, the team will have to be aggressive in the transfer market over the next three years if they hope to rejoin the WorldTour in 2029, as they have lost their top points scorers during the uncertainty surrounding their future, some of whom have made a step up to the WorldTour.

Their GC hopeful Jordan Jegat, who finished 10th overall in the Tour de France and won the Classic Grand Besançon Doubs in April, has already signed for Lidl-Trek. Classics specialist Anthony Turgis and Nicolas Breuillard have already inked deals with XDS Astana, and Alexandre Delettre, along with Emilien Jeannière, a podium finisher in the Scheldeprijs, and Sandy Dujardin left for Groupama-FDJ. Pierre Thierry signed with Cofidis.

Meanwhile, Mathieu Burgaudeau, Thomas Bonnet and Mattéo Vercher jumped ship for ProTeam Burgos-Burpellet BH, while Lorrenzo Manzin, Geoffrey Bouchard and Fabien Greiller retired.

Bernaudeau may yet hold on to Jason Tesson, winner of the Classic Var, who was their fourth-best scorer in 2026, and Tour of Mentougou winner Joris Delbove, who are among the 14 riders who have not yet announced their 2027 contracts.

The outfit have a long history in the peloton, having been founded in 1986. They were briefly a professional team as Castorama before returning to a development programme. In 2000, Bernaudeau landed Bonjour as a title sponsor and, under that banner and later as Brioches La Boulangère, Bouygues Télécom and Team Europcar became fixtures in the ProTour, the predecessor to the WorldTour.

Thomas Voeckler's ten-day stint in the maillot jaune in 2004 was the team's biggest highlight, but by 2009, the team were forced to drop out of the top tier and almost disbanded in 2010 as they struggled to find a sponsor until Europcar came along.

The team brought on Direct Énergie as a sponsor in 2019 and, as TotalEnergies, signed superstar Peter Sagan with high ambitions of rejoining the WorldTour, but the three-time world champion won only a single race for the French outfit, a stage of the Tour de Suisse in 2022, and the team did not meet the promotion criteria by the end of 2025.

In 2026, the team fell short of the top three ProTeams, being beaten by Pinarello-Q36.5, Tudor and Cofidis, so they will not earn automatic invitations to the Grand Tours. However, they remain eligible for wildcard entries as they made the top 30 in the UCI Team Rankings, and as the fourth-best ProTeam, will be invited to the one-day WorldTour events.

Welcome to this special episode of the Velo Podcast from our 2027 Field Test , where we asked one very important question: What does the future of gravel look like? We took six bikes that couldn’t be more different and compared them head to head.

This podcast is part of our 2027 Velo Field Test. All episodes are streaming now!

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: James Paxton
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
After the 2018 season, the Yankees’ pitching staff looked thin. Young ace Luis Severino gave them a top-flight starter atop the rotation, and Masahiro Tanaka was a more-than-capable No. 3 starter with a tendency of stepping up in big spots, but Sonny Gray and Domingo Germán were disasters while CC Sabathia and J.A. Happ were on the wrong side of 45. Compared to the Boston Red Sox — led by Chris Sale, Nathan Eovaldi, and David Price — and the three-headed monster of Justin Verlander, Gerrit Cole, and Dallas Keuchel in Houston, it was clear that the Bombers had a lot of catching up to do in the arms race.

To that end, the Yankees opened the 2018-2019 offseason by swinging a deal for James Paxton, sending a package centered on top pitching prospect Justus Sheffield to the Seattle Mariners.

November 6, 1988 (Richmond, British Columbia, Canada)2019-20

Born and raised in British Columbia, Paxton made a name for himself on the Canadian youth baseball circuit, ultimately helping to lead Team Canada to a bronze medal at the 2006 World Junior Baseball Championship. Following his high school career, the Big Maple took his talents to the United States, joining the University of Kentucky. Between his performance with the Wildcats (first as a reliever, then as a starter) and with the summer Alaska Baseball League, he quickly found himself on the radar of Major League ballclubs.

After a junior year in which he struck out 115 batters in 78.1 innings, he was drafted by the Toronto Blue Jays with the 37th overall pick of the 2009 draft (the compensation Toronto received when the Yankees signed A.J. Burnett). Unfortunately, they were unable to come a deal, and Paxton opted to return to Kentucky for his senior year… that is, until the Blue Jays told the media that they had been negotiating with Scott Boras, not with Paxton’s family. Back in the pre-NIL days, hiring an agent changed your status from an amateur to a pro, and he was declared ineligible; an attempt to sue in order to be reinstated led nowhere, and eventually, Paxton withdrew from Kentucky to begin his professional career.

Paxton spent the 2010 season with the Grand Prairie AirHogs, an American Association team which allowed him to retain draft eligibility. On the back of a solid, albeit unspectacular, performance there, he was selected by the Seattle Mariners in the fourth round of the 2010 draft. After a lengthy negotiation, he finally put pen to paper in March 2011, and began what would be a rapid ascent through the minor leagues. He reached Double-A by the end of 2011, received an invitation to spring training in 2012, and finally made his Major League debut on September 7, 2013.

Thanks to a strong cup of coffee in 2013, Paxton began the 2014 season in the Seattle rotation, where he would spend the next five seasons. Unfortunately, he fell into a rather predictable pattern. When healthy, he was one of the league’s premier pitchers: his 13.2 fWAR from 2014 to 2018 ranked 26th out of the 88 starters who went at least 550 innings, and his 18.8 K-BB% ranked 14th — just one-tenth of a percentage point behind Cole and three-tenths behind Tanaka. And on May 8, 2018, he became just the second Canadian-born pitcher to throw a no-hitter in baseball history — a testament to his ability.

However, Paxton was hardly healthy for a full season: he made more than 20 starts just twice in that span, having hit the IL with a lat strain in 2014, a strained tendon in his finger in 2015, a forearm strain and a pec strain in 2017, and back inflammation and a forearm strain in 2018.

When the Yankees acquired Paxton that winter, they gambled that his ability on the mound would be worth the risk of his lengthy injury history. In 2019, that was absolutely the case. In the year where pretty much every member of the Yankees spent time on the injured list, the oft-injured pitcher put together the healthiest season of his career, making 29 starts and spending just a few weeks of May on the shelf.

Despite a nasty tendency to surrender home runs in the first inning, Paxton anchored the Yankees rotation, and when the Yankees needed him most in October, he delivered. Getting the ball with the team down 3-1 in the ALCS and having dropped three consecutive games, Paxton shook off two less-than-stellar postseason starts to shut down the Astros lineup, striking out nine and allowing just one run in six innings to send the series back to Houston. Sure, things didn’t get any better from there, but that’s another story (and not any of Paxton’s fault, either).

As good as things went for Paxton in 2019, however, that’s how bad 2020 went. On February 5th, he underwent lumbar surgery, which would have sidelined him for 3-4 months if the season hadn’t been delayed because of the pandemic. Although he made it back in time for the late-July Opening Day, he put together the worst season of his career, posting a 6.64 ERA in 20.1 innings across five starts before hitting the shelf again, this time with a left flexor tendon strain — perhaps the reason for the diminished velocity that made him suddenly very hittable.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Yankees opted to let Paxton walk in free agency, and he returned to the Seattle Mariners on a one-year deal. After just 1.1 innings, though, he left the game with an elbow injury, and later that week, it was announced that he needed Tommy John surgery.

A free agent again that winter, Paxton returned to the AL East joining the Red Sox on a one-year deal with a two-year club option and a one-year player option. A lat tear ended his attempt at a comeback in 2022, prompting Boston to reject the club option and Paxton to accept the player option. Due to a right hamstring strain, he began the 2023 season on the IL, and finally, on May 12, 2023, he made his Boston debut. Over the next two months, he pitched well, posting a 3.34 ERA in 13 starts in his first bit of extended action since 2020. Boston floated Paxton at the deadline, but ultimately held onto him in an attempt to make a bid for a Wild Card spot after a dominant July. That would turn out to be a mistake for everyone involved: a mediocre August and terrible October sent the Red Sox to the basement of the AL East, and Paxton battled inconsistency before being shut down with knee inflammation at the start of September.

Paxton signed with the Dodgers on a one-year deal in January 2024, a contract that was originally $11 million but reworked and lowered to $7 million with playing-time incentives due to unspecified health issues. He made 18 starts for Los Angeles, helping them deal with a rash of injuries to the rotation, before being surprisingly and unceremoniously designated for assignment to make room for River Ryan and Clayton Kershaw on the active and 40-man rosters, respectively. The Red Sox claimed him off waivers, and after three starts, he suffered a calf tear that ended his season.

The Big Maple retired from Major League Baseball after the 2024 season, but that wouldn’t be the last time we saw him on a mound. Paxton accepted the invitation to pitch for Team Canada during the 2026 World Baseball Classic. Working out of the bullpen, he touched 97 mph on his fastball in two appearances, including 2.2 scoreless frames against Cuba to advance out of the group stage. Despite potential interest from pro teams, Paxton has reiterated that he will remain retired. Aside from spending time with his family, he is in the process of completing the business degree he abandoned at the University of Kentucky when he was declared ineligible more than 15 years ago; after that, he intends to pursue a Master’s degree in sports psychology.

Happy birthday to James Paxton!

items.title: 'If you like it, then why would you stop?' – Approaching his 40s, Wout Poels continues into 19th and final pro season with Unibet Rose Rockets in 2027
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Wout Poels will continue racing into his 19th season as a professional in 2027 with Unibet Rose Rockets, the French-registered ProTeam confirmed on Friday.

The 39-year-old joined the Rockets at the start of 2026, and after maintaining his love of training and racing, particularly at the Giro d'Italia – the team's first and his 26th Grand Tour – and his high levels of performance, Poels didn't want to hang up his wheels just yet.

Born out of a YouTube channel and owned by Bas Tietema, Josse Wester, and Devin van der Wiel, the Rockets are approaching their fifth season in the pro peloton, with Poels part of a 26-rider roster that also includes Dylan Groenewegen. In 2027, they will look to secure invites to the Giro and a first Tour de France.

Poels' extension was confirmed in an accompanying video featuring him and Tietema at the former's fan club cafe in his home village of Blitterswijck, where the pair discussed plans for 2027 and played darts.

"Now I have to say, because of the Giro, it triggered a little bit more. It was a really nice three weeks and a really, really good level," said Poels.

"The most important thing is that I really like to do it. I like to train. I like to race. I like to do training camps. If you like it, then why would you stop? And the level is still there. That's the most important one.

"I imagine if I would have really did shit in the Giro and you get all the time dropped, you never go in a break, you never make a result, then I think I would not continue. I also like to be in the mix to do results, but even at a small race like Sibiu Tour, I was fourth in the GC and then second in the mountain stage – it's not the biggest race, but I still enjoy to race and get a result."

Poels will turn 40 on October 1 next, and while this is supposed to be his final year of racing, he still didn't rule out potentially keeping going into a 20th year.

"Is this really the last one?" asked Tietema. "Normally, yes… The door is always a little bit open," said Poels.

A former Liège-Bastogne-Liège winner, Tour de France stage winner, and Vuelta a España stage winner, Poels isn't landing the same calibre of results he was in his prime years at Team Sky and Bahrain Victorious, but he's still been able to land several impressive top 10s for the Rockets.

Poels finished in the top 10 of two stages at the Giro, including on the brutal mountain day to Pila on stage 14, where he was eighth and only lost out to the top GC favourites. He also finished fourth on GC at the Sibiu Tour in Romania, and seventh overall at the Arctic Race of Norway.

"The Giro; that's the highest level of the WorldTour, and it's really nice to perform there, especially on the mountain days to do top ten there from the peloton, that gives me a really good feeling," he said.

"OK, for me, I did, I think, 26 Grand Tours. But then I really come to my best after one week of racing, and I still feel that I get less fatigue.

"The WorldTour teams and Pro Teams, just to be in the top ten is always really high level. If you really want to perform there, then you need to be 100% ready."

But it's exactly that process which the Dutchman is still enjoying, having trained at altitude for the Giro this past season. Not only can he operate as a climbing leader, but Poels – as one of the most iconic super domestiques of the Team Sky era – is one of the most valuable riders for the Rockets' young talents to learn from.

For now, his win tally reads the same as his Grand Tour appearances at 26, but he's looking to bump them both up to at least 27 in 2027. It would maintain a run of winning a race on every team he's raced for as a pro, and a streak of starting a Grand Tour in every season that extends back to 2011 when he was on Vacansoleil-DCM – this was the season when he finished second atop the Alto l'Angliru behind Juan Jose Cobo at the Vuelta.

"I really would like to win a race for the team because I didn't do that last year. I was close to it, but I didn't do it," said Poels.

"That would be really nice, also for myself, just for my stats to say that I won a race in every team. But I just want to approach it like last year; have a good time, go to some nice races, perform well, try to do good GCs, just make good results. That's what I like to do."

items.title: "Exhausted" Russell set for Brazilian F1 grid penalty
Ferrari: Abolishing BoP should be “final goal” of 2030 WEC Hypercar regulations
What’s happening with Cadillac F1 buyout talks amid Fenway interest
items.author: Darren Cox
items.content:
Once upon a time, if you wanted to know who was buying into a Formula 1 team you could ask the bloke who owned it over coffee in the paddock.

Such is the way ownerships are now structured and managed in F1 there may only be one person in the paddock that actually knows something about the sale, someone with a freshly signed contract who appears to have let something slip on Thursday.

When I recently dug into who actually owns each F1 team, the distance we have travelled from the owner-operator days became very clear. The person running the team, the company whose name is above the garage, and the people who ultimately control the money can be three very different things.

That matters when considering the potential sale of a stake in Cadillac's F1 team.

There has been plenty of talk around the Austin and Mexico paddocks. But the reporting that has moved the story forward has come from American sporting and financial circles, led by Sportico, followed by the likes of the Wall Street Journal. The Race's journalists have been seeking confirmation in Brazil. That does not mean the answers are in Brazil.

I have been told that these negotiations are being handled personally by Walter and a very small circle around him. People working at Silverstone, at the American facilities, or in the garage at Interlagos, could quite reasonably know very little about it.

Cadillac has a struggling racing team and urgent challenges on track to resolve. Its owner has a collection of businesses and challenges of his own to manage, including federal investigations involving his insurance businesses.

That is why Cadillac's stance that nothing has doesn’t mean that nothing is .

My sources have indicated, for months, that a sale process is under way. Getting formal confirmation or anyone willing to speak on the record has proved rather harder, as is often the way with these things. The remaining question is what the outcome of that process will be. That is where the interest lies.

The least surprising part is that somebody wants to buy in.

Fenway among the prospective buyers

Walter has meanwhile been selling sporting assets, including his interests in the Lakers and Chelsea, against the backdrop of reported financial pressures and federal investigations involving his insurance businesses. TWG denies wrongdoing. That wider situation matters far more to this transaction than Cadillac's latest qualifying position.

It does not follow that Walter needed to begin by putting up a "for sale" sign. Prospective investors have been knocking on his door. In his circumstances, those conversations would be difficult to ignore.

The Guardian has reported talks about a majority purchase by Fenway Sports Group, which owns Liverpool FC and the Boston Red Sox among others. The preference on Walter's side appears to be a minority sale that allows him to retain control.

A preference is not a completed deal. But the distinction matters.

Lawrence Stroll provides a useful example. As we explored in the ownership article, he has brought successive investors into Aston Martin while retaining commanding voting and governance rights. Economic ownership and control are different things.

An owner can take money off the table, bring in another investor and still decide who sits in his second F1 seat.

So, the percentage sold will tell only part of Cadillac's story. The rights attached to those shares may tell us considerably more.

It is generally understood that Walter holds 67%, Dan Towriss 3% and General Motors 30%. Those figures have not been publicly confirmed and they do not tell us what approvals or protections GM has.

That is a significant unknown.

When I interviewed Flavio Briatore about Otro Capital's proposed sale of its 24% Alpine stake, he made a practical point about Renault's position. Its formal veto period ran until September. But who would commit hundreds of millions of dollars to a minority stake without a workable relationship with the majority shareholder?

A date passing on a contract does not remove the need to get along.

GM's position at Cadillac is different and we should not assume identical rights. But any buyer would need to understand its relationship with the manufacturer whose name, investment and long-term commitment are central to the proposition.

Seemingly well-informed in such matters, Sergio Perez offered a reminder of that in Brazil on Thursday, speaking to media including The Race.

Perez pointed to GM as "one of the biggest manufacturers", before considering whether the TWG investors wanted to "get some of their investment back".

"But I don't think it will change any structure at all," he said.

Having just signed a new long-term contract, Perez would have had every reason to ask what a sale might mean for the team before committing. He sounds unsure about why the investors would sell, but rather more certain about what happens afterwards. He may know more than most in Brazil. And that last line may have just let it show.

Naturally, there are plenty of other people being linked to said new structure.

An apprentice mechanic's job could become available in F1 and somebody would mention Christian Horner. His name appearing in this conversation is therefore hardly a revelation.

More interestingly I have also heard considerably wilder suggestions involving prominent paddock figures. As far as I can establish, those have not developed into firm outcomes. Yet.

Of the names reported, Fenway Sports Group, I've been assured, looks the most likely to progress.

Why Fenway's interest deserves attention

The very American nature of Fenway is of particular interest.

Informally, GM and senior management have been very pleased with the particularly strong response when Cadillac leans into its American identity. That has strengthened the appetite for an American driver, with Colton Herta increasingly central to that ambition, and for an American investment partner. The Race's audience data backs up this assertion. Our US audience figures spike on Cadillac and Herta stories. Obvious but important.

The process of getting Herta into F1 has, in my view, exposed the inexperience around the decision-making at a sporting level within the team. That deserves a piece of its own, which I will return to if, as seems increasingly likely, he is confirmed around the Las Vegas Grand Prix as Cadillac's second driver for 2027. For now, the decision remains publicly unresolved and Valtteri Bottas has been told there is still a route to him staying.

The commercial logic is easy enough to see. An American manufacturer, an American driver, and an investor experienced in American sport make a coherent proposition to sponsors and supporters.

Herta would still have to deliver behind the wheel. But the appeal of that combination helps explain why the driver discussion and the ownership discussion belong in the same article.

For Walter, the task is now to realise as much value while preserving as much influence as possible. For GM, it is to ensure the funding and stability is in place to support its long-term ambitions.

The negotiations that settle those questions will tell us more about Cadillac's future than anything said outside its garage this weekend.

items.title: ‘It Definitely Wasn’t Good’: Ineos Vowed the Transition Was Over. 2026 Shows It’s Only Just Starting.
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Netcompany Ineos head of racing Geraint Thomas sees signs of recovery in the former superteam. An exodus of talent will test the momentum in 2027.
items.lbText:
Netcompany Ineos is on the way back to its former glories – still .

Speaking this week on his Watts Occurring podcast, team head of racing Geraint Thomas insisted that 2026 was only the start of the newly financed squad’s quest to regain relevance in the WorldTour.

“It’s all about that progression, and it’s where you’re starting from as well. This might be a headline now, but let’s say we’re at 20 percent of what we used to be, to pick a number. You can’t just go from 20 to 80 straight away,” Thomas told his co-host Luke Rowe.

“It’s like climbing a ladder, isn’t it? It’s the same thing with a team, and I think we’ve gone up the ladder a couple of steps, for sure,” Thomas said. “We slipped a few times as well, but that’s all part of it.”

2026 was promised to be the year for Netcompany Ineos.

Seven years after the last of its seven Tour de Franc e titles, this would be the year of reboot.

Thomas, freshly retired from a career devoted to the team, was bringing his racing nous and good vibes to the directors’ chair.

Former yellow jersey mastermind Dave Brailsford was back pulling the strings.

The mid-season arrival of Danish IT brand Netcompany offered a path back to superteam status with its pledge to invest €100m over five years.

As Thomas said at the start of the year: “There’s been a lot of talk about transition – ‘the team’s in transition, blah blah blah. The transition’s over now, mate.”

UAE Emirates XRG, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and Visma Lease a Bike were warned.

Netcompany Ineos learned that transition takes time in an era defined by a small few phenoms.

In 2026, the team finished eighth in the WorldTour rankings, only a squeak ahead of Uno-X Mobility and Soudal Quick-Step.

A total of 36 victories through the season was the team’s best return since 2023, but strip away the filler and it’s not so pretty.

Eight of that haul came from national championships, the bulk were lower-ranked races, and only 13 were from the WorldTour.

That baker’s dozen is only a fraction of what was gobbled by the teams Netcompany Ineos is aspiring to beat. Tadej Pogačar, Isaac del Toro, Jonas Vingegaard, and Matthew Brennan powered UAE and Visma to two and three times that number, respectively.

Looking further forward, Netcompany Ineos’ two marquee wins in 2026 came from a rider who’s on the way out.

After a sensational victory at Dwars door Vlaanderen and the inevitable time trial victory at the Giro d’Italia, Filippo Ganna is leaving for Lidl-Trek this winter. More on him later .

Thomas insisted the results didn’t tell the whole story as he appraised his team’s season on Watts Occurring .

The Welshman highlighted how a myriad of mechanicals and crashes pulled the handbrake on a young team focused on three newly recruited captains.

“I think it’s all learning as well. Even though results weren’t particularly sensational, we had a lot of wins, but they were smaller wins,” he said.

Thomas’ positive spin on the season was well founded.

Oscar Onley, Dorian Godon, and Kévin Vauquelin all came to the team in the winter to fill high-stakes leadership positions.

Godon harvested victories in tough guy sprints. The Frenchman was one of the revelations of the season.

Onley was denied the chance to do what he was signed for – lead the team at the Tour de France – due to injury . But the rising young Scot rebounded for sixth overall and the white jersey at La Vuelta.

Vauquelin managed to get at least something on the board at the Giro d’Abruzzo after he was whacked by sickness in summer and lost time on day 1 of the Tour de France.

It’s good, but it’s not good enough for a former powerhouse that still judges itself against its own past.

Thomas was confident that there were green shoots behind a season of misfortunes and what-ifs.

Thymen Arensman and Egan Bernal put the team into the picture at the Giro d’Italia while its three new leaders began to acclimate to the team.

“People have said, ‘you can say was our season good or bad?’ And purely from results, I’d say it definitely wasn’t good,” Thomas said.

“I feel like Dorian, Oscar, and Kévin are all new to the team. That takes a bit of gelling,” he said. “The fact that they executed is a big plus. I think they all learned. And I think they’ll all take that forward, and it’s part of that growing. They’re all still young.”

The long-promised transition isn’t over. It’s only just starting for a team with a new identity and new leaders.

The question is, can the transition hold momentum into 2027?

Eight months after Netcompany bowled in, and a year after the arrival of Thomas, Onley and Godon, the team is facing more overhaul.

Ganna, one of the team’s biggest stars and a guaranteed source of time trial wins, broke his contract to join Lidl-Trek.

Rising U.S. talents Artem Shmidt, Andrew August, and Magnus Sheffield are all leaving as part of a talent exodus that’s seen eight riders find contracts elsewhere.

Also, the retirement of Ben Swift feels symbolic. The 39-year-old was the one survivor of the original Sky team that once upended and then dominated the sport.

Netcompany Ineos might struggle to fill the void left by so many significant departees in 2027.

After rumor of poaching Paul Seixas flittered out, the wannabe super team followed a moneyball recruitment policy focused on young talents or mid-career journeymen.

Benjamín Noval is the headliner of the nine arrivals confirmed so far, despite him only being 18 years old. Netcompany Ineos saw so much potential in the kid who dominated junior worlds that it reportedly gave him the biggest contract ever for a rider his age.

Speaking at the time, team CEO John Allert said Noval is the team’s future.

“At the heart of our team is a belief in long-term development and investing in the next generation of talent. Benjamín represents that future – and we’re delighted he’s chosen to grow and develop with us,” Allert said.…

items.title: 'I think she has grown a lot mentally' – Lars Boom highlights reason for Demi Vollering's stunning season, outlines 2027 goals
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
FDJ United-SUEZ manager Lars Boom has outlined Demi Vollering's main goals for the 2027 season and talked about what went right in a stunningly successful 2026 campaign.

Vollering enjoyed her most successful season yet, with wins at the Tour of Flanders, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Giro d'Italia Women, Tour de France Femmes, and the World and European Championships, among 16 victories.

She added another trophy to her collection on Monday, taking home the Keetie van Oosten-Hage trophy as the best Dutch female cyclist of the year. It's her second time winning the award, having previously triumphed in 2023.

At the ceremony in Utrecht, Boom told about Vollering's 2027 goals, with her schedule likely to follow a familiar pattern.

"Well, I think the Tour de France again. And defending her world title," Boom said of her top priorities for next season. Her early season goals and starting point have yet to be defined, however.

"She will ride some Classics and maybe the Giro again. It's a bit obvious, of course, but I think the Tour and the World Championships will be major milestones again."

Vollering has been in the USA in recent weeks, travelling through California and Oregon and taking part in events and rides with sponsors Specialized, Red Bull, and visiting Nike HQ in Portland.

Attention will soon turn to the 2027 season, though, and renewed hostilities with rivals including Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney at Lidl-Trek, new Movistar pairing Paula Blasi and Marlen Reusser, Visma-Lease a Bike leader Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and UAE Team L'IMAD's Elisa Longo Borghini, among others.

She beat all of them in 2026, and Boom hinted at what she did right.

"I think she has grown a lot mentally. If I take the Giro as an example, she was quite nervous back then," Boom said.

"In the Tour, however, there was total calm, and we basically didn't say anything on the bus or just before the start. That really made a world of difference."

items.title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Fernando Cruz
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
One of the most beautiful parts of baseball is how many different personal journeys we fans get to learn about as players chase their dreams. Fernando Cruz’s story aside, let’s dive into the season that earned him a B- from the staff here at Pinstripe Alley.

Cruz’s 2026 really started at the World Baseball Classic, representing Team Puerto Rico. After rejoining the Yankees, he picked up where he left off last season as a trusted member of Aaron Boone’s bullpen. From there, it became a story of two halves.

61 games, 54.2 IP, 3.13 ERA (135 ERA+), 4.17 FIP, 4.39 xFIP, 28.6 K%, 13.7 BB%, 0.0 fWAR, 1.2 rWAR, 4-6 record

Arbitration-eligible

Before the All-Star break, Cruz was excellent. He was a borderline All-Star, striking out 50 batters over 40 innings while holding opponents to a .191 batting average. His best month of the season was May, when he appeared in 14 games and posted a 1.02 WHIP while allowing just two earned runs over 13.2 innings. He was one of the more dependable pieces out of the bullpen during the first half of what was an underrated unit.

The key to this effectiveness was his splitter, which he deployed 51.3 percent of the time. He paired that pitch with a four-seamer, sweeper, and sinker to keep hitters off-balance. The splitter continued to be his best weapon, generating a 52 percent whiff rate and limiting hitters to a .161 average against it. 

After the break, however, his performance began to slip. Something seemed off as Cruz started losing some control in late July, and August became his roughest month of the season. He posted a 6.75 ERA over eight innings, allowing six home runs and four walks. Following a blown save against Houston on August 25th, the Yankees announced that Cruz had suffered a partial tear of his right ulnar collateral ligament, and he landed on the injured list the following day.

The ultimate team guy, Cruz opted to pursue a non-surgical approach after receiving a second opinion with the hope he could make it back in 2026. He received a cortisone shot and started rehabbing trying to find his way back into the mix for the postseason. However, a month after landing on the injured list, the Yankees transferred Cruz to the 60-day injured list on September 25th, ending his chances of returning during the 2026 season. 

On the season, Cruz had some impressive underlying numbers. He ranked in the 91st percentile in average exit velocity and the 99th percentile in whiff rate. He also landed in the 82nd percentile in xERA, the 88th percentile in strikeout rate, and the 85th percentile in extension. However, his hard-hit rate ranked in just the 22nd percentile, and his walk rate was in the third percentile. The right-hander was also effective against left-handed hitters holding them to a .180 batting average.

Losing Cruz after the Trade Deadline was less than ideal, especially with the Yankees having few options capable of replacing his production internally, which led to the Michael Fulmer experience. As the page turns to a new season, with the injury question mark hovering over him, Cruz becomes an interesting offseason decision for the Yankees.

The team has until November 20th to tender him a contract for the 2027 season. Depending on the outlook for his elbow, it would not surprise me to see the Yankees retain him and try to work out a deal before arbitration. Given the injury uncertainty, it could be a buy-low opportunity for the club, provided they believe he can return to form and he is willing to accept a similar salary to last season. However, professional baseball is a business and the team might opt to use the money and roster spot they would spend on Cruz elsewhere this offseason.

Personally, I gave Cruz a B for this season, and in hindsight, I feel that might have been a touch low. What grade would you assign Cruz, and what are your thoughts on him in pinstripes in 2027?

See more of the Yankees Roster Report Card series here.

items.title: McLaren's 2027 F1 front wing breaks cover in Brazil
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
McLaren’s new front wing, which will be the same concept it launches its 2027 Formula 1 car with, has been revealed at the Brazilian Grand Prix.

As part of an end-of-season push by the Woking-based squad to deliver continuous improvements to its MCL40, the squad has brought its latest upgrades to Interlagos.

This includes tweaks to its floor, an updated rear wing, but also a front wing that will form the starting point for next season’s MCL41.

The front wing is a change of concept for the team as it features many revisions across the spectrum of wing elements.

The attachment point for the main plane and the endplate has been revised to now run across the lower edge – where it marries up with the refined outboard element.

The attachment between the nose and the main plane has been adjusted to sit on the second flap now rather than the mainplane, while the new wing also features an adjustment in the height of the flap elements.

Speaking ahead of the weekend, McLaren explained that the changes delivered were about both delivering more downforce and improving car balance.

Chief technical officer of aerodynamics Peter Prodromou also made clear that these changes were the launchpad for its 2027 project.

“The season isn't over yet: these upgrades are designed to improve the car now and help us in our fight for third in the championship,” he explained.

“While the learning we take from these upgrades will feed into next year’s development, we also expect to carry over the concept of the new front wing into the launch specification of next year’s car.”

items.title: The Traka Goes Global in Major Gravel Racing Shakeup
items.author: ahood
items.content: The new seven-round Traka World Series replaces Gravel Earth, with equal prize money, global events, and plans to livestream every race.
items.lbText:
The Traka World Series is a new format with seven events. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The Traka is taking its flagship brand beyond Girona and putting its stamp on a new gravel racing circuit.

Organizer Klassmark will launch The Traka World Series in 2027 to replace the Gravel Earth Series , officials announced .

The new project will include seven rounds, with equal prize money for women and men, and the promise of live broadcasts.

The series is built around growing Traka brand, and will leave several familiar stops from the Gravel Earth Series outside the new-look format.

Stages races Migration Gravel Race and Oregon Trail Gravel Grinder, as well as The Hills and Ranxo Gravel are among the events absent.

The Traka debuted in 2019 in Spain’s Girona region, and has since grown into one of the marquee events on the world gravel racing calendar.

On the back of that success, promoters launched the Gravel Earth Series in 2022. It closed out its final season in 2026 with 11 events across six countries, with Specialized Off-Road teammates Mads Würtz Schmidt and Geerike Schreurs winning the elite titles.

The new slimmed-down format puts the Traka brand front and center.

The move comes after Klassmark partnered this summer with Grupo Godó , a Barcelona promoter behind the Titan Desert and Barcelona Marathon.

The biggest change for fans in 2027 could be the ability to watch live coverage for every round, though details are not finalized.

Prize money will include a series-wide purse of €76,000 (about $85,000), divided equally between women and men in the pro category.

Racing opens at Santa Vall in February. Girona’s Traka anchors the calendar on May 1, with Iowa’s CORE4 and Belgium’s The River among the later stops.

Another event outside Europe in April and a series-ending finale called The Last Dance have venues still to be confirmed.

There are few interesting twists to the new series worth mentioning.

Riders must register as either “pro” or “open” and remain in that category all season. Only pro riders will race for overall standings and prize money, but open riders will be classified in age groups in certain events.

Cross-gender drafting is banned. Pro riders cannot use headphones, phones, or radios, and outside assistance is limited to official zones. Riders may share food, water, and basic tools, but cannot swap out bicycles or other components.

Participation also counts toward future access to the headliner event, now called The Traka Girona. Riders earn one point for each “By The Traka” event completed to count toward entry for the 2028 and 2029 editions.

items.title: Marquez quickest as Qatar MotoGP weekend kicks off
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
MotoGP championship leader Marc Marquez led the way in the opening practice session of the Qatar Grand Prix, heading Marco Bezzecchi by a tenth of a second.

Marquez led virtually the entire session on the dusty Lusail track, and ended up on a 1m52.278s. He never fitted a spare rear tyre - but neither did virtually anyone else, with no incentive to use up any of the valuable rubber in the less-representative daytime session (compared to Friday afternoon practice, the sprint and the grand prix all taking place in the evening under the lights).

Fabio Di Giannantonio was third behind Marquez and Bezzecchi, four tenths down on the leader.

Pedro Acosta was fourth as the lead KTM, but his RC16 seemed to either fail or run out of fuel in the end as he had to pull over to the side of the track.

Jorge Martin, who had withdrawn from the Sepang weekend last time out due to his wrist fracture from Phillip Island, had a livelier start here, logging 16 laps and placing fifth.

With the Yamaha riders absent as the manufacturer elected to skip Qatar, a total of 18 riders took part. Honda's new stand-in Jake Dixon was last of them, after crashing on his very first flying lap.

But Dixon was just 3.1s off the pace in the end, so will have zero trouble clearing MotoGP's 105-percent pace rule for race eligibility.

There was another crash early in the session, for KTM's Brad Binder, who likewise returned to action shortly.

items.title: Should the Yankees non-tender Luis Gil?
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
In 2024, New York Yankees right-hander Luis Gil impressed with a brilliant first half and a full campaign worthy of the American League Rookie of the Year Award. At that point, the Bombers thought they had unearthed another pitching gem, controllable for multiple years on the cheap.

A severe lat strain in 2025 and shoulder issues in 2026 have hampered his progress and affected his fastball velocity and command, though. Last year, he posted a 3.32 ERA in 57 innings, but with very ugly peripherals. This season, the wheels completely fell off. The shoulder woes limited him to 39.1 innings between the majors and the minors. He finished with a 4.61 ERA and a rough 7.12 FIP in 27.1 MLB frames, with 18 walks and 17 strikeouts.

The right-hander started to transition to a bullpen role during the season, which could actually represent his firmest, most concrete way into the team’s plans. With the non-tender deadline looming on November 20th, however, the Yankees will have to make a decision. Is holding onto Gil worth the headache? The right-hander is projected to get a modest raise in his first year of arbitration, to $2.3 million, according to MLB Trade Rumors. Money, in this case, is not the primary issue, though.

Is Gil good or promising enough to warrant a place in the team’s future plans? Well, it will entirely depend on his ability to thrive out of the bullpen, which could be both his short and long-term home.

The concept of Gil as a multi-inning reliever is certainly enticing. Potentially increased velocity and not as much wear and tear on his shoulder sound excellent for his long-term prospects, but he does have short-term goals: looking good on the mound and getting closer to that 2024 version of himself, regardless of role. He was a completely different pitcher back then:

He is currently pitching for Tigres Del Licey in the Dominican Republic League, and boasts a solid 1.50 ERA in six frames, spanning over three games. The problem? He has issued six walks against seven strikeouts. Control has never been Gil’s calling card, but anything that starts with a five next to his BB/9 stat would represent a big problem.

The Yankees would probably love to trade Gil, hoping to get something in return for his name value and the fact that he won the award for the league’s best rookie just two years ago. They are probably dangling his name in the market as we speak. If they can’t reach a deal with any team, they will need to make a decision. They can give their promising, yet erratic right-hander one last chance, probably in the bullpen, or they could choose to cut ties and not tender him a contract, making him free to sign with any squad.

Complicating matters is the fact that Gil does not have any minor league options remaining. The next time the Yankees want to remove him from their 40-man roster, they will need to put him through waivers and risk losing him for nothing. If the Yankees can’t find a deal for him, they could opt to keep him around and try the bullpen experiment full-time to see if he can give them anything there, considering that it’s an area of need at the moment. It’s hard to see him sticking over the long term unless something drastically changes, though.

items.title: 'Miraculous' – Tadej Pogačar's heart rate data and sleep scores revealed in new documentary
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar has a resting heart rate of 38 beats per minute, a heart rate variability of 100, and a 'miraculous' prowess for sleep, according to new up-to-date figures revealed by his physiological data tracking sponsor, Whoop.

The numbers were disclosed in the first of a new documentary series on Eurosport, TNT Sports and HBO Max, titled ‘Anatomy of a G.O.A.T’, which aims to "decode the science behind the greatest athletes of all-time".

The first documentary, which airs on Saturday, looks to piece together the puzzle of Pogačar’s startling superiority over the rest of the peloton.

"Tadej’s resting heart rate, right, which is a very nice kind of global picture of your cardiorespiratory fitness, is 38," says Whoop’s Global Head of Human Performance, Kristen Holmes.

Holmes states that the average resting heart rate for a male of Pogačar’s, 27, age is 59, while also revealing that the other 27-year-old riders on UAE Team Emirates-XRG are a good bit higher.

"The average of the six other teammates is 42. He’s about four beats per minute slower than his teammates. And what this points to is a more efficient cardiorespiratory system, because he’s got this very efficient engine."

Pogačar’s resting heart rate of 38, while putting him a cut above his teammates, is not other-worldly like the 28bpm reportedly associated with another five-time Tour de France winner, Miguel Indurain.

Earlier this year, Pogačar’s top Classics rival, Mathieu van der Poel revealed his resting heart rate was the same, on average, at 38, though he noted the lowest he’d recorded was 34.

Heart rate variability – or a 'readiness indicator'

Whoop, as with Van der Poel earlier in the year, also revealed Pogačar’s heart rate variability, which is a measure of the variation in time taken between heart beats, measured in milliseconds over a long period of time, such as overnight.

It tracks the balance of the body’s autonomic nervous system but is described by Whoop in layman’s terms as a “readiness indicator”, with a higher HRV indicating superior physical fitness and recovery.

"The more variable that time interval, the more kind of ready you are to take on load," says Holmes. "So Tadej, his heart rate variability is 100. The other six riders on his team, their average is in the 80s. So he has to work less hard for the same output."

While the average HRV for active individuals is said to be between 40 and 65, Pogačar’s score of 100 pales in comparison with Van der Poel’s claimed HRV of 200.

"I’m really high in HRV," Van der Poel said earlier this year. "I think it’s a bit genetical, but fitness is important also. For sure, it’s something that makes me stronger and better recovered."

The HRV scores tie into the most important factor when it comes to recovery: sleep, and here is another area where Pogačar is said to be "remarkable". Whoop’s wearable technology monitors riders overnight, and gives them a ‘sleep score’ in the morning.

"Sleep consistency is when you go to bed and when you wake up, and the stability of that. And it’s expressed as a percentage. So on a scale of 0 to 100, again, you know, Tadej is 84%," says Holmes in the ‘Anatomy of a G.O.A.T’ documentary.

"Over the course of the 2026 Tour de France, none of the cyclists on the UAE team had sleep consistency that compared to Tadej’s 84%. They were mostly in the 70 to 80% range," adds Research Scientist Gregory Grosicki.

"One of the things we see very clearly in our data is that, when our members and even our elite athletes on Whoop do very high intensity efforts, the quality of their sleep tends to suffer. But with Tadej, he takes that even a step further. Going into the [Tour de France], he was sleeping about 7 hours. During the entire 2026 Tour de France, he was sleeping 8 hours. Miraculous. He’s sleeping more. He’s sleeping more regularly."

Asked about his sleep skills, Pogačar said: “I’m not a big hour sleeper, but if you eat clean and good for the dinner, I think it’s the biggest impact on the sleep then. And yeah, you just need to be relaxed and be organised for the next morning.”

Pogačar's powers of recovery were further underlined by his former coach Iñigo San Millán.

"He has an astonishing ability to recover," said the Spaniard. "We did some metabolic testing. We can see between 1000 and 2000 metabolic parameters, and one of them is ability to recover. Some of the antioxidant parameters are very important for recovery. When we saw his results, Tadej was far ahead of everyone else."

'Anatomy of a G.O.A.T' premieres on Saturday November 7 and will be available to stream in the UK, US, and Europe on
