items.title: How much has bad luck really cost George Russell in F1 2026?
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell says he's only had six race weekends without an issue in a bruising 2026 Formula 1 season.

But, on a Brazilian Grand Prix weekend where he's facing another grid penalty, does his claim stack up, and how much does bad luck explain his clear defeat to Kimi Antonelli? 

Antonelli has destroyed his Mercedes team-mate Russell this year, winning nine races to Russell's three and wrapping up the title with four rounds to spare last weekend in Mexico.

Facing the media for the first time in Brazil since that crushing title loss was confirmed, Russell admitted to "feel[ing] a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up". 

"When you get kicked to the ground, you pick yourself back up, then you get kicked down again, you pick yourself back up, and I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season, not every other weekend really," he said. 

"When you get to a point of this season, you're away from home three weeks in a row, and you have another race like what happened in Mexico, where a chance of victory, a chance of the podium, just disappears totally outside of your control, it's tough to deal with. It's very tough to deal with. 

"So Brazil's a place that I love, I've got great memories of. Do I come in with high expectations? Honestly, no, to be honest. But looking forward to next year for sure. And just continue to work on the things that I can control, and pray that things outside of my control sort themselves out." 

Russell said he went through every race of 2026 with his engineers and found "we've only had six races this season where we had not an issue". 

"So 14 [likely 13, as there have been 19 weekends so far] of those races we've had things that have been what we thought was bad luck, but we need to start questioning things more deeply when it's happening so often, and especially on our side. 

"That was the main feeling for me." 

So, we put that claim to the test: we've gone through F1 2026's 19 weekends so far and found the following:

Russell's campaign started in dream fashion with a dominant victory in the Australian season opener, while Antonelli paid the price for a costly final practice crash that left him compromised for the rest of the weekend on a suboptimal, unrefined set-up. 

He could probably still count Australia as an 'issue' weekend as he had to fight back from having a depleted battery before he started the race - costing him positions to the Ferraris and requiring him to fight back into the lead.

Russell followed it up with a sprint win in China, but his first real bit of bad luck came in grand prix qualifying when his car ground to a halt at the start of Q3. This left him needing a late lap to salvage second on the grid. 

Reflecting on that session, Russell told media including The Times: "I pulled the clutch half a second too early in the qualifying, which led to my car breaking down. 

"Should we have known about that? Maybe yes. Maybe not." 

Russell had been faster than Antonelli all the way through the weekend up to that point, so you can make a case he'd have won there with a normal Q3. 

At Suzuka, poor safety car timing helped Antonelli to victory and cost Russell a shot at it. But Antonelli looked the faster driver and may have won on sheer pace. It looked more like a fight between him and Oscar Piastri's McLaren.

But Russell was also then further compromised on the safety car restart by his car being put into an extra harvesting mode, leaving him fourth at the chequered flag. 

"Then in Japan, doing the upshift at the exact same time as I clicked another button...on the steering wheel...should we have known about that? Maybe yes. Maybe not," Russell reflected. 

Antonelli won from pole in Miami while Russell finished fourth on what appeared to be a clean weekend for both cars.

Russell and Antonelli then scrapped for victory in Canada when Russell's engine failed while he was leading. 

Antonelli won again in Monaco while Russell had a double-hit of penalties, the latter for Mercedes not serving his first, a five-second penalty for pitlane speeding, correctly. 

Given the circumstances of the pitlane speed limit penalties that weekend and Russell being blameless for the second penalty, it was another unlucky weekend and a lost podium (as he was third on the late-race restart). 

Russell finished second at Barcelona; Antonelli had passed him (and may have challenged Lewis Hamilton for the victory), but his Mercedes broke down with an electrical issue late on.

Russell won in Austria, beautifully judging the yellow flags in qualifying while Antonelli mistook double-waved yellows for single ones and backed off, ending up fourth on the grid and third in the race. 

Russell struggled with power unit deployment issues at Silverstone and Spa. At Silverstone he salvaged second (so probably did not lose any points) while Antonelli loses a likely victory to a front-left wheel-shield failure. At Spa, the issue cost Russell 0.2-0.25 seconds in qualifying, while on the opening lap it left him vulnerable on the Kemmel Straight. 

This led to contact with Lewis Hamilton, who was penalised for the collision - which put Russell out on the spot. Antonelli won the race from pole. 

At Hungary, Russell cracked a sump running slightly wide over a kerb in Q3, which left him seventh on the grid prompted engine-swap ramifications down the line. Then in the race he stalled and sank like a stone because of an engine rev anomaly, and an ill-timed virtual safety car stunted his recovery, while Antonelli took third. 

Antonelli and Russell finished second and third at Zandvoort, while at Monza Antonelli's excellent charge through the field - from 19th, owing to an engine-change grid penalty - was aided by the red flag and another well-timed virtual safety car.  

Antonelli's pace was so strong he may have still won without those anyway, but he was certainly aided by fortune on Sunday. 

A virtual safety car helped Antonelli beat Lando Norris's McLaren to victory in Madrid while Russell was fifth, off Antonelli's pace all weekend. 

Russell won in Baku while Antonelli crashed in qualifying before recovering to fifth. 

Another power unit failure at Sepang cost Russell a likely podium meant he had to take a grid penalty in Singapore. Russell blew a sprint victory there by crashing out of the lead at the end of the first lap, while he recovered to ninth in the grand prix.

Russell picked up a five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage at Austin and labelled his own pace "rubbish" en route to eighth, while Antonelli won again.

Then in Antonelli's title-sealing Mexico weekend, Russell had a deployment issue that dropped him from his front-row start. He clashed with Isack Hadjar's Red Bull and was penalised 10 seconds. 

So really, there have been 12 weekends where Russell has some publicly disclosed bad luck - 10 of which cost him points - not counting issues that he or the team have not revealed. It is true that this dwarfs Antonelli's misfortune, as he only really lost points to factors outside his control at Silverstone and Barcelona.   

Ultimately, Russell can only make a case that he lost victories in China (Q3 problem), Canada (power unit failure) and Monza (red flag and VSC timing that helped Antonelli), but even all three of those were far from guaranteed. Maybe Antonelli would've just been quicker even if Russell had a normal qualifying in China, maybe Antonelli would've won their dogfight in Canada, and maybe Antonelli had the pace at Monza to win regardless.

We'll never know the answer to those questions, but only the most ludicrously generous estimates of the points Russell has lost this season put him marginally ahead of Antonelli right now, if you then subtract the points Antonelli gains from it.

Russell's lost points to bad luck - A (very) generous view

China - 7 points (1st not 2nd) Japan - 6 points (2nd not 4th)

Montreal - 25 points (1st not DNF) 

Monaco - 15 points (3rd not 12th) 

Belgium - 15 points (3rd not DNF) 

Hungary - 6 points (4th not 7th)

Italy - 7 points (1st not 2nd) 

Malaysia - 15 points (3rd not 20th) 

Singapore - 6 points (6th not 9th) 

Mexico - 10 points (2nd not 6th) 

Total = 112 lost points New gap to Antonelli = Russell leads by 6 points 

*accounting for Antonelli's net points loss as a result

This would be an impossibly fortunate season for Russell, taking very generous liberties such as assuming he wins in China, Canada and Italy, plus presuming he maintains his second place in Mexico, and crucially not removing of Antonelli's own bad luck.

And even in this highly unlikely scenario where Russell is leading by six points, you'd back Antonelli to overturn it comfortably in the final four races on this season's form. 

In reality, even if you balanced out the reliability dramas of both cars, of which Russell has had more, Russell would still be over 60 points behind Antonelli instead of 130. 

Russell called it "difficult to put a number on how much [reliability] has impacted the championship" and pointed to one important factor. 

"It's often about momentum. When we start the season, we had the issue in China with the failure in qualifying, we had the issues in Japan, we had the engine failure in Canada, we had the drivethrough penalty that wasn't a drivethrough penalty in Monaco. These things compound," Russell explained.

"If you're in the championship fight, or you're within touching distance, you don't feel like you're having to do catch-up. And maybe that contributed towards overdriving and trying to overachieve. Maybe not." 

Again, we'll never know how a cleaner start to the season would've changed things for Russell or put more pressure on Antonelli. Russell's bigger problem was how quickly Antonelli became the faster Mercedes driver. 

Has Russell had more bad luck than Antonelli this year? Yes. But has Antonelli been the better, faster driver on more weekends? Absolutely yes. 

And it's something Russell himself acknowledged in Mexico on the eve of Antonelli's coronation: "The truth is he's been at a higher level than me this year."

The bad luck ballooned the gap and made the defeat all the more crushing, but the speed and execution difference this year meant the intra-team fight was only ever going one way.

items.title: EF Education-EasyPost continue post-Carapaz rebuild for 2027 with two more development team graduates
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The former had started his path to the pros in Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe's junior setup at Team GRENKE-Auto Eder, but joined EF Education-Aevolo for 2026. Despite setbacks due to crashes and injury in the first half of the season, Capello closed out the racing calendar strongly and has now earned the step up he's dreamed of.

They join Tao Geoghegan Hart, Ivan Sosa, Nicholas Milesi, Tobias Bayer, and Emil Herzog as EF's new arrivals for 2027. Team boss Jonathan Vaughters had already confirmed that Carapaz's departure was due to overstretched finances, with development team graduates allowing them to bolster their roster size closer to the 30-rider maximum while keeping the costs down

"I’m looking forward to the future and not looking back. It’s been my dream to race pro since I started cycling. I can’t wait to race with the best riders in the world, and EF Education-EasyPost is a really cool group," said Capello.

"I’ve had my fair share of bad luck this season, but I’m confident I’m in a good position to join the WorldTour with EF Education-EasyPost. They have shown a lot of patience and faith in my qualities as a rider, and I’ve worked really hard since joining the development team at the start of the year. I’m confident I can have a successful 2027 with the team and be a strong rider and teammate.

"Next year I want to try my hand at some short stage races but mostly just gain as much experience as possible. I want to learn from my teammates, and give everything that I can. I can’t wait to start."

His best results so far came as a junior in 2025, taking second at the European Championships road race, sixth in the World Championships time trial, and winning the Italian junior ITT title. Despite the injuries, which mostly prevented him from kicking on fully in 2026, EF are still confident in his abilities as a GC prospect.

"If you see Roberto’s results, he was one of the top riders in 2025. I’m super happy that we signed him," said head of scouting Sebastian Langeveld.

"This year was a bit on and off because of injury, but you can see from his training that he’s super talented. He has an incredible capacity on climbs and against the clock. He’s a very promising GC rider. It will take time, maybe a few years, but he has the qualities even though he’s still super young."

Hlady rode as a stagiaire for the WorldTour squad back at the end of 2024, and then raced for two seasons on the Aevolo squad to earn his way up to a full spot. A two-time under-23 national road race champion, Hlady also finished on the podium of the elite men's road race at the US national champs in 2025 behind Quinn Simmons and Evan Boyle.

"I’m excited to be stepping up and into the next phase of my career with this amazing team," said Hlady.

"Honestly, over the last few years, I always thought joining the WorldTour was possible, but I never thought it was guaranteed, so having this opportunity means so much to me. I truly believe that I have more to give and more room to develop as a rider."

In 2026, he finished second on a stage of the Alpes Isère Tour, and netted top-10s on stages at the Flèche du Sud and Le Tour de Bretagne Cycliste. For 2027, Hlady is looking to improve on his versatility, with the team confident he can go in any direction when it comes to specialising.

"Obviously, EF Education-EasyPost has strong American roots, but even if you took that aspect out of the equation, this is the team that I’d want to join. If you lined up all the teams in the men’s WorldTour, I’d choose EF Education-EasyPost every time," he said.

"I’m grateful, and I appreciate that we still have this cool international flavour and culture. I think we’re a really diverse team, and what sets us apart is that at the biggest races we always seem to punch above our weight. It’s an all-or-nothing and fun racing attitude. From the outside, they seem like the best team too because all the staff seem really cool too," he added.

"I want to get stronger, better and faster in every possible way and then see where that takes me. From there, I’ll sit down with the team in November at our next camp, and that’s when we’ll formulate a plan in terms of expectations and race calendar."

"Gavin came with Aevolo, and he’s shown throughout the last couple of years, with his national titles, that he has a lot of upward potential. He raced with the WorldTour team this year, and he did really well as a teammate, and he’s ticked a lot of boxes for us this year," added Langeveld.

"It’s a bit early to determine where he will end up as a rider, but he still has a lot of untapped potential, and we’re going to work with him on getting the best out of himself in the coming season. He can climb, and he might even go in the direction of the classics, but really, it’s about taking our time with the young riders and not rushing them."

items.title: Permane to stay as Racing Bulls team principal
items.content: <article>Red Bull extend Alan Permane's contract as boss of their second team until the end of 2031.</article>
items.lbText:
Red Bull have extended Alan Permane's contract as boss of their second team until the end of 2031.

The 59-year-old Englishman was promoted from racing director to team principal of Racing Bulls in July 2025, when predecessor Laurent Mekies was moved to the same role at Red Bull following the sacking of Christian Horner.

The team secured their first podium finish in four years at last season's Dutch Grand Prix with Isack Hadjar, and this season are fifth in the championship - the leading outfit behind the 'big four' - after 19 races.

Oliver Mintzlaff, who runs Red Bull's F1 programme as chief executive officer of corporate projects and investments, said: "Alan is doing a tremendous job, and the progress the team has made is a direct reflection of his experience, commitment and competitive mindset.

"He brings clarity, composure, and a deep understanding of what it takes to perform in Formula 1, while creating an environment where people can consistently deliver at their best.

"The results Racing Bulls has achieved in recent seasons underline the strength of the team and the work being done throughout the organisation.

"Alan has played a key role in that progress, and we are very pleased that he will continue to lead the team as we look to build on this momentum in the years ahead."

Before joining Red Bull, Permane spent 34 years at the team based in Enstone in Oxfordshire through various guises as Benetton, Renault and Lotus, winning two world titles each with Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso.

He said: "I am immensely proud to be continuing this journey and I would like to thank everyone at Red Bull for the trust and support they have given me.

"What makes this team special is the shared spirit of everyone; trackside, in Faenza and in Milton Keynes, and it is a privilege to lead such a talented and committed group every day.

"Fighting for fifth in the championship is something we should all be very proud of, but it is the result of years of hard work from a lot of people, and we are not done yet.

"We have the right people, the right culture and a clear sense of where we want to go, and I am excited to keep pushing together."

items.title: Michael Vanthourenhout fined for post-race clash with Cameron Mason at Middelkerke cyclo-cross
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Round two of the Superprestige ended in controversy on Thursday evening after series leader Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels-Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) was fined following a post-race altercation.

The incident occurred after he clashed with Cameron Mason (777TV) late in the Superprestige race at Middelkerke, the Belgian rider shoulder barging Mason on the eighth of 10 laps of the Nordzeecross circuit.

After the race, Vanthourenhout was seen on TV coverage approaching and shouting at Mason, who turned round and remonstrated with the Belgian, the two arguing briefly. Organisers have confirmed to that Vanthourenhout was fined 200 Swiss francs (€218) for the post-race incident.

Vanthourenhout had led onto the eighth lap, but was in second place behind eventual winner Joran Wyseure when Mason made a move on a straight section. Seeing the Scottish rider coming up on his left, Vanthourenhout moved out and barged into him, but in doing so seemed to be concentrating too much on Mason and not on the race, losing balance and crashing on the next left hand bend.

Consequently, Vanthourenhout dropped back to seventh place and was forced to chase back to the leading group. Meanwhile, Mason also crashed, after failing to negotiate a set of barriers, falling from second to sixth place, Vanthourenhout clearly commenting to the Scot as he passed, pushing him wide on the next bend.

"It was in the heat of the battle, adrenaline got the better of us," Vanthourenhout said in his post-race interview.

"I don't think he should have come on the inside there, but it is a manoeuvre that is allowed. I lost my balance, and from sixth or seventh place it is difficult to get to the front."

When asked whether the incident prevented him winning he said: "It plays a role, but that is a race. I was disappointed, but I am also happy that I still made the podium. My second place is good for the standings."

For his part, Mason was seen laughing with team staff after the incident, later adding the caption "Something something, 'own medicine' something something. Another solid race. Onto the next" on his Instagram story.

The race was a fast one with hectic, exciting racing throughout, Joran Wyseure (Crelan-Corendon) taking the win ahead of Vanthourenhout. Swiss champion Kevin Kuhn (Heizomat-Cube) was third, one place ahead of Mason.

Vanthourenhout has had an excellent start to the season, winning four of his seven races to date and never finishing off the podium. Having won the first round of the Superprestige at Overijse on October 25, he started Thursday’s race leading the series, his second place enough to retain his lead in a series where he finished second overall last season.

Though not matching his Belgian rival, Mason has also had a good season, with eighth place in the first of six races the lowest placing so far. The two riders will line up against each other at Sunday's European championships, which Vanthourenhout won ahead of Mason in 2023.

items.title: TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Which is the best app to support your structured training?
items.author: Paul Norman
items.content:
TrainerRoad and TrainingPeaks offer an objective-driven approach to training, helping you to target specific events or develop a plan to cover your whole season.

They also focus on offering more detailed analysis of your performance than other platforms, such as Zwift and MyWhoosh and are generally used by riders whose priority is training and data or who don't need an immersive virtual training world.

They go about this in rather different ways, though. While TrainingPeaks delivers workouts via its TrainingPeaks Virtual app, TrainerRoad is more old-school, with a simpler ramp-based graph interface.

Where TrainerRoad scores, though, is its AI-driven workout selection. It also caters for missed workouts and changed schedules via its Train Now functionality.

TrainingPeaks was bought by Garmin in July 2026. It’s not clear how this will affect the app in future, but for the moment it continues to operate as normal.

Garmin may be looking to strengthen its own indoor training offering, which is currently delivered via the niche Tacx app.

TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Approach

Both TrainerRoad and TrainingPeaks are much more hardcore than apps such as Zwift and Rouvy. They aim to offer objective-driven, structured training based on goal setting and planned activities to meet your goals.

TrainerRoad provides AI-driven training, with its app assessing your performance after each workout and tuning your future activity schedule based on this. The assessment is across multiple aspects of your fitness, not just FTP. This, it claims, gives a more precise assessment of your strengths and weaknesses and allows it to more accurately target its workouts.

As well as structured, scheduled plans, there’s also the Train Now option, which allows you to fit in workouts around your other activities in a more flexible way.

TrainingPeaks is more focused on its structured plans, which offer less flexibility than TrainerRoad. There’s a wide range of plans available, but these are extra-cost items on top of the basic access.

TrainingPeaks doesn’t just work with cyclists; it offers training for other endurance sports and also strength training. There’s the option to work with in-person coaches to manage your training.

TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: User interface

TrainerRoad offers a fairly basic user interface while you work out, consisting of the classic ramp profiles on a black background, with stats on your performance. There’s no interactivity with other users. You do have the option to ride its workouts on other platforms, though – see below.

TrainingPeaks offers a virtual world with a similar, although less finished, look to Zwift or MyWhoosh. This can be explored solo, but you can also join up with other riders, join group rides and chat in-app.

Ride physics is simulated, so you’ll get a boost from drafting, and headwinds can slow you down. As with Zwift, there are virtual riders too, and you can upload your own GPX files to ride your own routes.

There are the same ramps in intensity as with TrainerRoad, just presented in a more visually appealing way. If you want to, you can select Focus mode and switch off the virtual simulation, or Zen mode and ride alone in the virtual world.

TrainingPeaks Virtual also offers a range of different races at different performance levels, adding an element of competition to your riding.

TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Workout alternatives

Both TrainerRoad and TrainingPeaks allow you to work out on other platforms, although you will need a separate account for the second app.

TrainingPeaks workouts can be ridden on Zwift, which offers a greater depth of immersion than its TrainingPeaks Virtual environment and all the Zwift add-ons such as power-ups, as well as a larger user base to ride with or race against.

You’ll need both a TrainingPeaks and a Zwift account, but then workouts in your TrainingPeaks calendar will appear in your Zwift workout schedule and, once you’ve completed a workout, it will automatically be synced back to TrainingPeaks for analysis and progress tracking.

TrainerRoad offers a feed out to Zwift too, so that scheduled TrainerRoad workouts appear in your Zwift account and you can ride them there, with data then transferred back to TrainerRoad for progression tracking and analysis.

TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Pricing

A TrainerRoad annual membership is priced in US dollars and annually works out at $17.45 monthly equivalent, but you can also pay monthly, which costs $21.99 per month. TrainerRoad offers a 30-day money-back period.

TrainingPeaks costs the equivalent of $11.25 per month if you pay for a year’s Premium access. You can also pay quarterly, which increases the price to $16.33 per month equivalent, while paying month-by-month costs $19.95. Again, there’s a 30-day money-back period.

But with TrainingPeaks, you also need to factor in the price of its training plans, which are not included in the basic price. Its 12-week Base and FTP Development plan, for example, costs $5, while the VO2max Booster costs $20. Other plans can cost as much as $500.

TrainingPeaks has the option to work with a live coach to develop a custom training plan. Three tiers of interactivity range in price from $149 per month to $359 per month. The lowest-priced option puts limits on your communication with your coach, while the most expensive option offers unlimited interactions and feedback on every workout.

TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Which should you choose?

TrainerRoad’s adaptive training and its sophisticated metrics will be attractive to cyclists wanting some flexibility in their objective-driven training. It’s a solitary experience, though, and it takes a certain mental outlook to follow a plan when the workouts are presented as ramp charts only; although riding on another platform does offer a more interesting alternative, it has to be said.

There’s more opportunity for interactivity with other users and with coaches in TrainingPeaks, which some may find more engaging. This does increase the cost of access, though, so TrainingPeaks is likely to be more expensive to use. Its analysis is also less sophisticated than that of TrainerRoad, but it does cover a wider range of sports.

items.title: 'Tom's pace is pretty mind-blowing' – Tom Pidcock swaps two wheels for four to tackle fearsome Nürburgring Nordschleife race track in Porsche 911
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
With the cycling off-season in full swing, Tom Pidcock has swapped two wheels for four, taking to the German motor racing circuit Nürburgring Nordschleife in a Porsche 911 GT3 RS.

The Briton has won world and Olympic titles on cyclo-cross and mountain bikes, but he's no slouch in the race car, either, joining Porsche brand ambassador Jörg Bergmeister for a track day at the legendary circuit in Germany's Eifel mountains.

Pidcock has previously recorded a 6:52.37 lap time around the fearsome 20.832km former Formula 1 circuit, which features 73 corners, leaving him just 27 seconds off the all-time lap record, set by Stefan Bellof in 1983.

The 27-year-old, who this year won Milano-Torino and finished ninth at the Tour de France, will soon be gearing up for his third season at Pinarello-Q36.5, where he'll be joined by new arrivals Giulio Ciccone, Mauro Schmid, and Ethan Hayter, among others. However, he took time away from the bike to explore the track with Manthey Kit on Wednesday.

"The organisation of the race team and where all the parts are feels very similar to how we have our service course in the cycling team. The parts storage, the packing lists – it's a similar world," Pidcock said of the company's headquarters, located near the famous 2km straight of the circuit.

"What I've learned from Manthey is that, if you're developing a car at the Nürburgring, the data doesn't tell you everything. You have to use feeling.

"And personally, I think feeling is even more valuable than data when I'm trying to develop a bike. The Nordschleife is such an unpredictable place, and Porsche and Manthey manage to make the cars feel as predictable as possible for the people driving them."

This time around, Pidcock took on the challenging circuit in wetter conditions, and Bergmeister said that Pidcock's pace is particularly impressive given he isn't a regular at the track.

"I know a couple of pro and ex-pro cyclists, and the line and flow that it takes to do a smooth, quick lap comes naturally to these guys. Tom gets in and knows exactly what he's doing and has great feel for the car – and also no fear," he said.

"For someone who isn't here regularly, Tom's pace is pretty mind-blowing. There are people on the Ring every day who go slower. The advice I could give him is to simply focus on hitting the marks: braking points, turn-in points.

"But you can see it all comes naturally. I guess there's a reason why he's so good on the descents in cycle racing!"

Pidcock explained what drew him to the track and racing high-performance cars, such as the powerful Porsche 911 GT3 RS.

"I guess it's because it's about 'high performance', just like cycling is for me. It's the same mindset," he said.

"Driving, in general, is a pursuit of improvement, which is constant in what I do daily. But here there's no pressure – I can also enjoy the fact that I don't need to push it to the extreme limit. When I'm competing [in my career], there's always so much pressure, so on track it's nice that I can simply just compete with myself."

items.title: How to turn an AI into your personal coach: Goal-specific prompts and setup instructions
items.author: Tim Perkin
items.content:
The world of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is moving so fast that even WorldTour cycling teams are now using it to help understand and interpret riders' data to aid with training and racing.

AI use is commonplace now, and cyclists are using it to their advantage. Following suit, I decided to see what AI could do for me.

My end goal was for AI to generate a bespoke training plan that could return me to my peak level of fitness, whatever that was. Simple, or so I thought. I wanted to learn about customising an AI training plan based on my own historical data, and improve my skills along the way.

The first challenge was choosing a platform. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot were all AI assistants that I investigated.

Some AI engines or apps are free, some aren't. Free versions limit what you can do and, in this case, how many files you can upload to be analysed. I paid a subscription fee as I was always going to need to use my full training history. After researching the different platforms, I settled on Claude because it could read and analyse my CSV files directly.

With Claude chosen, I paid for a subscription and began to see what it could do.

I decided to ask it to build me a 12-week indoor training plan using this simple prompt:

"Build me a 12-week indoor cycling training plan of between 7 and 10 hours a week. I can ride 5 times a week, but not on Thursday."

Claude then produced the plan below for me:

FTP test in Week 1, then sweet spot and tempo

Threshold and over under intervals

V02 Max intervals with some threshhold

The plan is perfectly acceptable, but it's limited. It offers nothing beyond what you can find in cycling training manuals or on hundreds of websites online.

The plan falls short because it is not based on my own data. Without access to my training data, asking AI to build me a plan will always result in something this generic.

Granted, you can input parameters such as how many rides you intend to do each week, how many hours you have available for training, and which days suit you best, but beyond that, the output will always be limited.

To create a bespoke plan and something tailored to my requirements, I realised that I needed to provide AI with my training data. Only with this could AI produce a bespoke plan. And for that, I knew where to go:

My Strava account held almost all my training data, and with the functionality to download it, I could then take the relevant files and have AI analyse them and utilise my training and riding history.

[Ed. Since undertaking this project, but prior to publishing, Strava launched its MCP connector, allowing direct plugin to AI assistants, enabling the sharing of historic datam, plus future data in perpetuity].

However, I had to undertake a slight side quest first. Strava did not have all my data. My early years of training results were held on spreadsheets, so I had to get these uploaded into Strava using a third-party app.

I reformatted the spreadsheets got the data uploaded into Strava, using a third-party go between. I then requested my complete set of training data from Strava. An email link soon arrived with a 1.7 GB archive, though I only needed one file from it.

The summary file was called "activities.csv" and contained enough data to enable AI to produce a tailored plan for me.

To download your own data in Strava, go to Settings > My Account > Download or Delete Your Account, then select Request Your Archive. Strava then emails you a link to the data.

Only activities.csv is needed, so there's no need to upload the whole thing. If you have many years of riding and the file is too large to upload, delete the oldest rows, but keep your best season so the AI can compare against it.

A word of caution: activities.csv includes heart-rate data, which is personal health information. I recommend checking your AI platform's privacy and data settings before you upload it.

Power figures only appear in activities.csv files for rides recorded with a power meter or smart trainer. Without them, the AI's FTP estimates and power targets will be much less reliable, so bear this in mind too.

The next challenge was writing the correct prompts to finesse my training programme. My first attempt was too simple. After some research, I learned that a good prompt needs four key components.

The first component is the persona, which assigns the AI a specific role, for example: "You are an elite cycling WorldTour coach."

The second component is the specific task, such as "Using my uploaded data, analyse and assess my current level and create me a 12-week training plan that gets me to and surpasses my previous best cycling fitness levels."

The third component is the context: including any important details, which in this case were the days I could train and for how many hours.

The fourth and final component is the format, or how I would like the answer to look.

The prompt I decided to use to build my specific training plan was as follows:

"You are an elite cycling WorldTour coach. Using my uploaded data in the spreadsheet only, analyse and assess my current level and create a 12-week training plan that gets me to and surpasses my previous best cycling fitness levels."

"I have 10 hours per week for training and can ride 5 times a week, with the exception of Thursday."

"Sessions in the week must not last longer than 90 minutes. I would like a detailed session plan, detailing how long each session should last, power output and heart rate."

I also find that going to a separate Claude chat window and asking it to suggest its own prompt is a good way to learn the phrasing and terminology that Claude itself understands. You can iterate on its suggestion more easily than create your own from scratch, and the wording is often less vague than anything I would generate myself.

I later refined these prompts into a shorter version that you can reuse:

"You are an elite WorldTour cycling coach. Using only the rides in my attached Strava activities.csv, assess my current level against my all-time best (estimated FTP, and best 20-minute and 60-minute power), then create a 12-week plan starting [date] to beat it."

"I have 10 hours a week over 5 rides. I can't ride on Thursday or [second rest day], and weekday rides must be 90 minutes or less. Give me my power and heart-rate zones, then a table for each week showing day, duration, session, target watts, and target heart rate. Include recovery weeks and FTP tests in weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12, and be honest about how realistic the goal is."

Before building the plan, the AI assessed my data. It estimated that my FTP had fallen from about 325–329 watts at my peak (December 2021 to February 2022) to about 260 watts, a drop of around 20%, and that my weekly riding had halved from 8–10 hours to about 4.5 hours. That told me straight away that this plan would be built around me, not a textbook.

The output, generated by the first of the two prompts above, was a very detailed plan with tailored power and heart-rate targets. The table below shows Week 1; the other 11 weeks are just as detailed.

The plan is not fixed. After each FTP test, I can give the AI the result and ask it to recalculate my zones and update the remaining weeks, so the plan keeps pace with my fitness. With the newly added MCP Connector, this could even be automated.

Example Block 1: Rebuild (FTP 260 W)

Week 1 (26th Oct), 8 hours, approx 430 TSS

20-min FTP test. 15 min Z2, 3 × 1 min at 290 W

(1 min easy), 5 min easy, 20 min max effort (start at 265 W, build). FTP = 0.95 × 20-min average

Easy, with 4 × 30 s spin-ups at 110–120 rpm

Endurance, last hour includes 2 × 10 min tempo (5 min easy between)

Prompts you may find useful

This prompt gets the AI to act as your personal cycling coach and build a 12-week plan that fits around your life and moves you towards a goal, such as beating your best FTP. It is a fuller version of the short prompt above, giving you more control over the output.

"You are an elite WorldTour cycling coach who builds periodised, power-based plans for time-limited amateurs. Using the 'Ride' and 'Virtual Ride' activities in my attached Strava activities.csv, create a progressive 12-week plan to [goal, e.g., beat my previous best FTP]. I have [X] hours a week across [X] rides; I can't ride on [days], and weekday sessions are capped at [X] minutes.

Remember to be specific in your demands; a degree of nuance and experience is needed here, and if you choose to experiment, the more you do, the better you will get.

I asked the AI to give me:

  • An assessment of my current level against my all-time best, with key numbers. Estimate FTP from Weighted Average Power in 20–60-minute rides, and include weekly hours, load, and consistency over the last 12 weeks.
  • A zones table: % of FTP, watts, and heart rate.
  • One table per week: day, duration, session (with intervals and recoveries), target watts, target heart rate, and weekly total hours. Include recovery weeks and FTP tests in weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12, with week 12 a taper that ends in the final test.
  • Up to five rules on fuelling, adjusting when fatigued, and updating zones after each test.
  • Be realistic about what 12 weeks can achieve.

This prompt uses your data to check whether you've been riding too hard too often over the past month without enough easy days or rest between hard rides. The aim is to catch fatigue before it leads to poor performance, illness, or burnout.

"You are a cycling physiologist specialising in recovery and fatigue monitoring. Using the 'Ride' and 'Virtual Ride' activities in my attached Strava activities.csv file from the last 30 days, find the days where my recovery was probably not enough. My FTP is [X] W, and my threshold heart rate is [X] bpm. Classify each ride as hard (above 85% of FTP), moderate, or easy (below 70% of FTP), using Weighted Average Power, Relative Effort, and heart rate, and treat a heart rate of 0 as not recorded. Flag hard days back-to-back, more than three hard rides in any seven days, and heart rate out of line with power."

I also asked my AI coach to give me:

  • A 30-day calendar table: date, ride, duration, Weighted Average Power, and Hard/Moderate/Easy/Rest.
  • Each day where recovery was not enough, with a one-line reason.
  • My hard-to-easy ratio compared with 80/20.
  • Three changes to my weekly structure.

This prompt checks whether your recent riding has prepared you for a specific event, such as a sportive, road race, or time trial, and tells you what to work on in the four weeks before it.

"You are an experienced cycling coach who prepares riders for races and sportives. Look at my rides from the last 12 weeks in the attached Strava activities.csv file. I'm riding [event, e.g., a 120 km sportive with 2,000 m of climbing] on [date]; my goal is [goal, e.g., finish under 4 hours], and my FTP is about [X] W. Tell me whether my training so far has prepared me for this event.

I also asked my AI coach to give me:

  • A short summary of how fit I am now, in three or four sentences.
  • A table of my last 12 weeks: hours ridden, longest ride, total climbing, and number of hard sessions (Weighted Average Power above 85% of FTP) each week.
  • What's missing. Check whether I've done enough long rides, enough climbing, enough long steady, hard efforts, and enough short bursts for attacks. For each gap, show the evidence from my data and why it matters for this event.
  • A four-week plan to fix those gaps, with the key sessions, the long ride for each week, and power and heart-rate targets.
  • An honest one-line answer on whether my goal is realistic.

Rather than building all of the above as a self-serve chat-based coach that you ask questions of and manually prompt when you want it to adjust or analyse your work, it could even be built agentically. An overarching AI Agent could be given the primary prompt, the database of Strava workouts uploaded as resources alongside your preferences, and improvements to your power duration curve or your FTP can be its reward signal.

The trio of prompts above - alongside others - could then be created as 'skills' - essentially tools that the LLM can call upon, and automations can be built to check your progress periodically, update the plan in real time, and flag whenever you're off track.

If you wanted, you could even connect it to your Whoop (if you use one), and your Calendar app of choice to slot the workout into your day.

There's a lot of potential here, and although the build essentially seeks to mimic much of what's already been achieved by TrainerRoad, Zwift Plus, Vekta, FasCat, Xert et al, there's a certain enjoyment and pride in building it yourself (even if Claude is doing the hard yards), and being able to tweak it to your liking.

AI can be a valuable tool for cyclists to understand their training and improve performance, and many are already experimenting with ways to use AI to improve their training.

The results are going to depend on the input. While generating a basic training plan is easy, creating a genuinely bespoke one is harder.

The real insights come when AI accesses your historical training data. It analyses past performances, assesses your current state, and builds a plan around your ambitions, time, and individual needs. This results in a more detailed and personalised approach.

For the plans and outputs to be relevant, the data must be accurate, prompts carefully constructed, and output critically evaluated. Training recommendations are only as useful as their underlying information and assumptions. AI should not replace professional coaching or understanding your body's response to training.

There's also a cost, both for AI platform subscriptions and the time to organise data and refine prompts. Yet, for cyclists willing to invest the initial effort, the reward is a plan built around their own numbers rather than a generic one.

I aimed to see if AI could help me regain peak fitness. I now have a structured, data-driven 12-week plan designed to do just that. Its success will ultimately be determined on the bike in the coming weeks.

items.title: Russell to take grid penalty at F1's Brazilian GP
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell will take a five-place grid penalty for this weekend's Formula 1 Brazilian Grand Prix for a new internal combustion engine, his second grid drop in four races.

Russell had a 60-place grid penalty for a suite of power unit component changes in Singapore last month, a necessity after he retired with a power unit failure in Malaysia the week before.

He knew then that he would have to take another grid penalty before the end of the year, and Mercedes has chosen Brazil to do so at Interlagos this weekend, with Russell confirming the decision on Mercedes' Instagram account.

"We always had to take a grid penalty at some point between Singapore and the end of the season," Russell explained.

"We felt like this was a good place to take it. Lewis [Hamilton] had a big grid penalty here a number of years ago [in 2021] and did pretty well.

"Five places doesn't seem that bad and we’ll try to come back through."

Driving for Mercedes in 2021, Hamilton was disqualified after topping sprint qualifying for a technical non-conformity (a misaligned DRS), yet charged from 20th to fifth in the sprint.

Back then, the sprint result dictated your start position for the grand prix but, after taking a new internal combustion engine, Hamilton was dropped back to 10th on the grid.

He still comfortably won the grand prix from there.

So Brazil is a logical choice for Russell to take the engine penalty, one that was originally going to coincide with the debut of Mercedes' Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities-assisted (ADUO) engine.

But the debut of that ADUO engine is uncertain, and there's no guarantee it will appear before the end of the season, with a maximum of three races remaining after Brazil.

Mercedes does not want to rush its introduction and will only introduce it when it is sure it is ready, with the drivers' championship already sealed and the constructors' championship all but guaranteed.

items.title: Ferrari set for crunch meeting as Hamilton and Leclerc tension reaches Brazil
'I felt quite lost and desperate' – How Ashleigh Moolman Pasio re-wrote the ending of her 17-year career, and how she's re-writing the future for African cyclists
items.author: Dan Challis
items.content:
Ashleigh Moolman Pasio's career could have ended very differently had she given in to a drawn-out and frustrating recovery to a fractured vertebrae. She considered hanging up her race bike during the 2025 season, a year earlier than planned, her confidence weakened after 18 months of trying to find form due to a crash at the 2024 Volta a Catalunya.

However, the South African was determined to write a different final chapter to her 17-year professional career, and saddled up for one last campaign.

Speaking to Moolman Pasio over a video call from her home on the outskirts of Girona, it's clear that this conversation would have been very different had it occurred twelve months earlier. The AG Insurance-Soudal rider is leaving the peloton satisfied to have bowed out on her own terms and in good shape, rather than being forced out through injury.

I didn't finish because I wasn't good enough any longer. I finished because I've decided it's time to put my focus into other things.

"At the end of 2025 I actually didn't know who I was as an athlete any longer. It was such a disconnect from the athlete I was in training and who I knew I was in terms of the power and the performance I could produce," Moolman Pasio tells a few days after her final bow at the gravel worlds. "I felt quite lost and desperate. It did cross my mind to retire sooner than planned."

Alongside her T10 vertebra fracture, Moolman Pasio also discovered at that time that she was suffering from high insulin sensitivity, causing her muscles to flush out glucose from her bloodstream; a physiological concept known as the 'athlete paradox'. After adjusting her diet, she got back in shape for the 2026 season.

"I decided that I wanted to finish my career on my terms and managed to get back to a level that I was very happy with," she says, having finished fourth at April's Brabantse Pijl among several other strong results in her final year.

"I finished on my terms and I finished the athlete that I know I should be. Whereas if I had finished last year having had all those performance issues I would have felt like I was forced to retire because I'm not good enough any longer. Now, I actually could continue… I still am at the level that I could hugely contribute to a team."

"I didn't finish because I wasn't good enough any longer. I finished because I've decided it's time to put my focus into other things," she adds.

Moolman Pasio was pleased with her final road worlds performance, finishing in the top-20 on a tough course in Montréal. Things didn't go quite as smoothly on the gravel two weeks later, however, as she endured a cold in the days before and ended her final race early due to a crash.

No "fairytale ending," she says, but turning 41 in December, Moolman Pasio is now taking time to reflect on almost two decades in Europe that have themselves had the twists and turns of a good novel.

An outsider infiltrating a European sport

No African woman precedes Moolman Pasio for her longevity and achievements in professional cycling. After qualifying as a chemical engineer at Stellenbosch University, the Pretorian discovered her talent for cycling later than most, encouraged and supported by her husband, Carl.

Moolman Pasio began racing on the South African scene while at university. She soon signed for one of the country's big teams, Cyclelab-Toyota, which in 2008 enabled her to race in Europe for the first time at the Tour Feminin de l'Ardèche. She finished the six-stage race in 39th, doing enough to convince Lotto Ladies to hand her a life-changing contract.

"The Tour of Ardèche was a big big eye-opener. [I was] totally out of my depth at that point in time; crashing, punctures, all sorts of nonsense. But thankfully I made contact with Lotto. We managed to negotiate this ride for a couple of members of the local team on the Lotto set-up. [It was] for free. We just got our bikes and support," she explains.

"It took determination, it took guts. I had to be really brave to make this all happen. It also took the support around me which I was very lucky to have."

Moolman Pasio describes racing a 'double season' in her first couple of years; competing in Europe during the northern hemisphere summer with Lotto, and then again throughout the summer months in South Africa. She survived on the small amount of pay from racing in South Africa as well as some personal endorsement deals from South African companies.

She says her first "proper contract" came along in 2014 when she joined the Norwegian Hitec Products team after a season in which she finished on the podium at La Fléche Wallonne. However, throughout all this time, she and Carl had been struggling with visa restrictions due to their South African passports. Utilising his Italian heritage, Moolman Pasio's husband managed to get Italian passports for both of them, solving their visa restriction woes.

Moolman Pasio went on to take a total of 49 UCI victories throughout her career. She became the first African woman to win a WorldTour stage race in 2022 at the Tour de Romandie, won the UCI eSports World Championships in 2020 and was twice overall runner-up at the Giro d'Italia Women. For much of that time, Moolman Pasio has been the only African rider at the top level of women's cycling, something which she plans to change in the next phase of her life.

'The hunger in their eyes' – Paying it forward with Team Amani

Moolman Pasio's career has not only been characterised by what she has achieved on the bike, but also her activities off it. She set up Rocacorba Cycling in 2021 alongside her husband, a boutique cycling hotel in a restored 17th century estate, nestled in the mountains near Girona and named after one of the local climbs. Alongside the hotel, Moolman Pasio established the Rocacorba Collective, a thriving indoor cycling community with a particular mission to uplift and bring women together.

In a sport that has become more insular, with riders able to focus on little else aside from their performance, Moolman Pasio has always ridden with a wider set of goals in mind. In 2023, during the middle of her Classics campaign, she travelled back to South Africa to support women from Khaltsha Cycling, a cycling project partnered with Rocacorba Collective in the country's largest township, to ride the Cape Town Cycle Tour.

"I've always been driven by impact, purpose, paying it forward, deeper than winning bike races," she says. "Yes, performing at bike races motivated me, obviously, to keep always giving my best, but my real inspiration as an athlete was so much more than winning bike races."

Now that she has hung up her wheels for good, Moolman Pasio will plough her full focus into her new role as general manager of Team Amani. She will guide the East African cycling project's women's Continental team, which aims to enable African women to race at the very top levels. The ultimate and immediate goal is to race the 2028 Tour de France Femmes.

Moolman Pasio's original plan in the latter stages of her career was to set up her own cycling team, linked in with the Rocacorba community. However, after speaking with Ethiopian former men's WorldTour rider Tsgabu Grmay, she recognised a synergy between her ideas and what Amani was already putting in place. Instead of competing with Amani, Moolman Pasio was invited to join the team staff, and has even spent time supporting its riders this season, hosting a small group at Rocacorba and spending a day coaching them in descending.

Instantly, Moolman Pasio was gripped by the potential of the riders from Ethiopia, Rwanda and elsewhere in East Africa.

"It was actually quite mind-blowing really," she recalls of her day coaching the riders in June.

"We went out for a session on Rocacorba to do some downhilling skills and it still gives me goosebumps to think of that day because it was just so high impact… The hunger in their eyes, that's something that really stands out to me with these girls. They have so many challenges back home, especially the Ethiopians with war that's looming [In October, fighting resumed in the Tigray region, where Amani's Ethiopian riders are from, following the 2020-2022 Tigray War between the Ethiopian Armed Forces and the Tigray People's Liberation Front – Ed.].

"Two of them have young children and their families are there, but the hunger and just how they were soaking up everything that I was showing them, everything I was saying to them. I could just see their eyes, I could see the sparkle, I could see the switch flick in their brains."

Days later, Moolman Pasio raced with her AG Insurance-Soudal team against Team Amani at the Volta a Catalunya, finishing 12th. Amani's best finisher was Ethiopian Eyerusalem Haftu Reda in 20th overall.

"Seeing how [Eyerusalem Haftu Reda] moved in the peloton, how she was fighting for her place. She transformed her descending just from spending a few hours with me. I was just blown away by it and that's when I was like these girls have it, you know."

"It's now moved from 'I want to pay forward, I want to help Africans, I want to give them opportunity', to saying 'We can get to the Tour de France, we can compete at the highest level'. If this is how quickly they can turn things around, imagine if they have a full season. They can do it."

"It didn't change my motivation, I was always motivated, but it just amplified everything. We need to make this happen. So that's when we really started talking quite aggressively. We want to be at the start line of the Tour de France in 2028 and we really do believe we can do that. So now it's about putting everything possible in place to make that happen."

The loss of Moolman Pasio's presence in the WorldTour peloton will be felt in 2027. This driven rider, with her punchy style and consistency, has been a constant figure in the bunch for 17 seasons.

However, speaking with this giant of African cycling, you get the sense that she is just getting started.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/6/26
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
We’ve made it to the weekend, and now that we’re a full week into November the holiday season is fast approaching. I’m personally brushing up on some fun fall recipes to have on hand for a Friendsgiving later in the month, which is how you know we’re fully into offseason mode when baking is the lede we’re going with. To be fair, it’s not like we’re anticipating much of a hot stove in the baseball sense with the lockout about to freeze transactions once the calendar turns over to December. The league is still rolling out award nominations, with the Silver Sluggers the most recent batch to be announced, and we’ve got a few weeks to go until we know who will be tendered a contract among arbitration-eligible players and who will accept their qualifying offers.

It’ll be a quiet day as we get your morning started. Andrés starts us off with his second look at a player on the fringes of the Yankees’ roster in Luis Gil and whether the Yankees should cut bait with him entirely. Jonathan looks back at Fernando Cruz’s season and hands out our next report card, and then John takes us through James Paxton’s career on his 38th birthday. Later on in the afternoon, I’ll return to answer your latest questions from the mailbag.

1. Would Ben Rice have better odds of winning a Silver Slugger had he stuck around at first base long-term this season and gone up against Pete Alonso instead of Yordan Alvarez, or is it a moot point?

2. What’s a random Yankee from the 2010s that you think about from time to time? (I’m picking Nathan Eovaldi personally, he’s been around the block for a while now but his Yankees days feel like a forgotten part of his career.)

items.title: Ingram stays put at Excelr8 in BTCC until end of decade
How Cyclists Can Start to Run Without Getting Catastrophically Injured
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Pro cyclists keep crushing crazy running performances in the winter – but riders should apply caution before they take off-training inspiration.
items.lbText:
Nothing screams “off-season” more than when pro cyclists start popping crazy running performances into your Strava feed.

Whether it’s Mathieu van der Poel blasting 10Ks while nose-breathing or Andreas Leknessund and Alexys Brunel obliterating half- and full-marathon races, the ride-to-run pivot is as seasonal as pumpkin-flavored everything .

But if you’re feeling inspired to do the same now the fondo season is over and the weather is turning grim, don’t lace up your runners just yet.

An overzealous new running regimen could leave you with DOMS so bad you’ve got to walk down stairs backward and might not be any benefit when you’re back on the bike.

There’s a reason why Tom Dumoulin waited to retire before he clipped off a sub-2:30 at the New York Marathon .

And even for the most experienced runners, the crossover benefit to cycling is still unproven. A marathon P.B. in winter won’t guarantee an FTP personal best in spring.

But what about the benefits for bone health? We hear your cries. Well, some pro trainers have thoughts on that, too.

Here’s what cyclists should know before they take up running this off-season.

We cover what the pros do, the risks and benefits for you, and how to start running without smashing your capacity to cycle.

“Pro cyclist does stupid-fast run” is like a meme that’s auto-posted every autumn.

Riders driven stir-crazy by weeks without structure, competition, and a mandate to stay away from the bike often lace up their trainers at this time of year for an annoyingly fast “jog.”

Adam Yates, Tom Pidcock, and Tiffany Cromwell are among the active pros who’ve laced rapid running performances in off-seasons past.

This year, Brunel of TotalEnergies and Leknessund of Uno-X Mobility stepped up to stoke the annual “cyclist runs fast” meme.

Brunel finished 20th at the Lille Marathon in a smokin’ fast time of 2:26 . Leknessund casually ran a 1:15 at the Amsterdam Half Marathon, despite having run little more than 100km in the past year.

Those are times even the most devoted enthusiast runner would lose all their toenails and get plantar fasciitis for.

Brunel and Leknessund’s cycling coaches might not have been so impressed.

Tudor Pro Cycling performance guru James Spragg told Velo that even the strongest pros tread a tightrope if they pivot to running too fast.

“Those guys can run very good times compared to regular runners because they’ve got that huge cardiovascular base. But they don’t have the mechanical adaptations, and that makes them very average against a world-class runner. And that’s also where the injury risk can come up,” Spragg said.

“Cyclists who suddenly cross over don’t have the shock resistance that’s built in the cartilage over time, or the tendon stiffness which gives you running efficiency. They are mechanical adaptations that you need to get from running,” Spragg said.

“Trying to go too far or too fast without those can be dangerous.”

Brunel and Leknessund appear to have built some running base before they blasted their recent races. Their injury risks might not have been extreme.

Riders who feel inspired to start running fall into a trap of pushing harder than their bodies, pampered by years of non-weight-bearing sport, can handle.

“The one thing we as coaches have in our ‘advantage’ with cyclists coming into running is normally they do one run, and then the DOMS protects them from themselves,” Spragg laughed.

“They run once and then don’t run again until the next off-season.”

Pros “have” to step away from the bike in autumn to reset themselves for the next season of self-flagellation.

Amateur riders don’t have 10 months of heinous workouts and 50kph racing to steel themselves for, but there’s a similar temptation to take a winter break.

Short, dank days, and the end of a season of fondos, races, and adventures can make bike rides feel pretty unappealing.

But if you’re considering taking up running as an off-season replacement, apply caution.

For beginners, the acute DOMS can be so devastating that a set of stairs can feel insurmountable. And more chronic conditions can crop up surprisingly fast. Tendinopathies will flare after even a fortnight of running beyond your experience.

The brutal demands of running are why any good training program will start with weeks of run-walk workouts.

These extra-easy “interval” sessions prepare the body for ground reaction forces more than three times a runner’s bodyweight. But be warned – they will do nothing for the fitness of even a moderately trained cyclist.

For noobs, the time investment is high, and the aerobic payoff is low.

Even veteran runners may feel little benefit when they return to the bike after spending winter pounding trails and tarmac – a recent study found no improvement in sport-specific performance if running and cycling were used to replace one another.

Because the mechanics simply don’t translate.

Even the most souplessed pedal stroke is a predominantly concentric (shortening/pushing) muscle contraction. Meanwhile, running incorporates an eccentric load into a push-pull motion that’s totally alien to even the strongest riders.

Running builds fitness, but it can only be expressed on the bike if you maintain the riding legs.

Riders who want to take up running to avoid the misery of the winter need to consider their longer-term goals.

If you’re in a rush to maintain bike fitness ahead of early-season challenges, look beyond the latest pair of Hokas.

The early run-walk protocols will wipe time off your schedule and do almost nothing for your aerobic capacity.

However, those who gamble by skipping those slightly embarrassing intervals are running toward injury.

Jayco-AlUla team trainer Peter Leo said the inefficiency of “learning” to run should give riders pause.…

items.title: Brandon McNulty Has the Rainbow Jersey. Is Grand Tour Leadership Next?
items.author: ahood
items.content: UAE boss Matxin still believes in McNulty’s grand tour potential. Could his rainbow season bring a chance to test it?
items.lbText:
McNulty took in an AS Roma soccer game last month after winning worlds. (Photo: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty won’t spend his entire season in the rainbow jersey fetching bottles for Tadej Pogačar .

That’s according to UAE Emirates-XRG boss Joxean Fernández Matxin, who said the American world champion will see opportunities to win in 2027. And he even hinted at the possibility of grand tour leadership.

“Yes, have no doubt that he will have freedom and his own opportunities,” Matxin told Eurosport .

The bigger question is where those chances might fall on the stacked super team roster built around Pogačar and rising star Isaac del Toro.

Matxin said UAE is committed to giving the 28-year-old Arizonan plenty of shots to honor the stripes next season. In fact, UAE already backed McNulty across the Italian fall classics , where he delivered his first win in the rainbow jersey at the Veneto Classic .

“People are now talking about Brandon McNulty as world champion, but in recent years he has been leader or co-leader in many of the races on his calendar,” Matxin said.

McNulty admits he will be taking pulls for Pogačar in the big races like the Tour de France, and he has no illusions that his new stripes will change the pecking order that much.

But even Pogi joked that he might be returning the favor for McNulty in a few select races.

For McNulty, the most intriguing part of his rainbow jersey season could be dipping his toes into grand tour leadership.

With strong time trialing and climbing skillset, he’s still seen as untapped potential across three weeks. Matxin said 2027 could give him a clearer pathway.

“We’ve also tried to see how far he can go in a grand tour,” Matxin told Eurosport . “In the end, for one reason or another, the stars haven’t all aligned for him, because I don’t believe he isn’t a grand tour rider.”

He pointed to the 2025 Giro d’Italia as an example of how quickly the hierarchy can shift. McNulty finished a career-best ninth overall at the 2025 Giro while helping Del Toro finish second overall.

“In fact, at last year’s Giro d’Italia we had two leaders, Adam Yates and Juan Ayuso, and two alternatives, Brandon McNulty and Isaac del Toro,” he said. “In the end, Del Toro emerged strongly and consistently, but McNulty could also have had the opportunity.”

Leading a grand tour wouldn’t be that far of a stretch. He’s already proven he can win shorter, week-long stage races, like the CRO Race, the Volta a Valenciana, the Tour of Luxembourg, and the Tour de Pologne.

With Pogacar all but certain to return to the Tour de France and likely the Vuelta a España as well, a shot at the Giro alongside Del Toro could be in the cards.

All that will be fleshed out in the coming weeks in the winter team camps.

McNulty’s worlds win in Montréal stunned many, and Matxin and the other UAE brass were half-expecting Del Toro to come up aces with Pogačar sitting out with injury.

Instead, it was Team USA’s superb tactics coupled with McNulty’s perfectly timed attack that won the day to deliver America’s first road world title since 1993 .

“It was a more open world championships. Because a rider like Tadej, simply by being there, imposes a certain way of racing,” Matxin said. “Brandon seized his chance.”

Matxin pointed to a key moment in the final lap when Tom Pidcock’s pursuit drew the lead chasers within a few seconds of McNulty. Instead of shutting down the move, the bunch sat up, and McNulty had the legs to power home the historic win.

“Brandon won, but if Pidcock had closed those six seconds and they caught him, maybe we’d be talking about [Matteo] Jorgenson having won,” Matxin said.

“McNulty has that ability to hold on. He’s a time trialist, a rider with unquestionable quality and a mentality for winning. When we target certain objectives, he generally very rarely falls short.”

McNulty now has the jersey and the promise of freedom. He said he’s dreaming of winning a Tour de France stage in the world champion’s jersey.

The question will be if UAE lets him chase something even bigger.

items.title: 'He'll regret it': The day Alex Ferguson quit Aberdeen for Man Utd
items.content: <article>It's 40 years since the legendary manager left the Dons after eight trophy-laden years. </article>
items.lbText:
When Alex Ferguson announced he was joining Manchester United after eight trophy-laden years at Aberdeen, there was shock among fans.

They had seen the legendary manager lead the Dons to three league titles, four Scottish Cups, the Cup Winners' Cup and the UEFA Super Cup.

One told BBC Scotland News at the time: "I think he's making the wrong move, I think he will regret it."

Ferguson went on to become one of the most successful football managers in history, winning 38 trophies during a 26-year tenure at Old Trafford.

On the 40th anniversary of Ferguson's decision to leave Aberdeen, some of those at the centre of the events have been reflecting on the day.

The story of Ferguson's defection to the English First Division on 6 November 1986 was broken by BBC Scotland football broadcaster Roddy Forsyth.

He had been tasked by his editor to head to Aberdeen to find out more about rumours that the Dons boss was in talks with Manchester United.

The flight he boarded in Glasgow was filled with journalists - but most were heading north to cover the Chinook helicopter disaster in Shetland in which 43 people died.

Once in Aberdeen, Forsyth eventually tracked Ferguson and the United chairman Martin Edwards down in an airport hotel.

He had called by chance asking to "speak to a Mr Edwards from Manchester".

The receptionist told him he was seated in the restaurant area.

"I heard some voices and made my way to them," Forsyth said.

"There was Martin Edwards and Alex Ferguson, and I said 'are you the new manager of Manchester United?' and he said 'yes'.

"They had a bottle of champagne which they were drinking and Fergie poured me a little champagne in a wine glass, and I toasted him as the new manager."

After a brief conversation, Forsyth got in touch with his newsroom confirming the story.

"Of course, the normal news led with the Sumburgh disaster, and then the sporting news led with Alex Ferguson," Forsyth added.

"It was a big day for news and sport and broadcasting.

"It was one of these utterly memorable days of your career and your life."

Ferguson had led the Scottish club to a period of success some fans thought would never end.

His departure was met with a mix of anger, disappointment, shock and acceptance.

The views of fans at the Pittodrie Bar were broadcast that day on BBC Reporting Scotland.

One was certain Ferguson would regret the move to the English giants.

"It is a sad case for Aberdeen, and I think he is making a wrong move," he said.

Another said: "Ferguson was preaching about having loyal players. He envied Rangers and Celtic for having that.

"In other words, he was condemning his players for leaving Aberdeen, he has set a perfect example he has just walked out."

Fast forward 40 years and fans today are generally a bit more measured on the whole episode.

Sandy Smith, 72, says he has "seen it all" in a lifetime of supporting the Dons.

"It was totally gutting," he said. "To be fair Man United and Aberdeen - there is no comparison.

"After all he did for the club, I was gutted.

"He had sticky first couple of seasons down there, but he got there in the end."

Ian Donald, the club's vice-chairman at the time, described it as a "shattering blow".

"It happened so quickly virtually overnight," he said in 1986.

"From yesterday morning perhaps having the best management team in Britain we are losing them both."

And it was a lot for the players to take in too.

Captain Willie Miller reflected on the time Ferguson left as a period of "uncertainty".

He thought all players missed the manager once he had gone, despite his famous temper.

"You would not get away with it now," he said.

"It was probably what we expected back then from a manager.

"I do not think the modern day player would accept anything close to it, you know, cups getting thrown around dressing rooms.

"He did not just want to win things, he wanted to win them with style. And it was OK with me.

"I was disappointed to see him go, I must admit, I think everybody was of the same opinion."

Ultimately, it was one man's choice to make and Ferguson made the move, taking his assistant with him.

In his first press conference as new boss he said: "I left probably the most secure job in British football with a life contract at Aberdeen.

"There's only one club that could possibly tempt me away from that and it is the only club I ever wanted to go to way from Aberdeen."

Thirteen Premier League titles, two Champions League victories, five FA cups and four League Cups later - maybe not.

items.title: Yankees news: Bellinger and Rice named Silver Slugger finalists
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
SNY | Phillip Martínez The finalists for the American League Silver Slugger Awards were revealed on Thursday, and two Yankees will have a chance to bring home some hardware. Ben Rice, who is competing in the DH position and hit 41 homers with a 149 wRC+, could earn his first award, and outfielder Cody Bellinger is a candidate to win his third. Rice will compete with AL MVP candidate Yordan Álvarez, though.

New York Daily News | Gary Phillips The Yankees would love to retain David Bednar, and bringing back some of their own free-agent relief pitchers, such as Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber, would also be a good idea. However, Phillips explains that for the team to build a quality bullpen, they need to bring in some external options, naming Adrian Morejon, Raisel Iglesias, JoJo Romero, and Alex Vesia as some of the potential alternatives.

MLB.com | Jared Greenspan Greenspan analyzed a player who could potentially be one of the Yankees’ X-factors heading into 2027: outfielder Spencer Jones. To be more specific, he took a close look at his unique swing, its steep path, and how it plays against pitches in the middle of the strike zone or lower. However, a key weakness also appeared in his analysis: Jones’ vulnerability to high heat. It’s definitely worth a read.

Jalen Brunson of the New York Knicks makes his scripted acting debut in Law & Order: SVU Season 28, Episode 5 (“Forsaken”). The show airs tonight at 9 p.m. ET on NBC and will stream on Peacock tomorrow.

Captain Clutch will play Detective Jay Madison (a nod to Madison Square Garden, obvs) across from Knicks superfan Mariska Hargitay (Captain Olivia Benson).  Official synopsis: When a wedding guest is assaulted at the reception, Benson and the squad uncover a secret that changes the course of the investigation; ADA Sonny Carisi’s pursuit of justice is complicated when key witnesses refuse to cooperate.

items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Lampard appreciation at Everton, Glasner sparking Forest fire, Zubimendi and Kroupi in spotlight and Carrick v Emery

Nothing better encapsulates the dysfunction that was Everton under Farhad Moshiri than the idea that an unknown vandal with a can of spray paint could influence the club’s managerial direction. “Pereira out, Lampard in” they daubed on a wall at Goodison Park when it appeared Vítor Pereira was in line to replace Rafael Benítez in 2022. Alarmed by fan protests, the Everton board opted instead for Frank Lampard and, while his tenure ended 12 months later with the club immersed in another relegation battle, there will be appreciation for the Coventry manager when he makes a first visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday. The connection between Lampard and Evertonians was genuine and a factor in keeping the club up in 2022. Both parties will be glad to see the other emerging stronger from those troubled times. Jack Grealish, meanwhile, will again be absent for Everton after his recent disciplinary breach, although the manager, David Moyes, said: “We will be working again with Jack soon.”
