items.title: Look 795 Blade RS: Much improved aerodynamically, a joy to ride, and French but in a good way
items.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
items.content:
£12,000 / $12,960 /€12,690 (in this spec)

6.95kg measured (no pedals or cages, with integrated computer mount)

Black Proteam, Silver-Red, Orange Shift, Iconic Prisme

Campagnolo Super Record, Shimano Dura-Ace, Ultegra, SRAM Force

Scope Artech 6.A, Fulcrum Speed 57, Mavic Comete 50, Look R45S

We are lucky here at to regularly test the best road bikes at the forefront of the technological arms race. Every bike is more than the last, with bold new advances in frame geometry (see the Ridley Noah and the Factor ONE) and aerodynamics (See the Factor ONE again, if you didn’t do it the last time).

The new Look 795 Blade RS doesn’t have one thing I can point to as being a progressive feature. In actual fact it’s perhaps the most ‘normal’ race bike I’ve ridden in some time, perhaps since the last Giant Propel (a bike it bears a striking resemblance to, it must be said), but I don’t think that’s a bad thing at all as it has done everything I’ve asked of it with supreme competence and with a front end in particular that makes it absolutely sublime.

Whether it’s flat miles, protracted climbs, or my boundless appetite for a punchy hill sprint, it’s eaten it all up and asked for seconds. It’s also been an excellent test bed for some of the fastest aero wheels from our latest LABS test, which made for a convenient excuse to hold onto it for a while longer.

As you might have gathered from the opening, I am quite fond of the 795 Blade RS. I’m not, however, enamoured with the aesthetics. It’s not a bad-looking bike by any means, but, insofar as a great many aero bikes now look almost indistinguishable, it looks like a generic aero bike.

Slap a Giant logo on, and you could convince me it’s a Propel, and maybe if I wasn’t paying too much attention you could do the same with a Merida logo and goad me into believing it was the old Reacto 9000. It’s also (shocker!) pretty similar-looking to the old one, just a little fuller in the tubes.

Still, with the Scope Artech wheels in, and in the matte black, mostly paintless pro spec finish, it does have a certain menace about it that cuts through the generic silhouette. I have warmed to it, but turning up on group rides it doesn’t turn heads like other machines can; perhaps that’s just down to the fact that it isn’t as hyped of a brand as many others that spring to mind.

The old Look Blade, according to our own wind tunnel testing, was a bit of a brick in aerodynamic terms. Look makes big claims of a 15-watt saving, which is frankly enormous, and also an unusually specific claim of a saving of 2 minutes and 27 seconds over the course of stage 19 of the 2026 Tour de France, which was the big hilly one with the murderous Col de Sarenne, a climb you should definitely do if you’re ever nearby. This stage was, unsurprisingly, won by Tadej Pogacar, a full 6 minutes and 33 seconds ahead of Ion Izaguirre, the fastest rider on the Look Blade on the day. Lucky he wasn’t on the old one, eh?

We have wind tunnel tested the new Look Blade 795 RS, and at the 40km/h we tested at, I think the claims of a 15 watt difference are somewhat fanciful. Despite this, however, the new Look Blade is among the fastest bikes we’ve tested now, especially with a rider on (how most bikes are ridden). If you want the full monty on how it performed then go read our in-depth write up, but considering the old Blade remains the slowest road bike we’ve ever tested as a bike only, and third from slowest with a rider on, it’s quite an astounding turnaround in aerodynamic terms from the French outfit.

In geometric terms, it’s pretty spot on for a race bike. Compared to the latest Cannondale SuperSix Evo, as I have reviewed that recently, it’s a little more compact in the frame, but with the same chainstay length, an ever so slightly (1.8mm) shorter reach and a significant 15.8mm lower stack height. The new SuperSix already has quite a low front end, and even with a couple of headset spacers fitted, the Look felt slammed. Peruse the geometry charts for yourself, but ultimately it’s bang on for, on paper, an excellent handling package, even if you might need the number of a good chiropractor.

As a coddled media darling, I had to make do with the top spec machine, complete with Shimano Dura-Ace (not long for this world now we’ve spotted the new one), and the extremely fancy, extremely expensive (a £2,500 upgrade), and by our reckoning extremely fast Scope Artech wheels.

All in all it’s a £12,000 bike ($12,960) or at least a tenner shy of that magic figure. You do get a pretty healthy degree of customisation at point of sale. Choose your groupset, paint, and wheels, and you can select your stem length and bar width independently as the cockpit is technically a separate system.

In an ideal world I’d have had the in-line seatpost, and a 36cm bar, not a 38, but if I was in a position to drop £12k on a French superbike I could have those options at no extra cost. There aren’t any options for crank length, however, and none of the groupset options come with a power meter; this is perhaps a blessing with Dura-Ace - generally regarded as being a little inaccurate, but certainly a frustration for those opting for SRAM Force. Red, at least in the UK, is off the table.

A final note on the cockpit, as I did break it… As I often do when a bike arrives, I simply pushed the levers in a bit (because the UCI has no jurisdiction over this maverick) and rode it home from the office. As it turns out, this was an error, and the hoods managed to bore their way through quite a bit of carbon in an hour, meaning I had to replace them.

This was very much user error, and I should have done it properly and used a torque wrench, but I didn’t, and I paid the price. This is basically just a cautionary tale. The flip side is I got to take the cockpit apart to replace the bars, which was beautifully easy; four big M6 bolts hold it all together, and swapping the bars in total took less than half an hour. More than that, the computer mount itself integrates into these big bolts, and while I am not always a fan of proprietary integrated mounts, this is a very good example, and I’d be much happier slinging a big heavy light or action camera off the bottom of it than I would with many others.

On my scales, with no cages or pedals but with the slightly overbuilt computer mount, it weighs a very respectable 6.95kg, and that's with a healthy glug of sealant in each wheel rather than the scant breath of pink fluid most test bikes are supplied with to cheat the inevitable weigh-in. That's good going for a very aerodynamic bike, and sporting 65mm deep wheels. Swap them out for a set of Hunt 5AM Limitless, and you'll have a setup that should be just as aero, but basically on the UCI weight limit.

In this spec, the gearing is a respectable 52/36t chainset paired with an 11-30 cassette. Bristol and the surrounding area are beset by short, steep climbs (it’s like Flanders, but with better food), and I could have done with a 32 or a 34, and this is something you can’t change at the point of sale. .

There are certain bikes that excel in one particular area. The Ridley Noah, for example, was astoundingly good in a race-cosplay scenario for the benefits of testing. Likewise, the Factor Elara on gravel has that mad fork, aero, and progressive geometry, but both felt like their race focus was both a strength and a detriment in some ways.

The new Look Blade falls, in my mind at least, into quite rarefied company alongside the Cannondale SuperSix and the Pinarello Dogma F, as a beautifully dialled all-rounder, at least in handling terms. The Dogma was close to perfect, while I think the spec choices of the SuperSix let it down, but all three have a poise and balance across nearly every scenario that is hard to ignore. Jacks of all trades in the best possible sense, and here at least there’s also a compelling aerodynamic package to complement the handling.

It doesn’t have quite the same lightness of touch that I found the Dogma had. It’s less deft, and a little less refined, but the differences are pretty marginal. The rear end isn’t hyper-short in a way that can leave a bike feeling a little unstable, but this is offset by a wonderfully responsive front end.

With my saddle slammed forwards and a healthy 120mm stem, coupled with the low position that perhaps wasn’t overly sustainable in the long term, the front end traction was sublime and on the twisty lanes around Bristol it was magnificent, picking up a top ten on a local descent while out filming, so not even going all-out. It did a pretty sublime job of making you forget you were on what is an extremely aerodynamic bike with pretty chunky tubes in comparison to the all-rounders it felt like riding.

Descending, whether it’s on twisty lanes or fast, flowy, open roads is sensational. If you want a confidence-inspiring descender then perhaps this isn’t the frameset for you, but much like with the Factor Elara on gravel, if you’re already confident it’s extremely rewarding. Playful, even when the speeds tick over that 55-ish km/h where you usually have to lock in a little more and pay attention. Get up to the 70s and you do need to actually concentrate though, as the playfulness can become twitchy.

It doesn’t greatly feel like an aero bike, fast though it is. Not in the same way as a Cervélo S5 or the aforementioned Ridley Noah, bikes whose is flat out speed. It never seems to coax you into an aero tuck on the flat, perhaps because there isn’t an unusual handlebar or whopping head tube or mental looking pair of forks reminding you that you should be trying a little harder please and thank you. Nevertheless, it barrels along with aplomb, and dare I say that with a 36cm bar it would be a force to be reckoned with.

Stiffness is right on the money, too. It’ll cope with high wattage sprints, but I never felt like I was being rattled to pieces, even over what passes for tarmac in some parts of Bristol. My hands never got booted off the bars and nor did I get bucked off the saddle unduly. It never felt unyielding like the Incolor SSR; there’s still some degree of compliance engineered in, but it’s plenty stiff enough where you need it to be to feel efficient and resilient.

It doesn’t have the feel of a true climber like the Scott Addict RC, though with really shallow wheels it would close the gap despite probably looking awful. It comes with a pretty small cassette (11-30), which makes steeper stuff either a challenge or very quickly dispatched depending on how the legs are feeling, but for your generic climbing efforts it’s pretty excellent here, too.

I will say it helps that it came with a set of Scopes. I have reviewed these wheels, on a Dogma as it happens, and they’re magnificent to ride but not necessarily a pair of hoops I’d want to live with. Even swapped out for different (but very good) new Hunts it was still excellent, so it’s not like the wheels are doing all the heavy lifting. The other wheel options, if you don’t upgrade to Scopes, are a little more lacklustre. The stock option is a set of Look own-brand wheels, or you can pay £700 for a set of Mavic Cometes or Fulcrum Speeds, neither of which are particularly compelling. I’d keep the base model and save up for something really trick, or conceivably just keep the fast wheels you already have.

Much like the Dogma and the SuperSix, then, it isn’t necessarily the best at one thing, but it does almost everything extremely well indeed. I think from a performance standpoint that low front end, a clearly pro derived feature that’s somewhat falling out of favour in recent seasons anyway, will perhaps be the achilles heel. It’s a shame to have a giant stack of spacers on a bike this fast, just from a visual perspective, and I can’t help but feel taking the stack up to match that of the SuperSix at least would make it a more compelling prospect for those who want to go fast, have a bike that handles beautifully, but aren’t as flexible as a WorldTour professional. Or Look could just develop a riser bar that could be bolted onto the stem for a slammed but seamless look.

One thing that I think is hard to cram into the ‘performance’ section, but nevertheless I’m going to do it anyway as it’s my party, is the cool factor. There is a certain about having a French superbike with heritage that’s also, now, very fast too. I’m not saying that everyone and their dog has a Specialized, but there’s something here that you don’t get with the all-conquering but expected performance of a Specialized, the cliche’d of a Pinarello, or the slight facelessness of a Giant. It does in a way Van Rysel doesn’t manage, but seemingly without any detriment to performance.

£12k, or $12,960 in yankee money, is big boy cash. It isn’t quite Dogma F money, undercutting the passionate Italians with a shrug by £600 or so. Like for like you get better wheels on the Look, if you opt for the Scopes anyway, and all else being equal it is definitely up there as a match for the Dogma in my eyes, so plus points there.

Compared to the much-yardsticked S-Works Tarmac SL9 it is a full £9 cheaper, so spend that on a pair of flat whites at the café and you’re talking absolute equivalence. The Look is more configurable, which to me works in its favour, but in the grand scheme of things you’re getting the same level of bike whether you shop from Burgundy or Morgan Hill.

Personally I’d probably have the Look so I could configure it to fit me a little better, and for the aforementioned cool points, and perhaps because I really like France, but you’ll not be let down in either case.

I really liked the new Look Blade 795 RS. It was aided by having the top spec, but like the best bikes I’ve tested, it does everything with confidence and composure without feeling like it’s leaning too hard into one particular wedge of the performance spider diagram.

It handles beautifully and with a playful front end that I’ve adored, it’s very aerodynamic now, you can configure it to a decent degree at point of sale, it’s French without being bad or silly and so is cooler for it, it climbs and sprints very well, the cockpit is pretty easy to work on, and while it looks a little generic you could spin that as ‘understated’ if you so wish. The only real issue I can point to is perhaps the stack figure is quite low, which may alienate a certain proportion of the customer base who don’t want a bad back or a massive spacer stack.

I’m glad it’s no longer aerodynamically equivalent to a wheelie bin, as that would have made this review a lot harder to write and the bike a lot harder to like, set against the manufacturer's claims. All in all, an excellent bike.

While it looks a little generic, it is very far from ugly. The cockpit is very well designed, and there's nothing mad on it anywhere. The front end is low though, which may be an issue for some if you want to avoid a stack of spacers.

I still have some questions about the longevity of the Scope wheels, but in this spec it's basically impossible to fault from a build standpoint for a bike at this price. A pair of the best wheels, Dura-Ace (and not having a power meter isn't a drawback in this case), Corsa Pro tyres in a 29c size, and a quality saddle too. Ceramic bearings in the headset and BB would have been the only think I expect that wasn't here.

Just surfing a hair above the UCI weight limit, as it should be. It's not illegally light, but for a clearly pro-derived race bike there isn't a great deal of point making it weigh 4kg.

Essentially impossible to fault. One of the fastest bikes we've had in the tunnel, light enough to climb with the best, stiff enough to sprint with zero issues, but more than all of that it handles sensationally well.

It's on a par in terms of price with the best bikes in the world. It's basically identical in price to an S-Works Tarmac, but I think I'd be just as happy to have this in the garage as I would the Californian option, and at least here you can spec your cockpit, colour, groupset etc

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I said it for you, I hope I don’t get in trouble’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
New York was so good on Wednesday that the Knicks made me hate them for effectively finishing my 2-hour night plan in 20 minutes.

I’m cool with the 4-1 in the last five, but let’s make it a bit more competitive for entertainment’s sake, please and thank you (I know I’m in the minority here. Alas)

Here’s everything said before and after yesterday’s bullfighting.

On the entire Knicks roster contributing to the victory over Chicago:

“I take my hat off to everybody on the roster, because everybody contributed in some way, shape or form.”

On the Knicks delivering their most complete performance of the season against Chicago:

“That was as close to a 48-minute game as our group has had yet.”

On the Knicks’ franchise-record-tying 84-point first half:

“It was a really good half, in terms of doing what we believe, what we should be doing offensively as our staples. Everybody was really good in those areas.”

On the Knicks’ spacing, ball movement and offensive execution against Chicago:

“I really liked how we started out. Spacing the floor well, touching the paint, and then re-spacing too. Our re-spacing was really quick and really decisive. We had some great, great looks early on. And everybody played well offensively. Our pace was pretty good, it’s something we’ve been talking about. Our offensive rebounding, for shooting a high percentage, was pretty good. Just a lot of good things.”

On Brunson finally making the shots he had been missing earlier in the season:

“He’s obviously missed some shots but he took the same shots tonight that he’s been taking. And, we felt we’ve gotten some good shots in previous games that just haven’t gone down. But the good part about it is, they went down tonight, and we defended. A great game by him as well as everybody else.”

On Jalen Brunson’s unusual endurance and how the Knicks track player fatigue:

“Our analytics guys [chart] how guys play in two-minute increments. Some guys, after six minutes, their three-point field-goal percentage drops. They also can track their movement — how quickly they’re still moving out on the floor, if that slows down or not. Jalen’s just seems to go up every two minutes.”

On Brunson’s toughness and why he must avoid overworking him before the playoffs:

“He’s about as durable as anybody I’ve been around. He’s mentally tough, physically tough, and he can push himself to go… But at the end of the day, it’s going to impact him, in my opinion, come playoff time, so I have to be conscious of not going to the well too much, especially at this point in the season.”

On why he did not let Brunson continue playing after his 22-point first quarter:

“No, because he played 12 straight minutes.”

On Brunson’s ability to maintain his production over extended playing time:

“Jalen’s numbers just seem to go up every two minutes and there’s really no time when it’s down. So, can he play 12 straight minutes? Yes. Can he play 36-38 minutes? Yes. But, at the end of the day, it’s going to impact him, in my opinion, come playoff time. I have to be conscious not to go to the well too much, especially at this point in the season.”

On Landry Shamet earning playing time through his performances:

“The tough part about it is I don’t remember when that happened last year, but it’s more so the reality [that] Landry is playing well. Landry, he played well in the last game. As you guys can see I’ll try to go with who I think is playing well. I’ll try to find minutes for them . . . Sometimes the other guys are playing good and that’s who you rock with to try to get the win at times.”

On Tyler Kolek replacing Jose Alvarado as the Knicks’ backup point guard:

“I said this before, every position coming off the bench is a competition, all the time. Nobody’s minutes are set in stone. … Jose had the first opportunity in our last game. And then I gave Tyler an opportunity in the second half [against the Nets] and Tyler played well. So I’m gonna go with Tyler. And if I think I need to make a change because Tyler’s not getting it done in my eyes, then I’ll go back to Jose.”

On limiting the Knicks’ starters’ minutes during the first games of the season:

“I don’t want to kill these guys because they played more games — if you’re talking about last season — than most of them had in their career. And the offseason was a lot shorter than what it’s usually been. And it takes a toll. Playing (19) playoff games, it’s a lot different than playing (19) regular-season games. It might be a game-and-a-half just because of how physical the games are and the mental stress that goes into it, the attention to detail in each individual possession.”

On the physical and mental toll of the Knicks’ championship season and balancing rest with winning:

“It can be a mental and physical toll that can impact everybody differently. I have to be careful of not overreacting and trying to lay the hammer, especially early, on every little thing. I got to let our guys breathe a little bit and get their feet underneath them, not just from a physical standpoint, but a mental standpoint as well, because we played a lot of basketball last year and we’re right back to it. I also need to be careful in making sure that I’m not overextending all of our guys early. I wanted to use a 10-man rotation. There were a couple of games I think I went to nine.

“I hate saying this — I want to win, I’m going to try to win, but I’m not going to do that to the detriment of our group later on. So, I’ve got to find the balance of how to use my bench a little better to give these guys some more needed rest during the course in games, so they’re not at 35, 36, 37 minutes right now. I thought that helped us out a lot last year. We’ll up their minutes as the year goes along. I haven’t been too good with that so far this year.”

On adjusting the rotation after the Knicks’ slow start:

“We experimented with different stuff and our players not getting it done caused us to start off a little slow. So, to get us on track, we’re going to hold the fort down with a veteran group of guys.”

On managing the Knicks’ practices and playing time:

“I have to be conscious of how we practice. And I have to try to be conscious of guys’ minutes.”

On calling out his players for losing track of the game at times:

“We hit a three, we celebrated the three and they got a layup on the other end… that’s one of the little things that we talk about embracing playing with next play speed, playing the right way no matter what the score is… (by not doing that), that’s how you build bad habits.”

On Dalton Knecht’s offensive versatility and defensive development:

“He’s a scorer. He’s not just a shooter. A lot of people think he’s a shooter because he’s white. I said it for you, I hope I don’t get in trouble. He can go get it. He can shoot from range, he’s got a medium game, he can get to the rim, and he can pass. He’s got to work defensively and I thought tonight, he tried to play within himself and contributed the best way he could.

“There were a couple things defensively that he can do a little better and that’s what he really has to concentrate on but I thought he gave us a nice little lift, especially offensively when he played towards the end of the first half.”

On the Knicks’ improvement despite their early-season inconsistency:

“You want it, but you can’t live and die by trying to have everything be great and-or perfect in a matter of a week or two weeks. We know we can play better. The crazy part about it is we’re 3-1 in our last four. Knowing that we’re hungry for more, and that strive for perfection is going to help us out when it really counts at the end of the day.

“So we just can’t let go of the rope, we have to keep trying to get better on both sides of the ball and make sure that we’re embracing the little things so that we can hit a groove so we’ll be where we want to be at the end of the season — but knowing that we’re going to go through ups and downs throughout the course of the year.”

On giving starters more opportunities to overcome their struggles than bench players:

“Our starters are going to get a lot more rope than the guy’s coming off the bench, you know? And that’s kind of how I look at it. Again, this is a process and I have to always be careful of not trying to want [perfection]. You want it, but you can’t live and die by trying to have everything be great and/or perfect in a matter of a week or two weeks.”

On finding his rhythm and creating offense through defense:

“Obviously, making 3s, but I think making our two-pointers are really important as well. When you have it going, it feels good. Just trying to play off that and use your gravity to make plays. I feel like it really started on the defensive side of the ball, we were able to get stops and get out in transition.”

On using his scoring gravity to get teammates involved:

“When you have it going, it feels good. And then just trying to play off that and using my gravity to get teammates involved.”

On whether he would ask Mike Brown to leave him in a game to pursue an exceptional scoring performance:

“Possibly, but it has to be the right moment, right time. I don’t want to say no because you never know when you’re in this situation, but I just want to respect the game as much as possible.”

On the Knicks’ defensive effort setting up their offensive breakout against Chicago:

“I feel like it started on the defensive side of the ball. We were able to get stops and get out in transition, create a comfortable lead, and I think we played well with the lead for the most part.”

On the Knicks’ familiarity with their Eastern Conference rivals and the advantage of roster continuity:

“I think everyone in the East knows each other. This is our third year now with each other, so you know, it’s rare. That’s one of our advantages.”

On comparing the current Knicks to LeBron James and the Miami Heat’s Big Three era:

“At the end of the day, people knew, when LeBron and the Big Three were there, you had to go out there and beat them. Everyone brings their best against the New York Knicks. You’ve got to protect the jersey, the city at all costs.”

On handling the distractions and pressure of playing in New York:

“I mean, we did it all last year. You’re in New York, you’ve got to play through distractions; that’s what comes with playing here. There’s a lot of pressure, a lot of noise.”

On the Knicks’ ability to accomplish something special by staying united:

“But as long as this locker room, which has shown it can do, stays together and continues to just believe and fall into each other when things get tough, we can do something special.”

On how the Knicks grew closer during their difficult stretch after winning the NBA Cup:

“We didn’t look our best version, and we heard about it. This team continued to fall into each other instead of splitting away and … separating. We got closer and closer.”

On the pressure of playing in New York and how quickly fans’ expectations can change:

“I guarantee you, I’m going to be sitting here rock bottom. I don’t think I’m ever going to be on my high horse, either. We’re in New York. Everything rides on the next game. We go on a 10-game winning streak and the next game we lose, they’re ready to burn the place down. We know what it is. It’s the tough part of being in New York.”

On the Knicks’ short offseason and the physical toll of the championship celebrations:

“We gotta go out there and win games. And we gotta get those championship habits back, because we were away from it for I don’t know how many months. I think it’s a tough spot. It’s kinda like a little conundrum, because obviously we played into mid-June. Then in the summer obviously you’re working out, you’re doing that, but you also are enjoying the fruits of the labor of winning in terms of going to brands, going to appearances. Off the court, it’s kind of booming for you. So, you’re doing all of that, so that takes a little bit of a wear on you. And then you get into it. So sometimes, the body has to kinda catch up.”

On the Knicks’ open communication and willingness to have difficult conversations:

“It’s open. Anybody can step up, whether it’s the [bench] guys or starters. That’s the thing about this team, our chemistry is so good and we have a lot of trust because we see each other putting forth a lot of work.”

On accepting a reduced role and contributing energy even when he isn’t playing:

“[Brown] knows I’m always ready. My teammates know that I’m always ready and am going to try to bring the energy. If that’s not on the stat sheet or paper, just trying to do the little things, that’s something that I’ve grown in since I’ve been here. That really took priority for me.”

On being ready when the Knicks activated him for his debut against Chicago:

“I wasn’t surprised, I just came in ready to go. The coaches said you’re active so that just means be ready.”

On his first Knicks points coming on a putback dunk and making his debut:

“It was great. Honestly I didn’t hear much just because I’m so locked in, but it was good. Pretty much my first play was a putback dunk so it’s cool, it’s great.”

On wanting to contribute as a scorer and defender:

“I think I just go out there and impact the game on all three levels. And I just wanna show on the other side of the ball, getting the ball pressure and stuff like that and going in and grabbing defensive rebounds.”

On staying prepared for opportunities and learning from teammates on the bench:

“Be ready so you don’t have to get ready. Just watching on the bench and talking to my teammates is really helpful and it was easy to get in there and play confident. All the guys out there gave me a good look.”

items.lbText:
Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain flexed their muscles, Manchester United fought back and an unlikely star stole the show for AEK Athens

Still without the recovering Vincent Kompany, Bayern Munich are among the favorites to win the Champions League , which would be their first European title since 2019-20. René Marić’s side produced a dominant display at the Metropolitano, playing Atlético Madrid off the field in a commanding 2-0 win. Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer made the difference, with Harry Kane providing Laimer with a fine assist in his first continental appearance since winning the Ballon d’Or. Bayern remain just outside the top eight, which guarantees automatic passage to the last 16, having won two and drawn two of their opening four matches.

It was also a massive week for Michael Carrick’s claim to the Manchester United job, as his side overturned a 2-0 half-time deficit to beat Roma 3-2 . United have now won two, drawn two and lost none, enough to enter the international break in the play-off places.

Villarreal manager Iñigo Pérez warned that if visiting Paris Saint-Germain “smell fear, they won’t forgive you”, and evidently his players must have reeked of it. The reigning European champions redefined “scoring for fun” with an early onslaught, putting four goals past the sinking Yellow Submarine inside 17 minutes. PSG ultimately cruised to a remarkable 6-0 thrashing, with their five different scorers led by Fabián Ruiz, who scored a brace.

Inter got their campaign back on track with a commanding 3-0 win away at Feyenoord, a strong response to their defeat in the Milan derby. An eighth-minute strike from Yann Bisseck put the 2025 runners-up in front and they never looked back. “Football doesn’t always go to plan, but you have to respond, make the right changes and find a way to get back on track,” Inter coach Cristian Chivu said afterwards. One such change may be giving Djed Spence a greater role. Named player of the match on Tuesday after providing the assist for Bisseck’s opener, Spence has seldom featured in his first season, having made his first Serie A start only in Saturday’s defeat to Milan.

Como continue to win matches, as well as hearts and minds, and followed their 4-1 victory over Manchester United with an even more emphatic performance. Lens were the latest victims, with Como thrashing the French side 9-1. Cesc Fàbregas’s team continue to defy expectations in their first Champions League campaign. They sit fourth in Serie A and the Champions League tables.

Aboubakary Koita, AEK Athens . While far from a vintage Real Madrid side, or even a vintage José Mourinho version of one, Los Blancos headed to Athens brimming with confidence. Madrid had won all six of their matches since play resumed after the international break, including a statement victory at the Camp Nou in late October. And yet, they seemed to have no answer for a player representing a nation ranked 110th in the world by Fifa.

Koita kept Madrid’s full-backs on their heels throughout a tireless 90-minute shift for AEK Athens . Having taken just two shots in his first 180 minutes of this season’s Champions League, the 28-year-old winger put Madrid on notice early on Wednesday. Koita collected the ball on the edge of the penalty area in the 12th minute and bore down on Marc Cucurella. He cut inside, twisting the left-back out of position, before driving a powerful effort between Thibaut Courtois and his near post.

It was the first Champions League goal scored by a player from Mauritania.

Madrid fought hard to equalize, with Jude Bellingham having one effort ruled out for a narrow offside before his clever left-footed finish caught Alberto Brignoli by surprise. The hosts held firm until the 75th minute, when Koita drew defenders towards him as he drifted towards the left corner before spotting a run from his left-back, Stavros Pilios. Koita threaded the ball into the defender’s path and Pilios coolly slotted it past Courtois.

Ultimately, Madrid had too much talent for AEK’s defence. Kylian Mbappé made no mistake, scoring his team’s second equalizer three minutes after Pilios’s effort. Federico Valverde had no intention of giving the hosts a happy ending, powering a long-range effort across goal and beyond the diving Brignoli. Nonetheless, it was a hard-earned winner forced by Koita’s brilliance at the other end.

Koita’s night ended on a sour note. Furious after being brought down as the final whistle blew, he earned a red card for telling the referee to “fuck off”, then remained on the pitch to plead his case.

An impressive hat-trick in its own way: a historic goal, an assist and a red card.

Recent history has cast Fenerbahçe as the ultimate nearly team, finishing second in every Süper Lig campaign since 2021-22. A poor start to the season prompted İsmail Kartal’s resignation, leaving Dirk Kuyt, who had joined the club only in June as Kartal’s assistant, to become caretaker manager.

Kuyt’s first European match in charge carried even greater significance given the visitors: Liverpool , with whom he became a legend.

“As soon as the draw came up, as a technical member of the staff I was really excited because everyone knows how much Fenerbahçe and Liverpool mean to me,” Kuyt said on the eve of the match. “Of course tomorrow will be a very, very special occasion for me. But at the stage we are in, I’m not the important person. It’s the club.”

A job well done for the club, then, as Fenerbahçe stormed back from 2-1 down with 20 minutes remaining. Former Derby County academy product Archie Brown made Liverpool pay, scoring the equalizer before setting up Vedat Muriqi’s winner. The defeat was Andoni Iraola’s first in European competition, although Liverpool remain comfortably placed to advance.…

items.title: The Traka World Series a 'natural evolution' of Gravel Earth Series with collection of seven races, €84,000 prize purse and promise of live streaming
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
After nurturing the Gravel Earth Series for four years, organisers Klassmark have revamped the global collection of races under their direction as The Traka World Series in 2027, announcing a compact framework of seven events, all with consistent prize money and live streaming.

Six of the seven events have been revealed, with Klassmark owning and operating all but one of the events under their 'The Traka' brand. The majority of racing will take place across Spain, with the multi-day Santa Vall by The Traka stage race, February 6-7, taking place in Catalonia, followed by Gravel Desert by The Traka on March 13, which moved from a July slot, in the Monegros region.

The Traka 300 will take place on May 1 as the only distance of three race days with points for pro fields. Two other distances, 100 kilometres and 200 kilometres, remain centerpieces for amateur fields on either side of the series race, April 30 and May 2, and as a set the event will now be called The Traka Girona.

The back half of the series will return to the US at Iowa's CORE4 by The Traka on August 21, revisit Belgium with The River by The Traka on September 11 and then conclude in Spain with the Last Dance, formerly known as Ranxo Gravel. The grand finale will be in October, that date yet to be confirmed.

"The story of The Traka World Series does not begin from scratch. It is the result of years of growth, shared experiences and an approach to gravel that has evolved alongside the sport itself. Gravel Earth Series has played a fundamental role in that journey, connecting races, athletes and organisers from different countries and helping build an international gravel community," organisers said in a press release about setting a foundation for 2027.

"Throughout 2026, this evolution was already taking shape through the development of By The Traka, a concept that connects different events under The Traka philosophy while preserving the character, identity and distinctive qualities of each race.

"The Traka consolidates its position as an international brand, By The Traka brings together the events linked to the project, and The Traka World Series provides the framework for elite competition, with a calendar and overall standings connecting the season’s races."

Unlike the Life Time Grand Prix which has a series prize purse for invited riders only, the open format for The Traka World Series remains in place, with a total of €20,000 on offer to the top 10 overall, split evenly among pro women and pro men. Klassmark will also offer €8,000 in prize money at each event. At CORE4, sponsor River Products Company will double the race purse to €16,000, which will bring the overall cash payouts to €84,000 for races and the series.

CORE4 has been part of the global series for two previous editions, and this year has an appealing calendar slot between Leadville Trail 100 MTB and Lauf Gravel Worlds. The Iowa gravel race has a new venue north of Iowa City in a new urban downtown area of Solon, and will create new courses to mark an expanded collaboration with the By The Traka family, while retaining local ownership.

"Being part of that next tier in the series allows another level of marketing support and other components too, such as our pursuit of a live stream. We'll have 100% control over all the components, it's still a community-based and grassroots-supported event," Alex Buhmeyer, race director and founder of CORE4, told .

"The last couple of years we've had some of the best athletes here. Since we joined [the series], we've seen a surge of top-level athletes. The move into downtown Solon and be able to grow and accommodate more athletes. We roll out the red carpet with our age groupers and youth riders and everybody, regardless if they're pro or not."

Live coverage was promised for all Traka World Series events, though details are yet to be confirmed. Last year organisers launched Gravel Earth Series TV, but streaming on the YouTube channel was limited to Santa Vall, The Traka 200 and The Traka 360.

A modified points-based scoring system was used the last two years, which was easier to follow, and was expected to be in place again to determine rankings. In 2026, Specialized Off-road teammates Mads Würtz Schmidt and Geerike Schreurs came away with the pro titles.

items.title: Elite Square smart frame review: A serious alternative to the Zwift Ride
items.author: Tim Perkin
items.content:
• Up to 80 hours
  • 165- 175 mm

Elite unveiled the Square at Eurobike in July 2024 and put it on sale in Europe in March 2025.

For me, it remains one of the strongest alternatives to the Zwift Ride. Although both products combine a dedicated indoor frame with a smart trainer, their approaches are quite different

At the time of writing, the Square costs $1,990 / €1,049.99 / £1,099. Those prices are for the frame; don't forget you'll also need a compatible trainer.

I've been using one since September 2025, putting it through months of regular indoor riding across different trainers and platforms.

The design of the Elite Square is, unsurprisingly, what gives it its name. I like the angular aesthetic, partly because I have always liked this type of design and still consider the early Volkswagen Golf and Polo among the most strikingly designed cars.

However, I appreciate that the angular design isn't going to appeal to everyone and doesn't necessarily follow the design language of a modern road bike. The Square features a clean, functional design built specifically for indoor riding, rather than attempting to mimic a traditional road bike.

Putting the aesthetic merits to one side, from a construction point of view, the frame is made from steel, powder-coated black and feels extremely solid. The detachable front support provides a solid base, while the rear of the frame connects directly to a smart trainer. Although the front support ensures great stability, it does bring the total weight of the product to 23kg.

At 23 kg, however, the Square isn't something you'll casually drag around the house. Moving it into position was cumbersome, and mounting it to the trainer was much easier with a second person. I did wonder whether wheels on the front support would make positioning easier, although adding them would inevitably add complexity and weight. The other major design feature is the belt drive, which replaces the conventional chain and cassette.

Elite's virtual shifting system manages gearing electronically and can be configured to replicate various drivetrain combinations, including 1x, 2x, and 3x setups, allowing for personalised gearing preferences.

The gear shifters are part of the well-padded handlebars, which measure 42cm and feel similar to SRAM's in the sense that one lever changes the virtual gear up on one side and down on the other. There are brakes, but on platforms like Zwift, they are not utilised.

The hoods have buttons to control your avatar and navigate menu systems, and Elite has worked hard to ensure that these function with major platforms like Zwift, ROUVY, and TrainingPeaks Virtual.

The handlebars connect via Bluetooth and use replaceable CR2032 batteries rather than a rechargeable battery. Elite quotes up to 80 hours of battery life. They are functional and practical, and the shifting feels very similar to what you would expect from a conventional road bike.

In addition, Elite notes that the handlebars interact with their fan, Aria. Practical details have also been considered. The Square includes an Elite T-Race bottle cage, though a second cage or a dedicated accessory holder would have been a welcome addition. Space for items like a phone or towel is limited, requiring users to plan their placement during long indoor sessions.

Setting up the Square is relatively straightforward but not a quick undertaking, and there are aspects where having an extra pair of hands is almost a necessity.

Elite has provided a series of videos that take you through the set-up process, and there are QR codes on the outside packaging that lead to the instructions.

Unfortunately for me, these were covered by shipping labels, so I reverted to using the manual. The manual is interesting in the sense that there are illustrations at the front; then you have to find your required language in the document, and it requires a lot of back-and-forth looking at the pictures, then reading what it means.

The most challenging part of the assembly was removing the cassette from the smart trainer and installing the one that comes packaged with the Square. This is specifically for the belt drive.

Elite provides the relevant tools to install the cassette. Installing the front support was the most challenging aspect for me. I initially struggled to get the bolts to thread fully. I eventually managed to secure the support, but this was the point at which having a second person was most useful.

Once the front support is installed, you will need to mount the frame onto the trainer. To do this, ensure that the drive belt is loose. There is a tensioner near the seat post that needs to be loosened by pulling it down. When the belt is slackened, you can install it on the trainer.

To tighten it, push the tensioner up; this will secure the belt in place on the newly installed cassette. When the frame is mounted to the trainer, you will need to attach the handlebars and optimise their position. The Square does come with a sizing guide that will help dial in your requirements, and there is a key that sits in the rear of the saddle that helps change the position of things like the saddle.

In summary, it is an involved but straightforward process. Fortunately, this is something you only have to do once.

Adjustability is one of Square's biggest advantages over a conventional indoor bike: it isn't built around a single rider.

The Square is designed to accommodate a wide range of riders and can be adjusted to provide a more personalised riding position. Elite states that it is suitable for riders from 152cm to 198cm tall, covering sizes from XS through to XL. There are multiple adjustment points. The saddle can be adjusted for both height and setback, while the handlebars can be adjusted for height and reach.

This allows the Square to be configured to closely replicate the position of your outdoor bike. A nice feature is the fact that the cranks can be positioned to your desired length. In total, there are five adjustable crank lengths: 165 mm, 167.5 mm, 170 mm, 172.5 mm, and 175 mm.

To change these, you loosen the bolt at the base of the crank arm and change the position of the pedal. It's not difficult and is far simpler than swapping cranks. The Square comes with a front support that provides a stable base and helps align the frame with the trainer, and can be set to different heights when installed.

The frame can also be used directly with Elite's Rizer system, which replaces the standard front support and adds gradient simulation and steering functionality. With this level of adjustability, the Square can be fine-tuned to suit individual riders, making it practical for households where more than one person wants to use the same indoor bike

The Elite Square app is primarily used to configure and manage the Square rather than as a training app in its own right. It allows you to connect the Square to the Elite smart trainer, configure the virtual drivetrain, and create individual rider profiles. You can replicate Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo gearing, or select from several preset options designed for flat, hilly, or mountainous riding.

Up to five rider profiles can be stored, which is particularly useful if the Square is being shared between several users, as each rider can have their own preferred gearing setup.

After the Square has been configured, you can use it with your preferred training platform, including Zwift and other cycling apps. The app also provides useful information such as battery level, trainer connection, and current gearing. If you don't want to use a training app, the Square can also be used in standalone mode, with resistance controlled directly from the handlebars.

The belt drive is one of the Square's unique features and sets it apart. Unlike a conventional chain and cassette, the Square uses a belt to transfer power to the smart trainer, resulting in a smooth, quiet pedal stroke free from the noise or vibration of a traditional drivetrain.

Gearing is handled electronically through the Square's virtual shifting system, allowing you to replicate your outdoor bike's gearing without a derailleur or cassette. Virtual shifting via bespoke handlebars: The Square doesn't use a conventional cassette and rear derailleur. Instead, its virtual drivetrain can be configured to replicate Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo gearing.

You can customise the number of cassette speeds, sprocket sizes, and chainring sizes, or select preset gearing profiles. There is also a sequential shifting mode with resistance adjustable from 5–24 levels. Shifting is controlled from the handlebars, which are fundamental to the product. Elite have crafted them to have the functionality for indoor cycling but with the same styling and feel as the setup for a bike you would use outside.

In terms of applications, the Elite Square is one of the most compatible dedicated indoor bike frames currently available. The Bluetooth handlebars have been refined so that they sync seamlessly with Zwift, and the virtual gearing is on a par with the Zwift Ride, which is something I can testify to, having provided feedback to Elite regarding the compatibility.

It also works with ROUVY as well as TrainingPeaks Virtual, which makes the Square particularly attractive if you use multiple indoor cycling platforms. In terms of hardware, the Square is optimised for Elite trainers, and these include the following: Avanti, Avanti Cog & Click, all Direto home trainers (Direto, Direto X, Direto XR, Direto XR-T, Direto XR Team, Direto XRCog & Click), Justo, Justo 2, Justo 2 Cog & Click. Rivo, Rivo Cog & Click, Suito and Suito-T.

The Square is at its most straightforward when paired with an Elite trainer, but I also tested it with a Tacx NEO 2T. The experience is slightly different because the Square becomes responsible for the virtual shifting connection rather than relying on the Elite trainer ecosystem.

I connected the Square to the Justo 2, creating a fully integrated Elite system that worked seamlessly. When connecting through Zwift, you simply select "SQUARE" in the Controls pairing section, and virtual gear works.

In the other pairing screens, I selected “JUSTO 2.” The Elite Square is also compatible with Elite's Rizer and comes with a bracket that replaces the front support and connects to the Rizer, creating the ultimate integrated system. In contrast, when used with the Tacx NEO 2T, when pairing in Zwift, you need to ensure "SQUARE" is selected in the Power Source, Resistance, and Cadence pairing screens.

One important point to note is that it is necessary to replace the cassette on your smart trainer with the Square-specific cassette. Tools and instructions to complete this task are supplied by Elite to install the bespoke cassette and may require a chain whip and cassette tool. There is an important caveat with Rizer. Elite says Square and Rizer should only be used with compatible trainers that support rear-carriage rotation and gradient simulation. Using Rizer with an incompatible trainer can cause severe and irreparable damage to the Square frame. Check Elite's current compatibility list before connecting the two.

The Square is very stable, thanks in part to the front support, which provides a solid base. Whether you are out of the saddle putting down the power in a sprint or standing on the pedals as you tackle a steep climb, the Square provides a stable and reassuring platform.

At the same time, because it is connected to a smart trainer, there is enough "give" to provide a natural riding experience. The belt drive gives the Square a noticeably different feel from a conventional bike. The first thing you notice is how quiet it is. There is no chain moving across a cassette and no mechanical clunk when changing gear; instead, the resistance changes almost instantaneously as you shift.

The belt drive does provide a different feel to riding with a chain; it’s noticeably smoother. I did experience one issue during testing. When putting out high power, particularly during hard climbs and sprints, I noticed a clunking noise from the bottom bracket.

Elite confirmed that this had been identified on some early models, including mine, and said improvements had been made to address it. The noise did not impact performance.

Other points to note include practical things such as the bottle cage. The bottle cage held my bottles securely, although a second cage would have been useful. The problem, however, is finding somewhere to put it.

I would also like to see an accessory holder included as standard rather than as an optional extra. There is nowhere obvious to put a phone or towel, leaving you to drape a towel over the handlebars and find somewhere else for your phone, which is particularly inconvenient.

Ultimately, the Square delivers a convincing indoor riding experience that feels much closer to riding a real bike than a conventional indoor trainer. Its stable platform, smooth belt drive, and virtual shifting all combine to make it a capable and enjoyable option for serious indoor riding.

The fact that your outdoor bike remains free and ready to ride is a bonus, particularly for riders who don't want to switch their bike between indoor and outdoor use

At €1349, £1,299, or $1,799.99 USD, this unit isn't cheap, particularly as you still need a compatible smart trainer to go on top.

There are far cheaper ways to train with a smart trainer. You don't need one of these. And if you are considering investing in a 'frame' option, you are probably fairly serious about riding indoors.

In terms of 'smart frame' offerings, The Square is a good one, but you will need to pay for it. It's a luxury; you don't need one, but if it means your whole family can ride indoors and you minimise wear and tear on your bike, the value offering starts to look a bit more attractive.

After several months with the Square, I still consider it the strongest alternative to Zwift's Ride.

It isn't a copy of the Ride and, in many respects, that is its biggest strength. The belt drive, virtual shifting, extensive adjustability and broad platform compatibility make it a more flexible proposition, particularly for riders who use more than one indoor cycling platform.

It isn't perfect. At 23kg, it is heavy to move, initial setup is more involved than it should be, and there is limited space for essentials such as a phone and towel. My early-model unit also developed a clunk from the bottom bracket under high power, although Elite has confirmed this was addressed in subsequent models.

Those issues aside, the Square delivers where it matters. It is stable, quiet, comfortable, and can be configured to closely replicate your outdoor bike. Add compatibility with Zwift, ROUVY, TrainingPeaks Virtual, and MyWhoosh along with the option of Elite's Rizer, and it becomes a genuinely versatile indoor cycling system.

If you spend a lot of time riding indoors, the Square makes a compelling case. Your outdoor bike stays outside, while the Square provides a dedicated indoor setup that is ready to ride whenever you are.

Testing scorecard and notes

The Elite Square works with the major platforms, it is fully integrated with Zwift and virtual gearing shows on screen. Square’s functionality works with other platforms but as of writing, it’s not integrated to the same level of Zwift. Work is ongoing with the platforms to obtain the same level of clarity.

The Elite Square is compatible with Elite’s fleet of trainers suchas the Avanti and all Direto home trainers and with a healthy range of other big name brands

The Elite Square is fully adjustable so you can tailor the setup to your needs. The only downside is that there is nowhere to put a towel or phone so a secondary table is advised which means you are having to keep reaching for things. To buy the device holder, which can be used for such a thing, comes at an additional cost.

Very quiet as this is belt-driven however, the cranking noise from the frame under load was off putting. Elite have confirmed this fault has been fixed on future models.

The fact that the Elite Square can used with multiple platforms differentiates it from the Zwift Ride. It has extensive adjustability, particularly with the crank length, over the Zwift Ride version 1. However, it has a higher price point that than the Zwift Ride.

items.title: 'I didn't agree with their way of working' – Ellen van Dijk critical of Picnic-PostNL management but says she didn't experience culture of fear
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Former Time Trial World Champion Ellen van Dijk has shed light on the management culture within the Picnic-PostNL team after the leadership was accused of creating a culture of anxiety and fear.

Van Dijk spent the 2017 and 2018 seasons with the team when it was called Sunweb, and described the management structure as "special", saying their methods contributed to her leaving the team after her two-year tenure brought 10 victories.

However, she does not recognise the culture of fear exposed in an extensive recent report from the Dutch public broadcaster , though she accepts it might have existed.

"They have a strong opinion on how to work with riders, and they really believe in their approach. And for them, it's only that way that works," Van Dijk told .

"There's a lot written about an anxiety culture, and I never experienced it that way. The management wanted you to listen to them, but I never was scared of them. I mean, if I wanted to say something, I would say it. But maybe if you're a younger rider, you can experience that.

"I just didn't experience the anxiety they are they are writing about, and for me that's a that's an important nuance to it. Maybe some people did experience that, but I didn’t."

'We were not a perfect match'

During an investigation into the team, and the podcast spoke to 71 current and former riders and staff members, revealing accusations of a culture of fear and a "form of tyranny", with some staff leaving the organisation feeling traumatised.

The report further spoke of a lack of support for riders’ mental welfare and a management culture that feared losing control of its staff and was unwilling to allow riders any room outside the organisation’s decision-making.

Van Dijk’s time at the time came in the middle of a storied career that saw her take 71 victories, including three World and four European time trial titles. With Sunweb, her 10 race victories contributed to almost a third of the team’s total, but she left after two years, joining Lidl-Trek where she now works as a coach after retiring at the end of the 2025 season.

Though the team have a reputation for recruiting younger riders, Van Dijk was 29 when she joined, with one world title and victories at the Tour of Flanders and the Boels Ladies Tour GC already on her palmarès. The equally established and mature Lucida Brand arrived at the same time.

"I had quite some discussions with the management, they have a special way of working, and it didn't always fit my way of working, I kind of knew when I signed there that they are like that, but it was a bit more than I expected and yeah, we were not a perfect match together.

"But elite sports, being at the top level, it is really hard, and you need a special character for that. I think in this team, let's say, the characters that are less suited for pro cycling, they are offended a bit more easily, maybe.

"I think it's kind of part of the job that sometimes at the highest intensities, the highest emotions, people say things which are not okay, and then it depends on how sensitive you are at that moment. Sometimes it really hurts, and sometimes you think 'I don't care'. But it's a complicated subject for sure."

Harder for the youngsters

Picnic-PostNL has always had reputation for recruiting younger riders across its two WorldTour teams and that certainly applied to the women’s team, the 17 women on their 2026 roster averaging only 23 years of age. This has advantages and disadvantages, according to Van Dijk. On one hand riders are developed, but on the other they lack the maturity to challenge poor practice.

"I think they were really good for young riders to develop them and to guide them in the process of developing," she said. "I didn't agree with their way of working, but that's why I left, and maybe I had a bit of an easier position because I already had my place. It’s definitely easier than when you are young and you still are fighting for your place in cycling."

Van Dijk’s time with Sunweb was a hugely successful period for both the men’s and the women’s rosters. On the men’s side Tom Dumoulin was at the height of his powers, winning the GC at the 2017 Giro d’Italia and four stages across the two years, while other riders took multiple stages at the Tour de France among the 31 wins in the two years.

In the same period the women’s squad bagged victories at the Tour of Flanders, Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, the Ride London Classique and Madrid Challenge by La Vuelta among their haul of 29 wins. And both teams won the now defunct Team Time Trial World Championships in 2017.

"That was a surprise, and I wouldn't say that was because of their structure, I think; it was because of many things together," Van Dijk said of that success.

"But they got the confirmation that their way of working was going well, and from what I heard after that year it only became more strict because they started to believe in it even more."

Since the allegations emerged the team have appointed a prominent Dutch sports lawyer to lead an independent commission.

items.title: Knicks 135, Bulls 105: “We’re so back…”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
As the second quarter started last night between the New York Knicks and the Chicago Bulls at Madison Square Garden, Josh Giddey was bringing the ball up for the team from the Windy City. He tried to maneuver through a high pick-and-roll when all of a sudden a large human named OG Anunoby appeared in his path. The Australian must have thought he’d run into a boxing kangaroo, as he was so freaked out that he immediately lost his dribble. As the ball was bouncing away from him, Anunoby lunged after it but couldn’t quite grab it. So Mikal Bridges joined the scene as well for the orange and blue, also diving on the floor to ultimately force the refs to call a foul on poor Mr. Giddey.

Just for the record, the Knicks were leading 43-21 at that point.

The game was essentially over long before both of New York’s high-priced wings draped themselves across the shiny Garden floor, but this is exactly what makes the symbolism of the aforementioned play so much more distinct. The Knicks decided to show up last night. They decided to put it together and be the hard-nosed, all-out championship team we all love so much. Not only for the layup lines or the press conference but for the entire game. They not only cut up the Bulls into sirloins, briskets and ribs, they surely also took their hearts. And announced, if not to the league, then to their fan base, what Keef so aptly commented in : “We are so back…”

Knicks play complete game against Chicago

A critical comrade might point out that it had more to do with Chicago being gone than with New York being back, but this isn’t the day for such rationality. It’s a day of basking in the glory of being a good basketball team and showing it for 47 minutes and 58 seconds, maybe even longer. It’s exactly what this Knicks team needed after sluggish weeks to start their championship defense, and some of us fans might have needed it even a bit more. We all knew they were good enough to win it all, we all knew that there’s a level to their quality that might be unrivaled across the Association. At some point you have to see it, though, and we sure did last night.

From Jalen Brunson to Landry Shamet, from OG Anunoby to Mohamed Diawara, even from James Wiseman to Dalton Knecht, there basically was no Knick who didn’t look like his very best last night, at least not if we ignore garbage time and a rusty Jose Alvarado being dealt the thankless job of driving the party boat into the harbor. Maybe our Finals hero was a bit tired from all the clapping and cheering he did for a seemingly gazillion beautiful basketball plays from his teammates—even if SGA Anunoby gave him plenty of breaks standing at the charity stripe. All in all, the Knicks definitely played at a completely different speed than the Bulls, who only a week ago had raced out to a 19-point lead against New York. Watching this game, you wonder how that ever happened.

No matter what conclusion you might come to answering that question, last night proved that it’s a lot more fun to bring your A-game and best effort from the get-go than midway through the fourth, fueled by desperation. Jalen Brunson danced through the Bulls D like he was Barry Sanders playing a high school team early on and also had no mercy shooting the ball. As so often in the past, it inspired his team to follow him. The Knicks did it all the way to the highest-scoring half in their history, tying a 38-year-old franchise record. It’s nice to be back doing historical things just as they routinely did last season. And just like your starters and stars diving on the floor in a lopsided game, it is a reminder that these Knicks are still those Knicks.

Young Knicks make a good impression

Whether they might be even a bit more here or there could start to show itself in games like last night’s laugher. It is here where younger, unproven bench players like Mo Diawara, Dalton Knecht or James Wiseman will get their chances to make an impression on Mike Brown and the coaching staff. All of them have a ways to go, but watching last night, you at least feel a little intrigued by Mo’s and Wiseman’s physical profiles. Their length could give New York a different defensive dimension (5 blocks between them), and Diawara once again looked like the promising role player he teased last season. The herky-jerky is still there, yet he also flashed strong playmaking ability (tied for the team lead with 4 assists) and defensive awareness against supposedly strong wings like Caleb Wilson or Matas Buzelis. Maybe he can be a specialist for matchups like that, who knows? We’ve got 74 games to see more of it and figure out if it can really be a factor in important games.

We’re not going out on a limb saying that it will take some time before the Bulls get to experience such games again. This doesn’t diminish what our Knickerbockers did last night, playing as complete a basketball game as you dare to imagine. As beautiful as some of the passes, shots or dunks were, in the end, the foundation was the little things, many of which are exactly what a large part of the team’s identity is built upon. Things like boxing out your opponent, making the right rotation or flying hard around a screen. Things like making the pass that leads to an assist or pushing the ball when it truly makes sense.

Or diving on the floor after a loose ball, for that matter.
