items.title: Bianchi’s €100 Million Lesson: You Can’t Mass-Produce Heritage
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Bianchi built a volume-focused factory when it should have protected its prestige. Here is why the world's oldest bike brand must pivot its strategy and return to what it does best.
items.lbText:
A Bianchi bicycle factory worker works on a bicycle in Treviglio, Italy. Bianchi is known for its racing bikes. | Location: Treviglio, Italy. (Photo by James L. Amos/Corbis via Getty Images) (Photo: Getty Images)

Bianchi is in trouble right now. First came the news that Bianchi is out of the WorldTour , and then we heard that the brand had entered into financial restructuring with €100 million in debt after losing €28 million between 2023 and 2025. How did the world’s oldest continuous bicycle manufacturer land itself in this spot, and what could possibly help?

In the heady days of the pandemic bike boom, Bianchi made a big strategic investment. With consumer demand surging and global supply chains in chaos, the brand decided to reshore its infrastructure in late 2021. It was not a small bet. Bicycle Retailer reported a €40 million ($45 million) investment to build a 30,000-square-meter (325,000-square-foot) facility. Roughly 17,000 square meters were devoted to bike production, creating a capacity of 1,000 bikes per day by 2023. The plan would increase employment from 180 to 250 personnel, prominently featured e-bikes in the strategy, and even included a museum.

These plans came from aggressive financial projections. According to Road.cc, Bianchi’s turnover was €50 million in 2018, but the brand expected growth to €120 million for 2021 and an unheard of €200 million by 2022. Much of this projected growth hinged on e-Omnia e-bike sales in the German and Italian markets, combined with a strong internal belief that it was the absolute right moment to return control of production to Italian shores.

As we all know now, Bianchi chose what might have been the absolute worst time in history to bring production back to Italy (or not but more on that shortly). The new Treviglio factory opened in June 2024, immediately becoming a black hole for cash just as the global cycling market cratered. As BikeItalia reported, “total operating costs exceeded €118 million, more than revenues. Personnel costs rose to €10.6 million to support a team of approximately 180 employees… Added to this are the depreciation of the plant and machinery.”

Instead of the projected €200 million by 2022, Bianchi reported €114.4 million in revenue for 2024. The brand saw growth, but nowhere near fast enough to become profitable with a massive factory and debts to service. Debts are sky-high, growth has stalled, and the company is in serious trouble.

If I were in charge of Bianchi—with no actual business acumen, mind you—I would have argued that reshoring production when it happened was actually a genius move. Well, almost genius. It was so close, but it completely missed the realities of the market.

Bianchi is never going to survive going head-to-head with the pricing and manufacturing scale that Chinese factories bring to the industry. XDS is massive, and its products are amazing. Bianchi cannot win that fight, but the brand has something those brands won’t have for at least another 20 years: a story.

Bringing production back to Italy is smart for supply chain reasons, but it is even smarter because it tells a better story. When your bikes are made in the same factories as everyone else’s, it’s to stand out. When you make your bikes in your own factory, in the exact same place you’ve been for longer than anyone else, you have a passion story. Unfortunately, you have to pair that passion with exclusivity, and that was the first mistake Bianchi made. Instead of scarcity, the brand reached for volume.

The second mistake was spreading too thin while delivering unremarkable halo products. Bianchi seems completely unable to make a decent gravel bike, operating with no real understanding of the modern market. On the road, the brand launched the latest Oltre and Specialissima with bold, polarizing designs. Unfortunately, the Oltre was too polarizing and, frankly, not that good. The previous Specialissima was pretty good— I wrote about loving it —but when it was time to launch the next generation, things went sideways. The latest Specialissima isn’t a climbing bike anymore, and it doesn’t really have a personality. It seems to exist as much to carry the Bianchi name as anything else.

Unfortunately, I was not in charge of Bianchi when someone was deluding themselves that the brand was poised to compete on volume with Asian manufacturing. Those decisions were made, and the fallout now has to be managed. In the short term, I imagine the hope is that a favorable agreement can be reached with creditors to get things back on track. Perhaps billionaire Ivan Glasenberg wants to add Bianchi to his Pinarello and Campagnolo portfolio and share that Treviglio factory space? Or perhaps not, but from my seat, I can see a path to at least selling bikes.

The first thing Bianchi has to understand is what the brand actually means to consumers. No one dreams of a Bianchi e-bike, and its gravel reputation needs serious rehabilitation. The core road lineup has to carry the weight, which means the Oltre needs to immediately be very good. It is already a weird-looking bike; let that be, but take a note from Factor and turn it into an asset. Let it look weird so it’s distinctive, but don’t lose what matters: it has to be fast, and it has to ride incredibly well.…

items.title: 'We have already taken some incredible steps, but we are far from finished' – Unibet Rose Rockets add new head of racing as invite to Tour de France targeted
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Unibet Rose Rockets have welcomed on board a new head of racing as Aike Visbeek joins for the 2027 season. The team will aim for a Tour de France wildcard invite next year, after making their Grand Tour debut at this year's Giro d'Italia.

The 50-year-old Dutchman previously worked at Sunweb, SEG Racing Academy, Intermarché-Wanty, and, for half of the 2026 season, Lotto-Intermarché.

He surprisingly departed Lotto at the end of June, wanting to spend time with his family after the death of his father-in-law. Now, he's heading for a new start next season with the Dutch ProTeam.

"What attracted me to the Rockets is that this is a team that is still building and has a clear ambition to keep moving forward," Visbeek said upon signing with his new team.

"I have been fortunate to work on similar projects before, where you really have the opportunity to develop something together."

Visbeek has more than a decade of experience in various roles across several teams, with his longest stint coming at Sunweb between 2013 and 2019. At Lotto, he worked as chief performance officer.

Unibet Rose Rockets chief sports officer Eelco Meenhorst said that Visbeek has "an impressive track record of developing teams and improving performance at the highest level.

"His knowledge, strategic insight, and experience will be extremely valuable as we continue to strengthen our performance," he added.

Unibet will field a largely similar squad for 2027, with only Axel Mariault (CIC Pro Cycling Academy) confirmed on the incoming list to date. Major names including Dylan Groenewegen, Wout Poels, and Lukáš Kubiš stay on board, while several other riders – including Clément Venturini, Odd Christian Eiking, and Victor Lafay – are departing.

Visbeek's addition isn't the team's only behind-the-scenes change this offseason. Bas Tietema, Unibet co-founder and main 'face', is stepping away from the sporting side to focus "even more on positioning the team as well as possible", including media and business duties, reported .

"The fact that [Visbeek] has chosen to join us says a lot about how far we have come as an organisation, but even more about where we believe we can go," said Tietema.

"We have already taken some incredible steps, but we are far from finished."

The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Subscribe for unlimited access to our comprehensive news coverage, industry-leading CN Labs testing, expert columnists, and so much more. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

items.title: Why Man Utd's Roma comeback has echoes of Mourinho and Solskjaer
items.content: <article>After their memorable comeback victory against Roma, can Manchester United avoid a repeat of the past and follow that up with a successive victory?</article>
items.lbText:
It was impossible not to get swept up in the emotion and delirium of Manchester United's late 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

Old Trafford was transformed from a mutinous, baying cathedral of distrust and fury to one of joy and celebration.

Nine games and almost eight weeks is an eternity to wait for a victory at a club of Manchester United's size.

It didn't take Michael Carrick long to calm the mood.

"It's one win, so we're not getting too carried away with things, but it was an important win."

It was a huge result in the sense it bought Carrick some time. But given United's general state, no-one can be sure how much.

And, as was quickly pointed out in the aftermath of the victory, Manchester United have been here before.

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'

As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.

As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable.

Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.

Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.

After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.

While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".

Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.

As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.

Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.

Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.

Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.

Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks

Fernandes critical of media 'lies' about Carrick relationship

One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with £70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December. Given he beat Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games as interim boss.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

items.title: Amflow PX Carbon Pro e-MTB review: More power, more choice and a premium price tag
items.author: Jamie Darlow
items.content:
• £8,999 / $10,199 / €9,999
  • Fox Float 36 Factory, GRIP X2 damper, 160mm travel, 44mm offset
  • Fox Float X Factory, 210x55mm
  • Avinox M2S Drive Unit
  • Avinox Integrated Battery, 700Wh
  • Avinox SL alloy cranks, SRAM X0 Eagle AXS Transmission
  • Magura Gustav Pro, 4-piston callipers, Magura Sensor 203mm rotors
  • Amflow XMC-30 Carbon Mullet (29in front / 27.5in rear)

Amflow carries no legacy pedigree in the mountain bike world. Until mid-2024, the brand was virtually unheard of outside China. Formed under the umbrella of drone titan DJI to showcase its proprietary Avinox electric drive system, industry lore has it that Amflow was born only after established mountain bike brands turned down DJI’s motor partnership.

True or not, Amflow has bypassed the usual apprenticeship: it is already setting the benchmark the rest of the industry is scrambling to match. But does its PX Carbon Pro offer genuine trail dynamics, or is it merely an exercise in raw wattage?

What is now clear to me and many others is that Amflow is now one of the most desirable e-bike brands, thanks to its combination of power and performance. It now represents the industry standard that every other bike brand is playing catch-up to. But does this bike represent more than just the best watts-to-cash ratio of anything going? And can it match the established brands for ride feel and sheer joy?

The original Amflow (launched in 2024) was arguably a more radical step forward for e-bike design, introducing 1,000W of peak power and 120Nm of torque. The latest Amflow bike uses a new Avinox M2S Drive Unit that generates 150Nm of max torque (130Nm nominal) and 1,500W of peak power, which is unmatched by anything from Specialized, Bosch, Shimano, Bafang, Mahle, Fazua, Yamaha or Brose. In short – everyone else.

The Amflow range comprises three new models, all powered by the same DJI Avinox Drive System.

The PL weighs a claimed 19.2kg with a 2.27 kg carbon frame, 105 Nm continuous torque (120 Nm Boost), and 600Wh or 800Wh removable battery options. The PR is burlier, with heavier-duty FOX AWL HD/Float X suspension, SRAM Eagle Transmission, and Magura or Tektro brakes.

The range-topping PX I'm reviewing here has 150 Nm of torque, adjustable geometry (including chainstay lengths and head angles), a non-removable 700Wh battery, and SRAM X0 Eagle components.

You’ve probably heard plenty about the motor already, but it’s pivotal to understanding this bike and I can’t move on without filling in a few more details.

The Avinox M2S Drive Unit is almost exactly the same size as the M1 from the previous generation bike, which only makes the increased power claims more impressive still. Amflow says it’s also quieter than the old motor, while the 700Wh fixed internal battery has greater energy density and will outperform the older 800Wh version of old.

Fitting a 700Wh non-removable battery might seem like Amflow has shot itself in the foot by not giving riders the option to fit their desired battery size or swap out batteries for big ride days, but it worked for me. Without it, the extra complexity of a removable battery would have made the svelte downtube bigger - which not only looks ugly, but actually gets in the way on some bikes, reducing space for water bottles, gear, suspension components and even your knees.

I’d also argue you’ll never need a second battery on this bike. There’s no incentive to swap out the new 700Wh version for an older-designed 600Wh battery that saves just a few hundred grams. But more importantly, the fast charger took my flat battery from empty to full in around 90 minutes, so you could conceivably top it up at your lunch spot or from a mobile power bank.

While the Amflow name is relatively new, the four-bar linkage (Horst pivot) suspension design, with its telltale linkage on the chainstay, and general frame layout most certainly are not. It’s strikingly similar to bikes like the latest Specialized Stumpjumper Gen 3, YT Capra, Megamo Reason and many more bikes. It’s a sensible choice - long proven, easy for engineers to tune the suspension performance, and it leaves plenty of space around the bottom bracket and uninterrupted downtube for a big battery.

It uses a carbon fibre frame that Amflow says has 40 different geometry configurations in total, something we’ve seen before on bikes like the Stumpjumper. It has a choice of two bottom bracket heights, five head angles, and four chainstay lengths. You can run the bike with 29in front and rear, or as amixed wheel mullet using a 27.5in at the back. This adds complexity for Amflow, but it takes away any last-minute buying jitters about which wheel size to opt for.

This is the flagship bike for Amflow, and uses Fox Factory suspension components. It has a 160mm 36 fork with a GRIP X2 damper providing four-way high/low-speed compression and rebound adjustments, and a 210×55mm Float X shock with low-speed compression and rebound tuning.

That’s a lot more complexity than most of us need, but it means you can tinker and learn as you go. Using the smaller 36mm stanchioned fork with 160mm travel, and generating just 150mm travel through the rear wheel proves Amflow has done its research and will appeal to the majority of mountain bikers.

It has a wireless SRAM X0 Eagle Transmission setup, consisting of an X0 derailleur, XS-1295 10–52T cassette, X0 Flattop chain, an AXS Pod Rocker controller, and a 38T SRAM Direct Mount chainring on Avinox SL cranks (155mm on M/L, 160mm on XL/XXL). The rear derailleur is powered directly from the main e-bike battery via an internal Avinox power cable.

Four-piston Magura Gustav Pro hydraulic disc brakes paired with thick 2.5mm, 203mm Magura Sensor rotors front and rear. The bike rolls on an Amflow XMC-30 carbon mullet wheelset (29″ front with a 28H hub; 27.5″ rear with a 32H XD freehub) laced with SAPIM E-Light spokes. These are fitted with radial-carcass Schwalbe tyres: a 29×2.5″ Magic Mary Radial in Ultra Soft compound up front and a 27.5×2.5″ Albert Radial in Addix Soft compound at the rear.

I first rode an e-bike at Copper Mountain, Colorado, in 2013 and spent most of the ride giggling uncontrollably as I whined and wheelied past bemused riders. I then spent the next 10 years enjoying e-bikes in a more sombre, jaded journalist way. But I’m right back in 2013 with the Amflow, it’s a huge leap forward even from bikes with more than 100Nm of torque.

There are five power modes to choose from, and a boost button that will temporarily raise the torque to 150Nm for 30 seconds. There’s no limit to the number of times you can press this during a ride, except the ultimate limiting factor of the battery capacity and range. More on that in a minute.

I spent time in all five modes, and they’re genuinely useful. Set the power low enough and you can ride this e-bike with friends on naturally aspirated bikes… and really tedious a time you will have. I finished a ride like this recently, and proceeded to complete a second powered ride afterwards. If it sounds like I’m antisocial, it’s more that I can’t leave 700Wh of battery power burning a hole in my bike.

Set the power high enough and you’ve got the jump on everything you’re legally allowed to ride on a mountain bike. It will pick its way up the steepest of climbs, and on occasion I’ve used it to winch me straight back up the fall line tracks I’ve just descended… just because I can. And because it’s often the quickest way back up to the top.

Traditional e-bikes rely on frame-and-spoke magnets recording a single data point per revolution of the wheel. The Avinox system pairs with Magura’s Sensor rotor using an optical pick-up that measures 42 pulses per revolution. The resulting traction control is uncanny: instead of breaking traction and tearing up soft trails or scrabbling in the dust, the motor micro-modulates power delivery the instant wheel-slip is detected. Combined with a balanced front-end stack that prevents the front wheel from wandering, you can winch up technical, fall-line singletrack that would defeat almost any other machine.

The riding position suits this setup. There’s a 40mm high riser bar that shifts rider weight further backwards, but it’s not pronounced enough to stop me weighting the front wheel even when the winch uphill seemed impossibly vertiginous. I’m talking about those trails that have you hugging pressing yourself against the stem, as the front wheel hovers dangerously just a few inches from the ground.

As much as I enjoy climbing on the Amflow (and I really do, because it’s so easy and natural), I’m more interested in the descents. The motor cuts out at 25kph, like on any (UK and Euro) legal e-bike, but I’d hazard that most of us are under this threshold for most of the time when descending. It’s often either too steep or too tight. And it’s here I really noticed the beautiful way the DJI motor delivers its power - there’s a huge groundswell of support, but it’s never snatchy or unsettling, and it fires you out of a corner when you mess it up, or up a little rise in the trail to keep your speed up. It’s a lovely way to ride, keeping the bike fast and fluid, and a sensation I’ve honestly not had on any other e-bike.

Fox’s 36 Factory fork with the GRIP X2 damper strikes a sound balance between tracking and compliance, something I love on home trails in Surrey or rocky tech at BikePark Wales. I think the Amflow could easily justify the 38mm chassis of a Fox 38, the 36 saves a few hundred grams, and only fully formed enduro riders will miss the extra stiffness of a 38. Out back, I found that the Float X shock was supple in its initial stroke with a reassuring ramp-up through the mid-stroke. This let me run slightly deeper sag in the low BB setting without suffering harsh bottom-outs on squared-off square edges and drops.

It offers incredible grip and plenty of high-speed support to keep the bike nice and flat on janky stuff, but I did have to work hard to set it up perfectly, systematically winding on damping until I found the sweet spot. I think the Amflow could easily take a bigger 38 fork, which wouldn’t be out of place on a bike with enough stiffness like this one, but it adds weight, which is something Amflow has been keen to avoid on this bike, with its smaller 700wh battery and carbon bar and wheels.

The rear suspension is very good indeed. I found it beautifully supple when you’re charging over rough ground and feeling the trail under your wheels fly past, with the shock free and active and rear wheel eager to move out of the way of small rocks and roots. It’s also controlled and supportive when it’s time to slow it down and pick through rocks or over big roots, and I didn't have a harsh bottom out on drops or landings.

There’s a lot of support when you get to the mid-stroke, and that let me run more sag and drop the already-low BB down even further to improve the bike’s stability and cornering aplomb. The fantastically well-damped Schwalbe Radial tyres add to the grip and control this generates, taking some of the pressure off the bike’s suspension, and my hands. I didn’t like the Trail version of the Schwalbes on a previous bike, but the Gravity casing and Ultra Soft compound is probably the best tyre I’ve ridden in a long time.

It’s not just a low bike, though; it’s also slack (both the head angle and seat angle), and long. I kept the bike in its standard headset angle, because it’s still plenty slack enough even for proper enduro riding, and plonked the bike into its low BB setting for stability. For my kind of riding, the bike felt best with the longest chainstay setting, which seemed to calm the bike down on steeper trails. In the shortest setting, the rear wheel could break loose too readily.

This bike costs more than my car and my personal e-bike combined, and I would struggle to justify buying it. Price is subjective, though, and I think this is an astonishing machine for those who can drop nine grand on a mountain bike. The spec is fantastic - from Amflow’s own carbon wheels to the Fox Factory suspension - while the adjustable-geometry frame and ride feel show that Amflow have done their homework. And then there’s the motor, which other brands can’t touch right now.

That said, you can get a lot of the performance and most of the power from bikes lower in the Amflow range, or indeed other brands’ bikes using the M2S motor. When tested the entry-level original Amflow PL Carbon, Alan Muldoon said the basic in-line Fox shock was better than the Float X piggyback shock on the Pro model. I’ve yet to ride the entry-level, second-gen bike, but if they’ve got the tune right, there’s every chance it could pull off the same trick.

The Amflow has received so much praise online and on the socials that I wanted to hate it. But I absolutely fell in love with this bike. I’ve ridden scores of e-MTBs over the years and this one feels like nothing else. It’s so fast on singletrack and everything just short of full-on enduro tracks, where you come up against the inevitable - the end of its travel.

It reminds me of Whyte’s brilliant E-Lyte Evo. It’s comfortable and compliant in the same way, and absolutely razor sharp when cornering thanks to its brilliantly supportive suspension and geometry that means it can be whatever you want it to be.

It has a lot more power than the E-Lyte, though, much greater battery capacity, but the same light weight. And it’s here that the Amflow really makes the difference for me and noses ahead of other e-bikes: It’s stupidly good fun, easy to ride and move around, and forgives you when you mess up.

I said earlier the Amflow PX Carbon Pro is utterly soulless, and I love it for that. I have no idea who’s behind the DJI engineering, I don’t know where the bikes were designed and engineered, and which hills inspired their minutiae of design. Amflow just lets the power and performance do the talking.

A capable-looking bike that hides its e-bike battery and motor well. Handsome, not beautiful.

It’s solid without being harsh, stiff enough to work at the bike park but still supple enough to ride in the slop. Amflow has been sensible where it needs to - the suspension design and component choices - but hugely creative where it can with the motor.

Astonishing performance. Nothing else out there can touch this bike on the climbs, and it’s both thrilling and flattering on the descents.

A bike with this much power and battery capacity should not weigh this little - at 21.4kg it’s in the sweet spot to generate grip without feeling heavy,

This bike costs a lot of money, particularly when there are alternative Amflow models for less than half this. But it’s subjective, and I think it’s good value for the performance gains.

items.title: Roglič Is Running Out of Time: The Era’s O.G. Has No Contract and Few Options
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Primož Roglič suffers another setback in his search for a ride for 2027 as forced retirement becomes increasingly likely for a modern great.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Marco BERTORELLO / AFP via Getty Images)

Everyone’s obsessed with what’s next for Paul Seixas, but shouldn’t we be thinking more about Primož Roglič ?

The modern era’s grand tour OG is out of contract with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and he’s running out of time to secure his future.

Having been linked to seemingly half the teams in the pro peloton , Roglič’s options are becoming increasingly thin.

According to contract super-sleuth Daniel Benson, a previously muted link up with Tom Pidcock at Pinarello-Q36.5 is now off the table. Benson reported the news Wednesday on Twitter / X .

If correct, that will be another team crossed off the list of options for a rider who clearly has more to give.

Roglič dogged out second place at the Vuelta a España in September before he bounded to an unforeseen European time trial title one month later.

Despite Roglič’s late-season resurgence and his ongoing will to race into 2027, he’s accepted his days might be numbered.

“You never know when is the last [race],” Roglič said last month before he finished 10th at Il Lombardia.

When pressed on whether he will continue to race next year, Roglič said, “I don’t know yet. We will see. We will see.”

Benson’s reporting on Wednesday makes it seem increasingly likely that “The Race of the Falling Leaves” was Roglič’s last dance, whether he likes it or not.

“What’s next for Roglič” has become a saga worthy of its own Box Set.

He was linked to Lotto-Intermarché way back in summer but reportedly turned down the Belgian team’s offer.

Since then, the five-time grand tour winner has variously been connected to Unibet Rose Rockets, Tudor Pro Cycling, and his former team, Visma-Lease a Bike.

Het Laatste Nieuws reported last week that initial talks between Roglič and Visma have been called off.

Unibet Rose Rockets founder Bas Tietema revealed he had contact with Roglič ahead of the Vuelta a España, but made no suggestion of intent.

And the chances of a move to Tudor are looking increasingly slim – though Fabian Cancellara’s ambitious young team does still have a space on its roster.

With Pinarello-Q36.5 seemingly out of the running, Roglič’s time – and options – are running out.

Roglič may be without a contract for next year, but the four-time Vuelta a España champion and Giro d’Italia winner still holds some star power.

The Slovenian will do the rounds as a special guest at the Taiwan Masters Ride on Monday, November 9.

He and a selection of B-tier pros will be joined by a mob of local fans in a ride outside of Taipei.

But who knows, that could be Roglič’s last ride as a pro.

It would be a strange way to bow out for a rider who’s been so definitive of the modern era.

Having turned 37 just last week, Rogla is one of the few survivors of the pre-pandemic age – a time of rim brakes and 175mm cranks – to have remained competitive in his craft.

The riders who finished behind “the Slovenian who was a ski jumper” when he claimed his first Vuelta a España victory in 2019 reads like a pro cycling retirement home. Tadej Pogačar, then in his grand tour debut , is the one anomaly alongside Alejandro Valverde, Nairo Quintana, Rafal Majka, and the disgraced “superman” López.

In the seven years since Vuelta win No.1, Roglič has become the peloton’s enduring enigma, a rider who either crashes or crushes, and who says everything and nothing all at once.

With 93 wins on his palmarès, he’s one of the most celebrated riders in the bunch. Pogačar is the only active pro to have won more.

Roglič is far from his peak. With only two wins in 2026, this was the least successful year of his pro career.

But he’s refused to be pushed out of the picture altogether.

His defiant home victory at Ljubljana’s European time trial championships proves that point.

“It’s beautiful, it’s of course for me, but it’s also for all the people,” Roglič said after he accepted the white-and-blue Euro jersey.

“My radio stopped working. It cut out in the first kilometer of the race, so I was completely lost,” he added. “I just went with my instincts.”

Roglič’s European TT victory was as unlikely as it gets.

He might need to pull something equally unlikely to be able to wear that champion’s jersey in 2027.

items.title: UCI opens voting for its Fans’ Choice Awards with some surprising nominations - Who would get your vote?
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The UCI have opened voting for its Fans’ Choice Awards, which allows fans to select their riders of the year across five categories in road cycling.

Awards will be presented to the five winners at the UCI’s annual gala, which will be held in Benidorm on Wednesday, December 9. The shortlists in each category can be found below, with each consisting of 10 names, five men and five women.

The nominees include Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who has three nominations in the Feat of the Year classification, Paul Seixas (Decathlon-CMA CGM) for his win at Il Lombardia, and Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) for winning Milan-San Remo, though his fifth Tour de France win seems to have been missed.

Among the women, Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) has three nominations across the Young Rider, Domestique and Climber selections, while Vuelta Femenina winner Paula Blasi (UAE Team L'IMAD) was nominated in the Young and Climbers lists. Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) is nominated only for winning stage 1 of the Tour de France, though her other 23 wins aren't mentioned.

World number one ranked rider Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) was nominated for her victory in Liège-Bastogne-Liège but not the Tour de France or her incredible win in Montreal at the World Championships.

And, while Mathys Rondel's nomination in the Young Rider Performance of the Year category for his GC placings at Paris-Nice and the Tour of the Alps is correct, he is also mentioned as finishing 10th in the Giro d'Italia, when in fact he was 11th.

The UCI Gala is an annual event which celebrates the season and awards the best riders, teams and nations based on the World Rankings, with the fans’ awards a new addition, giving you a voice.

"Riders write the story of every season, but it is among the fans, at the roadside and in front of their screens, that it truly resonates," UCI President David Lappartient said. "It was only natural to give them a voice. The rankings tell us who was strongest; the UCI Fans’ Choice Awards will tell us which moments meant the most to the public."

The awards ceremony will be held at the Centro Cultural de Benidorm and will be broadcast live on the UCI’s YouTube Channel.

Want to Own Pogačar’s Winning Bike? It’s Up for Auction in LA28 Push
items.author: ahood
items.content: Pogačar’s winning Colnago and McNulty’s rainbow jersey: Bid for cycling history and help fuel America’s LA28 medal push.
items.lbText:
Pogačar's winning bike is up for auction to help USA Cycling. (Photo: MAARTEN STRAETEMANS / Belga / AFP)

Tadej Pogačar ’s monument-winning bike and Brandon McNulty’s signed rainbow jersey headline a USA Cycling Foundation auction opening Wednesday to help fund America’s push for medals at Los Angeles 2028 .

Fans worldwide can bid on the Colnago V5Rs that Pogačar rode to victory at the 2025 Liège-Bastogne-Liège, alongside a world champion’s jersey signed by his UAE teammate McNulty.

McNulty’s world title in Montréal has given American road cycling fresh momentum heading toward its first home Olympics since Atlanta 1996 .

Officials say the challenge now is to turn that rainbow breakthrough into Olympic hardware .

“Our athletes are proof of what private support can do,” said foundation executive director Molly Pickall. “LA28 is the first Summer Games on home soil since 1996, and we want to arrive with the strongest team we’ve ever fielded.”

The foundation’s fifth annual online auction runs November 4-9, with bidding closing at 6 p.m. Pacific time. Proceeds support programs that identify, develop, and prepare U.S. Olympic and Paralympic cyclists.

There’s already strong interest. Pogačar’s winning bike is already bidding at $25,000. Other bikes, however, are half-price ( at least right now ).

Other items include jerseys signed by Demi Vollering, Kate Courtney, and the U.S. men’s road world championship team, plus guided rides with Keegan Swenson, Christopher Blevins, and Alexey Vermeulen.

Entries to the 2027 editions of Unbound Gravel and Leadville, bikes, equipment, and VIP experiences are also available.

Bidding is open to the public. Registration is free and items can be previewed at this link .

Bikes : Pogačar’s 2025 Liège-Bastogne-Liège Colnago V5Rs, plus bikes from Specialized, Scott, Allied, Trek, Cervélo, and Canyon. Signed jerseys : McNulty’s rainbow jersey, plus memorabilia from Demi Vollering, Kate Courtney, Tejay van Garderen, Ashlin Barry, and the U.S. men’s road world championship team. Rides with the pros : Guided rides with Keegan Swenson, Christopher Blevins, or Alexey Vermeulen, plus a training camp day with Allen Lim. Race entries : Spots at the 2027 Leadville, Unbound Gravel, SBT GRVL, Rule of Three, Levi’s Gran Fondo, Rebecca’s Private Idaho, Stetina’s Paydirt, and Truckee Gravel. Gear : Wheelsets, tires, pedals, power meters, electronics, apparel, helmets, and wearables from leading cycling brands. Getaways and VIP access : Luxury stays across the U.S. and in Cabo, plus VIP access to the 2027 U.S. Pro Road Championships. Sports experiences : Golf at Sanctuary and Medinah, ski passes, UNC versus Stanford basketball tickets, an LA Galaxy suite, and a 2027 Summer X Games VIP package.

Ocon dropped - is it the end of his F1 career?
items.content: <article>Esteban Ocon's career as a Formula 1 race driver is over - at least for the foreseeable future - after falling out with Haas. Andrew Benson looks at what the future holds for the Frenchman.</article>
items.lbText:
Esteban Ocon's career as a Formula 1 race driver is over - at least for the foreseeable future - after a falling-out with Haas led to the Frenchman being dropped for the rest of this season.

Ocon, 30, was already going to be leaving Haas at the end of the year, with little prospect of finding a seat on the grid next season.

But the acrimonious turn of events in Mexico City last weekend brought that forward by a few races.

Ocon now faces a year on the sidelines, with the aim of finding a berth as a reserve driver, as he seeks to rebuild his career.

This is not the first time he has found himself in this situation.

Ocon was also without a seat in 2019 when he lost his drive at what had been called the Force India team after it was bought by Canadian billionaire Lawrence Stroll, who put his son Lance in Ocon's car.

This, though, feels like it has more potential finality about it. Not least because, 10 years into his career in F1, Ocon is well known within the sport for both his competitive level and his approach.

He's been around the block a few times. His career has not been especially stellar. He has a reputation for falling out with teams and team-mates. And there is a new generation breaking through in F1, led by new world champion Kimi Antonelli.

Ocon dropped by Haas for rest of season after row

Ocon denies reports of physical altercation behind dropping

The catalyst for Ocon's departure from Haas was a falling-out with team principal Ayao Komatsu after Friday practice in Mexico City last weekend.

Exactly what led to him being dropped is unknown. No-one is talking, not even off the record, and lawyers are now involved.

What is known is that Ocon objected over the team radio while in the car to being told by his engineer Laura Mueller that they were switching his run plan from using soft tyres for his race-simulation run to mediums.

Ocon said to Mueller: "No, no. I wanted the soft. Don't do that to me. Come on."

It seems the argument carried on after the session with Komatsu. The announcement that he was dropped for the weekend came on Saturday morning.

Later that day, Ocon put out a statement on social media admitting "a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved" but adding that he "categorically rejected any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature".

That followed a report in France's L'Equipe newspaper saying a meeting between Komatsu and Ocon "ended abruptly, perhaps even physically".

Haas said nothing more over the weekend in Mexico but on Tuesday evening put out what was already being seen as the inevitable announcement that he would not drive for the team again.

Haas had already run out of patience with Ocon long before Mexico City but whatever happened there was serious enough that Komatsu felt the relationship had to end on the spot.

The decline of Ocon's time with Haas has echoes of previous experiences.

Ocon has been beaten by team-mate Oliver Bearman over his two seasons at Haas, just as he was outpaced by Pierre Gasly and before him Fernando Alonso at Alpine, and Daniel Ricciardo before that when the team was known as Renault.

When Haas signed Ocon, his reputation was such that many were surprised they had taken him. Komatsu felt he could make it work.

But the team began to notice a pattern. When Ocon was struggling, he would become defensive and blame the team and car. Tensions would rise and the team felt there was a lack of accountability from the driver.

There were also clashes with his team-mate, for example in Monaco practice when they got in each other's way and Bearman ended up calling Ocon "an idiot" over the radio.

They also crashed into each other towards the end of the British Grand Prix last year.

Competitive tensions between team-mates are common in F1. A driver's team-mate is also their biggest rival - the only person with the same equipment so the only driver against which they can be directly measured.

The parallel need to work together to benefit the team's overall prospects can be an uncomfortable ask in such circumstances.

It's a problem that is causing tension at Ferrari between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, for example, as was also seen in Mexico.

But over the years, Ocon has built an unenviable reputation for both these sides of his character. To outsiders, this can be surprising because he is charm personified with the media, a delight to deal with.

He and Gasly - who were childhood friends before falling out nearly 20 years ago - crashed twice together at Alpine. The end of their two seasons together was the first occasion on which Ocon was released before the end of the season, dropped with one race to go.

Alonso and Ocon also fell out and the Spanish icon did not trouble to hide his distaste for his team-mate's behaviour at times. Ocon also had on-track clashes and team radio disputes with Sergio Perez when at Force India.

Alpine also saw the same pattern as did Haas more recently in terms of self-awareness and accountability.

Alonso put in a starring performance in wet qualifying in Canada in 2022 and stuck his midfield Alpine on the front row alongside Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

That lap was 1.6 seconds faster than Ocon's and team insiders say he simply could not accept that he had been that much slower.

Ocon is said to have insisted there must have been something wrong with his car and continued to do so for several races. The team checked and checked and there was nothing wrong. It was just Alonso doing what great drivers sometimes do and redefining perceptions of what was possible.

All drivers complain. It's part of their make-up. Their motivation comes from believing they can be the best, and finding weaknesses in the car and improving them is their job and how they make themselves and the team more competitive.…

items.title: Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro review: A modern aero package but it badly needs a change of seatpost
items.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
items.content:
7.3kg(cages, no pedals or computer mount)

SRAM Red, Shimano Dura-Ace, Ultegra

Scope x Atten Artech 6.A+

We first saw the new Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro back in August 2025 for a wind tunnel test when we had a paintless, lacquerless, menacing looking thing that seemed fresh off the factory floor. It was somewhat overshadowed that day by us also having a prototype version of the Factor ONE in the tunnel (yes, we were very smug), but nevertheless it caused enough of a stir at the time and hence to have at least piqued my interest.

Fastforward a year, and in order to review it properly, I took it on an extended trip home to Cornwall to see my family, where I sniffed out some familiar roads to calm my soul on the clifftops, and a few fresh sections to hunt out rare flat roads, where it does tend to shine. It is a fabulous place to ride, but absolutely murderous if you want an easy day out.

Reviewing it as I did straight after hopping off the fabulous Look 795 Blade RS - to be published in the coming days - left it with a tough act to follow, and one it didn’t quite manage to live up to. It certainly isn’t without merit though, and while I don’t necessarily think it’s quite up there with the absolute cream of the best road bikes (or indeed the best aero road bikes), it is certainly a good bicycle, and may well suit your tastes more than it does mine. Ultimately the front end felt a little languid for my tastes, but more presingly the combination of a slack-ish seat tube angle and a 20mm setback seat post stuck me in what felt like a rather old school position out of step with the modern era.

As always, let's tackle the subjective subject of how the thing looks first; I’m a fan. It manages to toe the line of looking hyper-modern without going absolutely bananas like the Factor ONE, with clear cues from TT bike design. Those hefty, extremely dropped seat stays would be just at home on the brand’s triathlon machines. Ridley also helped everyone out by normalising massive headtubes with the Noah Fast 3.0, something the Nitrogen Pro has up front to go with a relatively wide-set fork that’ll handle 34mm as measured tyres, which is a capacity matched at the back end.

While it can handle a 34 it comes with 30c Vittoria Corsa Pros on Scope Artech 6.A wheels, but not the standard set that I had the pleasure of riding on the Look Blade; these are a collaboration with Scope and Atten, Argon’s in-house componentry brand, and the extremely fast wheels have been reshaped to better suit the 30mm tyres and to better interact with the frameset, all while keeping the Scope hubs and that eye-catching fish scale texture. In reality they feel no different to the standard Artechs, but it is heartening to know they’ve at least been optimised to this machine in particular.

Back up front and you get the same CHB-01 cockpit as is found on the brand’s Anti Matter aero gravel bike that my colleague Tom loved so much. This you can spec when you buy it in either a 36cm or a 38cm width, and with a choice of stem lengths from 80-130mm at no extra charge.

What you cannot do is spec a zero offset seatpost, which is something I believe you should not only to do but also something you do. I’ll go into the why in a sec, but if you do want to do this it’ll cost you a cool £225.

Geometrically I do want to start at the back end. The seat post is pretty set back; 1 full degree slacker than the Look Blade. This is compounded by having a full 20mm setback seatpost, rather than a 13mm on the Look. It is the same as on a Tarmac however, though again with a less severe seatpost setback from Specialized.

Without boring you too much with maths, for my saddle height a 1 degree change in seat tube angle (STA) equates to roughly 13mm of increased saddle setback. Add in the 7mm differential in the seat posts and the Argon puts me a full 20mm further behind the BB; potentially manageable if you run your saddle in the middle of the rails but as someone who has theirs slammed forwards I would have needed a costly swap.

This is all compared to somewhat ‘normal’ geometry bikes. The seat tube angle is 1.5 degrees slacker than a progressive Ridley Noah, and a full three degrees slacker than the Factor ONE, though these are a lot more radical and not everyday machines.

Before I jump two-footed into the aerodynamics, it’s worth remembering the Nitrogen comes in two guises; the Pro, which I have with a lighter, stiffer carbon layup and more pricey build options, and the standard model with lower tier components and carbon, but ultimately the same aerodynamic shape.

With a rider on, at the time of testing it proved to be reasonably fast. Since then, though, we have been fortunate enough to test a load of other new releases, and it isn’t quite as fast as many of them, now sitting around ⅔ of the way down our power rankings of road bikes. While you should obviously read all of our wind tunnel content, and the one pertaining to the test in which the Nitrogen Pro was included, it’s worth bearing in mind that while ‘bottom third’ sounds bad, it is only shipping 7.5 watts to a Cervélo S5 in reality. If you need every watt then this may be of concern to you, but it’s perfectly plausible you could make this up elsewhere, though you could also make up that deficit elsewhere have a faster bike.

It’s easy to perhaps look at ‘bottom third in the wind tunnel rankings’ and conclude that this is a slow bike, but it isn’t really. Seven and a half watts is measurable, though only barely perceptible, and on the flats the Nitrogen Pro feels very much at home once you settle into a decent position, though as with so much of the performance of the machine the thing that seems to be holding it back is mostly down to the position it puts you in.

Having a relatively slack seat tube angle combined with a 20mm setback post means you do feel like you’re hanging off the back of the bike. On the flats, while the bike is certainly aero enough, it lacks that feeling of efficiency that comes with being more over the front of the bike. My hips felt impinged, and more than anything else it just felt quite old school.

On the flat it lacked that feeling of biomechanical efficiency (though it felt aerodynamically so), and on the climbs where your weight is naturally going to be further back I felt I had to spend more time on the tops than in the hoods just because that’s where my weight fell. When out of the saddle, either on climbs or in a sprint, these problems dissipated immediately, but that isn’t a sustainable solution. A shorter stem may have helped a touch, but only in terms of the overall reach and not what’s going on at the hips. Basically it needs a zero offset seatpost, and I think you should factor it into the cost of the machine.

I don’t think I’m alone; I did a basic straw poll (Instagram stalk) of Argon sponsored athletes. Chris Hall, Rasmus Bøgh Wallin, Linus Østdal, and the riders from Team Cranks appear to be on zero setback posts. It isn’t exclusive, and some other athletes weren’t, but from what I can see from a brief search it seems the majority are opting for the option to get them over the front of the bike.

Up front I found the fact my weight was off the back more than I’d like, combined with a slacker head tube angle (0.8º slacker than Tarmac, for example) meant the front end felt a little more languid and slow than I’d like, particularly at slow speeds. Moreover, being over the back means less weight over the front wheel, meaning reduced front end grip. This is, again, solvable with a costly seatpost swap, though only to a point; the head angle ain’t going to change. That being said, if you want a road bike that errs towards stability rather than waspish agility then this could well be a machine for you. On the twisty lanes of Cornwall I often found myself wishing I was on something a little more reactive, but on the flip side if you relish longer, steadier efforts on flat or rolling terrain (once you lock the position in) I think this would be a very decent machine.

At 7.5kg in this spec it’s not a superlight hillclimb machine but there’s a lot of carbon in the frame, forks and in those deep Scope wheels. It doesn’t have the immediacy of acceleration on steeper gradients that you get with bikes around the UCI weight limit (or below), but it’s also not absolutely leaden either. Certainly one more for fast, rolling terrain but if anyone tells me they can’t bear to ride a 7.5kg machine in the mountains I will tell them to go and touch some grass.

Sprints… now we’re talking. That super-compact rear triangle with large, boxy stays in combination with a bottom bracket shell that’s tall enough to sit proud of the outer front chainring just gobble up high wattage efforts and there’s no concerning play in the cockpit at all. I’d have like the tops to sweep forward a little sooner; the right angle transition is quite sharp and can sometimes leave your forearms contacting the bars when you're sprinting in the drops, particularly uphill, but it’s a minor quibble, and not something I cared too much about while bagging a few local, extremely low hanging ego-massaging KOMs.

The Nitrogen Pro, in this spec at least, is a funny old beast from a value perspective and is a little like the Force-equipped Factor Elara I reviewed recently. Everything besides the groupset is top drawer and as you would get on the best-of-the-best model, so you can look at it two ways: either you’re getting basically the performance of a £12,500 bike for £9,500 ($10,499), where a saving of three thousand pounds to Dura-Ace is significant, or you can look at it as £9.5k being a lot for an Ultegra-spec bike. An Ultegra Specialized Tarmac (not the S-Works, which this ‘Pro’ Nitrogen is more akin to) is £3.5k cheaper, but has less fizzy wheels, a separate cockpit, and it doesn’t say S-Works on the downtube.

Personally I actually like this new trend of top tier bikes but with a downrated groupset. Aside from weight, Ultegra is basically indistinguishable from Dura-Ace and Force is essentially the same as Red so it saves a huge wad of cash for a negligible performance hit.

Setback seatpost aside, as this is a problem that I think can be alleviated at a small cost, I think it accounts for itself reasonably well. Extremely fast wheels tuned to the frame and tyres, which themselves are a modern 30c width and not a cheaper option to bring the price down. A decent cockpit, and a stiff package that is pretty aerodynamic in the grand scheme of things, even if it isn’t world beating.

As tested I think there’s a lot to be positive about with the Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro. It’s stiff, an excellent sprinter, and while the handling isn’t lively enough for my liking it is certainly acceptable if you prefer something a little more stable and forgiving rather than hair raising and spicy. I think it’s a bike that, with a change of seatpost that I think is more of a necessity than an option despite the added cost, would be a fine mile munching fast bike for rolling and flat terrain.

I think if you’re looking for something of a do-it-all fast bike then you will perhaps have a better time with something with more of an all-rounder feel.

Looks good. Under the space age looks there isn't a great deal groundbreaking going on however, but neither is there anything crazy and superfluous.

Just a groupset away from top spec. Own brand Scopes are fun, that's for sure.

Perfectly acceptable for a chunky aero bike with big wheels.

The aero is decent in the grand scheme of things, though not world beating, but the geometry has too many implications for me to have truly fallen in love with the thing.

Top tier but with a step down in groupset can be viewed a couple of ways. I think it's a good entry point into superbike performance, but it's not an absolute bargain. Also you have to buy a new seatpost if you want an inline.

items.lbText:
Madrid hope to bring in forward during January

United to consider legal action if they feel rules broken

Real Madrid are closing in on signing JJ Gabriel, though Manchester United will consider legal action if the club believe any rules have been broken.

Madrid have offered the 16-year-old forward a multi-year contract and, subject to final talks, hope to bring him to the club in January. Gabriel is registered with United’s academy until the end of the season and it is understood the club have yet to be contacted by the player’s camp or Madrid regarding the proposed move.

Madrid intend to sign Gabriel via a Fifa loophole that allows clubs in the European Union to tie down young players to professional contracts if they have an EU passport, which Gabriel is eligible to acquire through both his parents.

Fifa would have to sign this off and United are on alert regarding any potential breach of regulations. A compensation fee would be due to United if Gabriel joined Madrid or any other team. Madrid have been approached for comment.

Gabriel walked out on United in September and is believed to be training in Spain. A move to Madrid offers the prospect of progression to senior football via their B team, Castilla, who play in the regionalised Spanish third tier.

Gabriel played in a pre-season friendly for United against Atlético Madrid in Stockholm in August at the age of 15 and had been training with the first team. If he had not informed United of his wish to depart , he would have been in Michael Carrick’s squad for the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat by Brighton on 16 September. Had Gabriel featured, he would have become the youngest player in the club’s history.

Gabriel last season became the youngest winner of United’s academy player of the year award and was the Premier League’s Under-18 player of the season.

Vingegaard’s Dilemma: Chase Another Giro or Risk Everything Against Pogačar?
items.author: ahood
items.content: Analysis: The Giro looks made for Vingegaard. But would defending pink leave him running on fumes against Pogačar at the Tour de France?
items.lbText:
Will Vingegaard return to the Giro or bet everything on the Tour? (Photo: Getty Images)

The Giro d’Italia just gave Jonas Vingegaard plenty of reasons to return in 2027 with a route that keeps pointing uphill.

A mountain time trial, the Mortirolo and Gavia, and a penultimate showdown on Monte Zoncolan serve up the defending champion a near-perfect course to defend pink as Visma-Lease a Bike maps out his return from a season-ending crash.

The Tour de France ? Some are calling it the Anti-Pogačar Tour , but in many ways, it looks even less inviting for Vingo.

With just three summit finishes and 71km of individual time trialing, the 2027 Tour offers fewer chances for the Dane to turn the screws with his Pogi-killer climbing power that delivered his two yellow jerseys.

So heading into the winter team camps, Visma and Vingegaard face a season-deciding quandary.

Would another run at pink give him a better chance of winning a grand tour in 2027 before another July clash with Tadej Pogačar ?

Or would another Giro take too much out of him and leave him empty in his pursuit of yellow?

The urgent question facing the Visma brain-trust now is how to win another grand tour while also giving Vingegaard his best shot at beating Pogačar.

Vingegaard is being squeezed from all directions as the 2026 season is a wrap.

He’ll be 30 in December, Pogačar remains his bête noire , and a new generation of GC riders is nipping at his heels.

King Pog keeps raising the bar in front of him, and after signing a blockbuster contract extension , he isn’t going anywhere. Behind him, Remco Evenepoel , Isaac del Toro, and Paul Seixas are pumping new hype and ambition into the grand tour conversation.

The Dane who twice beat Pogačar at the Tour now finds himself defending his place as the Slovenian’s most dangerous rival.

Vingegaard boasts four grand tour victories, yet some are already writing him off as the best candidate to crack the Pogačar code.

That’s a strange place to be for someone who ran away with the pink jersey just a few months ago.

And it puts huge pressure on Visma and Vingegaard for the choices they have to make for 2027.

Another pink jersey would underline how good he still is. A third yellow would silence those already writing him off.

So far, neither Vingegaard nor his team is giving much away.

Visma’s official reaction Tuesday to the Giro route offered zero clues. Head of racing Marc Reef praised the course without revealing the team’s plans for 2027.

“To win this Giro d’Italia, you need to have a wide range of qualities. That makes it a really exciting challenge,” Reef said. “We will study the route carefully before putting together the best possible plan.”

This year, Visma and Vingegaard took plenty of heat for attempting the Giro-Tour double.

The first part worked like a charm, with Vingegaard riding away with pink to complete the grand tour sweep.

The Tour went off the rails when he gave up time to Pogačar in the first week and then crashed out on stage 15 with a broken clavicle. He hasn’t raced since.

Team boss Richard Plugge told TV2 after the Tour reveal last month that the yellow jersey remains the central goal for the Killer Bees.

Whether a Giro defense fits into that calculation remains the big question.

Never one to go over the top on social media or give too many interviews, Vingo is leaving everyone guessing about his grand tour plans. No decisions have been announced.

Vingo remains the only rider to beat Pogačar at the Tour, winning in 2022 and 2023. Since then, the Slovenian has been unstoppable with three straight yellow jerseys, but Vingegaard has never given up.

Yet some are already suggesting that he will have a hard time even hitting the Tour podium in 2027 on a course that, on paper, doesn’t favor his strengths.

Ex-pro Michael Rasmussen believes the time trial-heavy, summit-light Tour route reflects the evolving hierarchy inside the elite men’s peloton.

“I don’t think ASO still sees Vingegaard as Pogačar’s main challenger,” Rasmussen said on Viaplay . “I see more potential in the riders coming up behind him.”

Yet fewer summit finishes don’t mean Vingegaard won’t a fighting chance for yellow.

He’s not that bad at time trialing, and the Tour still includes a late showdown on Col du Portet featuring the Tourmalet and 5,400m of climbing. That’s Vingegaard’s happy place.

And who could have guessed Pogačar would have crashed out of the Vuelta a España?

Visma remains one of the most successful teams of the decade, with grand tour victories hard-wired into its DNA. It won’t give up on yellow easily.

The ultimate question for Vingegaard and Visma is what matters more: winning another Giro or going all in for a third yellow jersey?

That could make for a few sleepless nights inside the Visma bus.

There’s another wrinkle: This year’s Giro-Tour bet ended without a clear resolution for the brain-trust inside the Visma bus.

Visma won the opening team time trial in Barcelona, but Vingegaard steadily lost time and then crashed out two weeks later at the foot of the Alps. And even though he was already four minutes-plus behind Pogačar, the team’s data wizards never got the final week of racing to complete their assessment.

Missing from much of this discussion is Vingegaard himself.

The last official team update came on August 17, when Visma confirmed Vingegaard wouldn’t race again this year. Since then, it’s been crickets and his 2027 program remains under wraps.

It’s hard to imagine Vingo not racing the Tour.

He’s Visma’s marquee grand tour leader, and winning the yellow jersey remains the assignment. And King Pog already confirmed where he will be in July.

Would going back to the Giro be read as waving the white flag for July? Some will inevitably see it that way.

But betting everything on the Tour and coming back empty-handed carries its own risk.

Repeating the double in 2027 would come with the same risk and potential reward.…

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’m a little excited that we’re struggling’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
New York hosts the 1-6 Bulls tonight for their second game in a week after beating them last Wednesday.

Chicago is not a team the Knicks should be too worried about, but hey, this is a matchup between sub-.500 teams, so who knows what will happen then and there.

Here’s some of what we heard from the Knicks heading into today’s game.

On a mediocre start to the season:

“Everything can get better… I’m not pissed about the start or upset about the start. There’s a part of me… I’m a little excited that we’re struggling. I want to see if we, right now, can figure it out.

“When you go through the offseason that we went through, everybody celebrates you the way that this lovely city did and the fans of the New York Knicks did, you want to be shaken and brought back to earth right away when the season starts because that grounds you.

“Right now, because we’re not playing our best basketball, we’re seeing some of the challenges that we need to work on. Right now we could be winning games, but it could be false reality.”

On Jalen Brunson’s early-season shooting struggles:

“He’s taking the same shots as in the past. In my opinion, he’s just missing shots. He’s taking the right shots. I think all our guys are, for the most part, taking the right shots. Right now, they’re not going in. And that can be for this reason, that reason, I don’t know, and I’m not going to try to overanalyze it. As long as they keep taking the right shots, keep working on the shots, I think eventually they’re gonna fall sooner than later.”

On the NBA’s best shooters’ slumps:

“It happens. It happens to the best of them because everybody is definitely human and every human has their ups and their downs when it comes to shooting. That’s why we have to keep embracing the little things, because they’re not gonna always fall.”

On Landry Shamet’s natural ability to create opportunities through off-ball movement:

“You could drill it, and guys will pick up on it, but you can tell (Shamet) is a natural with it.”

On the explanation for his unusually poor shooting percentages to start the season:

“Missing shots. I normally make.”

On whether his offseason wrist surgery has affected his shooting:

On Landry Shamet’s ability to create defensive closeouts:

“He creates great closeouts, whether he’s shooting or catching. He has a good knack for it.

“It’s just how he operates. He just finds the right windows, whether it’s benefiting him or someone else.”

On Jordan Clarkson’s role:

“He has a professionalism about it. For a person who is willing to do that — he makes our team better. Great person, great teammate. Off the court, he’s a great dude and someone I enjoy being around.”

On why the Knicks’ defense has been ahead of their offense early in the season:

“We have great coaches. [Brendan O’Connor] and [Darren Erman], they do a great job indicating to us what we need to be doing on the court, and then guys are executing defensively and we’re getting stops. That’s always our goal.

“We don’t think about it. Even when you said that, I didn’t think about it. There’s always room for improvement though, so always striving for better.”

On the Knicks finally increasing their pace:

“We finally played fast. We’ve been playing very slow, very stagnant. We finally got out, we ran.”

On the champion Knicks remaining a work in progress:

“It’s early in the season. I think everything’s a work in progress. Last year, I feel like we probably hit our best stride in the playoffs. So we were a work in progress the whole year. That’s the nature of the NBA season. You gotta keep getting better each and every day, each and every game, and be ready to go.”

On the Knicks’ dissatisfaction with their start to the season:

“I just think we’ve got to win, and I think it’s still early in the season, and I don’t think anybody in this locker room is satisfied with where we’re at. Happy to be in the win column tonight, but, you know, to point to 10 things offensively and defensively that we need to improve on. So the good news is there’s no panic there. Some nights right now, it might be the offense ahead of the defense and vice versa. We’ve had a hard time making shots so far early in the season. Tonight a few went in, but then we had some slippage defensively. So, a little give and take, but luckily that’s not the point. The point is for us to continue to get better and we’ll continue to do that.”

On Mike Brown holding the Knicks accountable and not allowing the Nets win to disguise their problems:

“We have to be real with ourselves. And Mike’s great with that, assesses things in film, calls it as it is. Our group’s great with that. We all understand that by no means — we’re not taking this as any potential fool’s gold. The whole goal right now is to continue to get better, and we want to do that. So that’s the thought process.”

On learning to move without the basketball by playing three-on-three without dribbling as a child:

“I remember growing up playing full-court three-on-three with no dribble, so you just learn how to move without the ball. I’m lucky I had that implemented for me at a young age. I wish more kids and hope more kids would do that moving forward in today’s game. I think it really helps you learn how to play and understand how to move and get open. So, it’s kinda always been something I’ve tried to continue to get better at.”

items.title: Tadej Pogačar's race-ridden Colnago and Brandon McNulty's rainbow jersey up for grabs in auction raising funds for US cyclists ahead of LA 2028 Olympics
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
The USA Cycling Foundation's annual auction goes live on Wednesday, with Tadej Pogačar's race-ridden Colnago, signed rainbow jerseys, and and rides with pros amongst the items up for sale to raise money for American cyclists.

Now in its fifth year, the online auction – which is open to anyone around the world – raises money to support US Olympic and Paralympic cyclists, with the upcoming Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028 making fundraising especially important this year. In the US, Olympic athletes do not receive any government funding.

The first items will go live on Wednesday, November 4 with the auction running through to Monday, November 9, and 99 items up for auction in total.

Topping the list in terms of value and intrigue is undoubtedly Tadej Pogačar's world champion edition Colnago V5Rs which he rode to victory at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2025. Donated by Colnago, the bike is valued at $80,000 and will go live on Friday with a starting bid of $25,000.

There's plenty of other pro memorabilia up for grabs, including signed rainbow jerseys from Brandon McNulty and Ashlin Barry, Tejay Van Garderen's white jersey from the 2012 Tour de France, and more from Demi Vollering, Enric Mas and Kate Courtney.

There are a number of money-can't-buy experiences included in the auction, such as rides with Keegan Swenson, Christopher Blevins and Alexey Vermeulen, plus several bikes, kit, helmets, and gift cards, as well as guaranteed entries to many of the biggest US gravel events, and even an entry to the Étape du Tour in 2027.

Supporters can also bid on plenty of non-cycling items, including sports and concert tickets, holidays and hotel stays, and food and drink.

Starting bids start at as little as a dollar with hopes of raising potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars for US cyclists.

"Our athletes are proof of what private support can do," said Molly Pickall, the USA Cycling Foundation's executive director.

"In Paris, American women won every one of Team USA's Olympic cycling medals. LA28 is the first Summer Games on home soil since 1996, and we want to arrive with the strongest team we've ever fielded. This auction gives every fan, anywhere in the country, a way to be part of the Foundation that supports USA Cycling."
